definition: A 401(k) is a workplace retirement savings plan in the United States, named after a section of the tax code, that lets employees save part of their pay with tax advantages, often with contributions added by the employer.
explanation: Employees choose a percentage of their salary to contribute, which is taken directly from their pay. In a traditional 401(k), contributions reduce taxable income now, investments grow tax-deferred and withdrawals are taxed. Many plans also offer a Roth 401(k) option, where contributions are taxed now but qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

Many employers add a matching contribution. For example, an employer might match half of what an employee contributes, up to 6% of salary, which is an immediate boost to savings. Employer contributions may be subject to a vesting schedule.
Employees usually choose from a menu of funds, often including target-date funds as the default. There are annual contribution limits, with extra catch-up contributions allowed for older workers.

Withdrawals before age 59 and a half usually face a penalty plus tax, with some exceptions. When changing jobs, savings can be left in the plan, moved to a new employer's plan or rolled into an IRA. Similar plans exist for public sector and non-profit workers, such as 403(b) and 457 plans.

definition: An abandonment option is a company's ability to stop a project before its planned end, and recover some value by selling assets or cutting losses, if the project performs worse than expected.
explanation: The abandonment option is a type of real option. It limits the downside of an investment, much like an insurance policy, because if things go badly, the company is not forced to keep losing money.

For example, a company opens a new mine. If metal prices fall sharply, it can close the mine and sell its equipment for 400,000, rather than continuing to operate at a loss. The possibility of recovering this value makes the project less risky and more valuable than a traditional analysis assuming the company must operate for the full term.

The value of an abandonment option depends on how much can be recovered and how uncertain the project's outcomes are. Projects using general-purpose assets, such as buildings or vehicles that can easily be sold, usually have more valuable abandonment options than those using highly specialized equipment.
Ignoring abandonment options can lead companies to undervalue risky projects. Recognising them encourages designing projects with flexibility built in.

definition: Absolute advantage is the ability of a country, business or person to produce more of a good or service than others using the same amount of resources.
explanation: The idea was described by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. If one country can produce something more efficiently than another, it has an absolute advantage in that product.

For example, if Country A can produce 20 tonnes of wheat per worker and Country B only 10, Country A has an absolute advantage in wheat. If Country B can produce more cloth per worker than Country A, each has an absolute advantage in one product, and both can benefit by specializing and trading.

Absolute advantage is different from comparative advantage. A country may have an absolute advantage in producing everything, yet trade can still benefit both countries if each specializes in goods where its relative efficiency, or opportunity cost, is lowest. This insight, developed by David Ricardo, shows that trade can be beneficial even when one country is better at producing everything.
Comparative advantage is generally considered the more important concept for understanding patterns of trade.

definition: Absorption costing is a method of calculating product costs that includes all manufacturing costs, both variable and fixed, in the cost of each unit produced.
explanation: Under absorption costing, each unit carries a share of fixed production overheads, such as factory rent and supervisors' salaries, as well as direct materials, direct labour and variable overheads. It is also called full costing.

For example, a factory makes 1,000 units with variable costs of 10 per unit and fixed overheads of 5,000. Each unit absorbs 5 of fixed overhead, giving a full cost of 15 per unit. If 800 units are sold, 200 remain in inventory at 15 each, or 3,000.
Absorption costing is required for external financial reporting under IFRS and US GAAP, because inventory must include all production costs.

A key feature is that profit can rise simply by producing more than is sold, because some fixed overhead is carried forward in inventory rather than expensed. In the example, profit is 1,000 higher than under variable costing, because 1,000 of fixed overhead sits in closing inventory. This can encourage overproduction, which is one reason managers also use variable costing internally.

definition: Accelerated depreciation is a method of depreciation that charges more of an asset's cost in the early years of its life and less in later years, compared with spreading the cost evenly.
explanation: Many assets lose value fastest when new and become less productive as they age. Accelerated methods reflect this by front-loading depreciation.

A common example is the declining balance method. Under the double-declining balance version, an asset with a five-year life is depreciated at twice the straight-line rate, or 40% a year, applied to its remaining book value. For a machine costing 50,000, the first year's depreciation is 20,000. The second year's is 40% of the remaining 30,000, or 12,000. Straight-line depreciation, by contrast, would charge 10,000 every year if the machine had no residual value.
The total depreciation over the asset's life is the same under both methods; only the timing differs.

Accelerated depreciation is especially common for tax purposes. Many tax systems allow faster write-offs to encourage investment, because higher early deductions reduce taxable profit sooner. When a company uses accelerated depreciation for tax but straight-line in its financial statements, the difference creates a deferred tax liability, which reverses in later years.

definition: Accounting is the process of recording, organising and reporting a business's financial transactions so that owners, managers, investors, lenders and governments can understand its financial position and performance.
explanation: Every business makes sales, pays bills, buys equipment and borrows money. Accounting captures each of these events, sorts them into categories and summarises them in reports, mainly the financial statements.

Accounting has several branches. Financial accounting produces reports for people outside the business, such as investors, lenders and tax authorities, and follows standard rules so that companies can be compared. Management accounting produces internal information for managers, such as product costs, budgets and forecasts. Tax accounting focuses on calculating what is owed to tax authorities.

Accounting is often called the language of business, because it gives everyone a common way to describe results. When a company reports revenue of 10 million and profit of 1.2 million, those figures mean something specific because they are prepared under agreed rules.

Good accounting builds trust. Banks need reliable figures before lending, investors need them before buying shares and managers need them to make sound decisions. That is why many companies have their accounts independently checked by auditors.

definition: The accounting equation states that a business's assets equal its liabilities plus its equity. Everything a business owns is financed either by borrowing or by its owners.
explanation: The equation is written as Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Assets are what the business owns or controls, such as cash, stock and equipment. Liabilities are what it owes, such as loans and unpaid supplier bills. Equity is what is left for the owners after liabilities are subtracted.

Suppose a small company has assets of 250,000 and liabilities of 90,000. Its equity must be 160,000. If the company then borrows 20,000 from a bank, its cash rises by 20,000, so assets become 270,000, and its loan rises by 20,000, so liabilities become 110,000. Equity stays at 160,000, and the equation still balances.

Every transaction keeps the two sides equal. Buying equipment with cash swaps one asset for another. Earning a profit increases assets and equity together. Paying a supplier reduces both cash and liabilities.

This is why the balance sheet always balances and why double-entry bookkeeping records every transaction in at least two places. The equation also makes an important point clear: borrowing to buy assets does not, by itself, make the owners any richer.

definition: An accounting estimate is an approximation of an amount in the financial statements that cannot be measured precisely and depends on judgment about future events, such as bad debts, warranty costs or an asset's useful life.
explanation: Many figures in financial statements involve uncertainty. Managers must estimate how many customers will fail to pay, how long equipment will last, how much a legal claim will cost, what an asset could be sold for or how much inventory is worth.
For example, a company estimates that 3% of its 2 million of receivables will not be collected and records an allowance for doubtful accounts of 60,000. That figure is an accounting estimate.

Estimates are based on past experience, current information and reasonable expectations about the future. They are reviewed at each reporting date. When new information shows an estimate needs changing, the change is applied from that point forwards, affecting the current and future periods, rather than restating earlier years.
This differs from a change in accounting policy, which is a change in the method used and is usually applied to earlier periods too.

Because estimates involve judgment, they create room for error and, potentially, manipulation. Auditors pay close attention to significant estimates, and companies disclose the key assumptions behind them in their notes.

definition: Accounting fraud is the deliberate manipulation of a company's financial statements to mislead investors, lenders, regulators or others about its financial performance or position.
explanation: Accounting fraud can take many forms. Common methods include recording fake revenue or recognising revenue too early, hiding liabilities off the balance sheet, overstating assets such as inventory or receivables, understating expenses by capitalizing them, manipulating estimates and reserves, and concealing related-party transactions.
Motives often include meeting earnings targets, supporting the share price, earning bonuses, meeting loan conditions or hiding losses.

Major corporate failures, such as Enron and WorldCom in the early 2000s and Wirecard in 2020, involved accounting fraud. At WorldCom, billions of dollars of ordinary operating expenses were wrongly recorded as capital assets, inflating profits.

Accounting fraud often leads to criminal charges, large fines, restatements, bankruptcy and heavy losses for investors and employees. Safeguards include internal controls, independent audit committees, external audits, whistleblower protections and regulations such as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act in the United States. Warning signs include profits growing much faster than cash flow, frequent changes in accounting policies and unusual transactions near period-ends.

definition: An accounting policy is a specific principle, rule or practice a company chooses and applies in preparing its financial statements, such as how it values inventory or recognises revenue.
explanation: Accounting standards often allow some choice or require judgment in how they are applied. A company's accounting policies set out the approach it has chosen.

Examples include which inventory costing method to use, such as FIFO or weighted average; how to depreciate property, plant and equipment; when to recognise revenue from long-term contracts; whether to measure investment property at cost or fair value, where permitted; and how to treat development costs.

For example, one company might depreciate its equipment over ten years using the straight-line method, while a competitor uses eight years. Their profits could differ partly because of these policy choices.
Companies must describe their significant accounting policies in the notes to their financial statements, so readers can understand and compare their results.

Accounting policies should be applied consistently from year to year. A company may change a policy only if a new standard requires it or if the change gives more reliable and relevant information. When it does, it usually applies the new policy to earlier periods as well, restating comparative figures so trends remain meaningful.

definition: Accounts payable is the money a business owes to its suppliers for goods or services it has received but not yet paid for.
explanation: Businesses often buy on credit, receiving goods now and paying later under agreed terms, such as within 30 days. Until the bill is paid, the amount is recorded as accounts payable, a current liability on the balance sheet.

For example, a restaurant receives a delivery of food worth 4,000 with 30 days to pay. It records the cost and 4,000 of accounts payable. When it pays the supplier, cash falls and the payable is cleared.

Accounts payable is a normal and useful form of short-term financing. Paying suppliers on agreed terms, rather than immediately, lets a business keep cash for longer. However, paying late can damage supplier relationships, lead to penalties or cause suppliers to stop delivering.

Managing payables is part of managing working capital. Analysts compare payables with purchases or cost of sales to see how long a company takes to pay its bills. A sudden rise in this time can sometimes signal cash flow problems.
note: Trade payables is another name for accounts payable, used especially under IFRS. It refers to amounts owed to suppliers for normal purchases.

definition: Accounts receivable is the money customers owe a business for goods or services they have received but not yet paid for.
explanation: Many businesses sell on credit, allowing customers to pay within an agreed period, such as 30 or 60 days. Until payment arrives, the amount owed is recorded as accounts receivable, a current asset on the balance sheet.

For example, if a supplier delivers goods worth 15,000 to a retailer on 30-day terms, the supplier records 15,000 of revenue and 15,000 of accounts receivable. When the retailer pays, the receivable is replaced by cash.

Receivables are valuable, but they are not cash. If customers pay slowly or not at all, a business can run short of money even while reporting healthy sales. Businesses therefore track how long customers take to pay and chase overdue accounts.

Because some customers will never pay, companies estimate likely losses and record an allowance for doubtful accounts, which reduces the reported value of receivables to the amount expected to be collected.
note: Trade receivables is another name for accounts receivable, used especially under IFRS. It refers to amounts owed by customers for normal sales.

definition: An accredited investor is a person or organisation that meets financial or professional criteria set by regulators, allowing them to invest in certain private offerings not available to the general public. The term is used mainly in the United States.
explanation: Private investments, such as hedge funds, private equity funds, venture capital funds and private company shares, are often exempt from the detailed registration and disclosure requirements of public offerings. To protect less experienced investors, regulators limit who can invest in many of them.

In the United States, individuals generally qualify based on high income or net worth thresholds set by the Securities and Exchange Commission, or by holding certain professional licences. Institutions such as banks, insurers, large companies and certain trusts also qualify.
For example, a start-up raising money privately might accept investments only from accredited investors, allowing it to avoid the costs of a public offering.

The idea is that accredited investors can bear the risk of loss and evaluate investments without the full protection of public disclosure. Critics argue that wealth is a poor proxy for financial knowledge. Other countries use similar concepts, such as sophisticated or high-net-worth investors in the United Kingdom and professional investors in the European Union.

definition: Accretion/dilution analysis shows whether an acquisition is expected to increase or decrease the acquiring company's earnings per share.
explanation: A deal is accretive if the combined company's earnings per share are higher than the acquirer's standalone earnings per share, and dilutive if they are lower.

The result depends on the price paid, how the deal is financed and the target's earnings. Paying with cash or debt adds interest costs or lost interest income. Paying with shares increases the share count.

For example, an acquirer earns 100,000,000 with 50,000,000 shares, giving earnings per share of 2.00. It buys a target earning 30,000,000 by issuing 14,000,000 new shares. Combined earnings are 130,000,000 over 64,000,000 shares, or about 2.03, making the deal about 1.6% accretive, before synergies and other adjustments.

Accretion and dilution are closely watched by boards and investors, but they are not a full measure of value. An accretive deal can still destroy value if the acquirer overpays relative to the target's risk and growth, and a dilutive deal can create value in the long run. Analysis should be combined with valuation and strategic assessment.

definition: Accrual accounting records income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash actually changes hands.
explanation: Under accrual accounting, the timing of cash does not decide when something is recorded. A sale is recorded when the goods are delivered or the service is performed, even if the customer pays later. An expense is recorded when the business uses the service or receives the goods, even if the bill is paid next month.

Suppose a consultant completes a 5,000 project in December but is paid in January. Under accrual accounting, the 5,000 is revenue for December, because that is when it was earned. The money owed is recorded as accounts receivable until it arrives.
This approach gives a truer picture of a business's performance in each period, because income is matched with the costs of earning it. It is required for most companies under GAAP and IFRS.

The downside is that profit and cash can differ significantly. A fast-growing business might report strong profits while running short of cash, because customers have not yet paid. That is why financial statements include a cash flow statement alongside the income statement.

definition: Accrual quality is the extent to which a company's accrual-based accounting profits are reliably backed by cash flows, rather than by estimates and adjustments that may later prove wrong.
explanation: Accrual accounting records revenue and expenses when they are earned or incurred, not when cash moves. This requires estimates, such as how much customers will pay, how long assets will last and what future costs will arise. High accrual quality means these estimates turn into cash as expected.

Analysts assess accrual quality by comparing profits with operating cash flow over time, looking at changes in working capital items such as receivables and inventory, and checking how often estimates are revised.

For example, if a company reports rising profits but its operating cash flow stays flat while receivables grow rapidly, its profits rely heavily on accruals. Customers may be slow to pay, or revenue may be recognised aggressively. This suggests lower accrual quality.

Research has found that companies with large accruals relative to their assets have, on average, tended to see weaker future earnings and share returns, although this is not true in every case. Accrual quality is a key part of assessing the overall quality of earnings.

definition: An accrued expense is a cost a business has already incurred but has not yet paid or been billed for by the end of the reporting period.
explanation: Under accrual accounting, expenses belong in the period when they are incurred, not when they are paid. If a cost has been incurred but the bill has not arrived or been paid, it is recorded as an accrued expense, with a matching liability on the balance sheet.

Common examples include wages earned by staff in the last days of a month but paid in the next month, interest on a loan that has built up since the last payment, and utilities used during the month but billed later.

Suppose employees earn 3,000 of wages between 26 and 31 December, to be paid on 5 January. At year-end, the company records 3,000 of wage expense for December and 3,000 of accrued wages as a current liability. When the wages are paid in January, the liability is cleared.
Without accrued expenses, a period's costs would be understated and its profit overstated. Accrued expenses are usually recorded through adjusting entries at the end of each period.

definition: Accrued revenue is income a business has earned by delivering goods or services but has not yet billed or received by the end of the reporting period.
explanation: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when it is earned. If work has been done but the invoice has not yet been sent, the revenue still belongs in the current period. It is recorded as accrued revenue, with a matching asset on the balance sheet.

For example, a consulting firm works on a project throughout December but bills the client in January. If 8,000 worth of work was completed in December, the firm records 8,000 of revenue in December and an 8,000 accrued revenue asset. When the invoice is issued in January, the asset is moved to accounts receivable, and when the client pays, it becomes cash.
Interest earned on savings or loans but not yet received is another common example.

Accrued revenue makes sure income is shown in the period when the work was done, giving a more accurate picture of performance. Because it is based on estimates of work completed, auditors often check it carefully to make sure revenue is not being recorded too early.

definition: Accumulated depreciation is the total depreciation charged on an asset since it was bought. It is subtracted from the asset's original cost to show its current book value.
explanation: Each year, depreciation is recorded as an expense on the income statement. On the balance sheet, rather than reducing the asset's recorded cost directly, these charges are added up in a separate account called accumulated depreciation.

The asset's net book value is its original cost minus accumulated depreciation. Suppose a delivery van cost 40,000 and is depreciated at 8,000 a year. After three years, accumulated depreciation is 24,000, and the van's net book value is 16,000.

Keeping cost and accumulated depreciation separate shows readers both what the business originally paid and how much of that value has been used up. A company whose accumulated depreciation is very high relative to cost has old assets that may need replacing soon.

Net book value is an accounting figure, not a market price. The van might actually sell for more or less than 16,000. When an asset is sold or scrapped, both its cost and its accumulated depreciation are removed from the books, and any difference between the sale price and book value is recorded as a gain or loss.

definition: In card payments, an acquirer is the bank or financial institution that enables a merchant to accept card payments, processing transactions on the merchant's behalf and depositing the funds into its account.
explanation: The card payment system has two sides. The issuer is the bank that gives the card to the customer. The acquirer, also called the acquiring bank or merchant acquirer, works with the merchant.

The acquirer signs up merchants, provides or arranges card terminals and online payment services, submits transactions to the card networks for authorisation and settlement, and credits merchants with the money from card sales, minus fees. It also bears some risk, for example if a merchant goes out of business and owes refunds to customers.

For example, a clothing shop opens a merchant account with an acquiring bank. Each time a customer pays by card, the acquirer processes the payment and later pays the shop, deducting fees that include the interchange fee paid to the card issuer.

Many modern payment companies act as acquirers or partner with them to offer simple card acceptance to small businesses. The word acquirer also has a different meaning in mergers and acquisitions, where it refers to a company that buys another company.

definition: An acquisition is a transaction in which one company buys a controlling stake in, or all of, another company or its assets.
explanation: In an acquisition, the buyer, often called the acquirer, takes control of the target company. The target may continue to operate as a separate business owned by the acquirer, or it may be fully integrated into the acquirer's operations.

Acquisitions can be paid for in cash, with the acquirer's own shares, or a combination of both. They can be friendly, when the target's board supports the deal, or hostile, when the acquirer makes an offer directly to shareholders against the board's wishes.
For example, a large technology company might acquire a small start-up for its software and engineering team, paying cash to the start-up's shareholders.

Acquirers often pay a premium above the target's current market value to persuade shareholders to sell. They justify this by expecting synergies, such as cost savings or increased revenue, from combining the businesses.

Acquisitions carry significant risks. The acquirer may overpay, synergies may prove smaller than expected, integration may be difficult, and key staff or customers may leave. For this reason, careful due diligence and integration planning are essential parts of the acquisition process.

definition: Active investing is an investment strategy in which a manager or investor selects investments and adjusts holdings in an attempt to outperform a benchmark index.
explanation: Active investors believe that, through research, analysis and judgment, they can identify investments likely to perform better than the market, or avoid those likely to perform worse. They may pick individual shares, adjust their mix of asset types or time their entry and exit from markets.

Active managers use a wide range of approaches, including fundamental analysis, technical analysis, quantitative models and macroeconomic forecasting. Styles include value, growth, momentum and income investing.
For example, an active fund manager might hold 50 carefully selected companies rather than all 500 in an index, aiming to beat the index by choosing companies they believe are undervalued.

Active investing offers the potential for higher returns and the flexibility to avoid overvalued areas or reduce risk during downturns. But it usually costs more, through higher management fees and trading costs, and many studies show that most active funds fail to outperform their benchmarks consistently over long periods after fees.

Active management may be more successful in less efficient markets, such as smaller companies or emerging markets, where information is less widely analysed. Many investors combine active and passive approaches.

definition: Active share is a measure of how much a fund's holdings differ from its benchmark index, expressed as a percentage from 0%, identical to the index, to 100%, no overlap at all.
explanation: Active share was introduced by researchers Martijn Cremers and Antti Petajisto in 2009. It is calculated by adding up the absolute differences between the weight of each holding in the fund and in the benchmark, and dividing the total by two.

For example, a fund that holds the same shares as its index in the same proportions has an active share of 0%. A fund that holds 30 shares chosen from a 500-share index, in very different weights, might have an active share of 85% or more.

Active share helps investors see whether an actively managed fund is genuinely different from its benchmark. A fund charging active fees but with low active share may be a closet indexer, closely tracking the index while charging more.

High active share is not a guarantee of good performance; it only shows that the fund differs from the index, which can lead to better or worse results. It is often used alongside tracking error, which measures how much the fund's returns differ from the benchmark's.

definition: Activity-based costing (ABC) is a method of assigning overhead costs to products or services based on the activities they actually use, such as machine setups, inspections or orders processed, rather than a single broad measure such as labour hours.
explanation: Traditional costing often spreads overheads across products using one allocation base, such as direct labour hours. This can distort costs when products use overhead resources very differently.

ABC first identifies the main activities that create overhead costs, groups the costs by activity, and then assigns them to products based on cost drivers, the measures of how much of each activity a product uses.

For example, machine setups cost 50,000 a year and there are 100 setups, so each setup costs 500. A specialist product needing 10 setups is assigned 5,000 of setup cost, even if it uses few labour hours. Under traditional costing, high-volume products would have absorbed much of this cost instead.

ABC often reveals that low-volume, complex products are more expensive to make than traditional methods suggest, while high-volume simple products are cheaper. This helps with pricing and product decisions. The drawback is that ABC requires more data and effort to set up and maintain.

definition: An actuary is a professional who uses mathematics, statistics and financial theory to measure and manage risk and uncertainty, especially in insurance, pensions and investments.
explanation: Actuaries estimate the probability and financial impact of future events, such as deaths, illnesses, accidents, natural disasters and investment returns. Their work helps organisations price products, set aside enough money to meet future obligations and manage risk.

In insurance, actuaries calculate premiums, estimate claim reserves and assess capital needs. In pensions, they estimate how much employers need to contribute to meet future pension promises, using assumptions about life expectancy, salaries, inflation and investment returns. They also work in banking, healthcare, government and consulting.

For example, a life insurance actuary uses mortality tables showing the probability of death at each age to set premiums for term life policies, ensuring the insurer can pay future claims and cover its costs.

Becoming a qualified actuary usually requires passing a demanding series of professional exams over several years, set by professional bodies such as the Society of Actuaries in the United States and the Institute and Faculty of Actuaries in the United Kingdom. Actuaries often have legal responsibilities, such as signing off on reserves.

definition: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) is a home loan, common in the United States, whose interest rate is fixed for an initial period and then changes at regular intervals in line with a benchmark interest rate.
explanation: An ARM typically starts with a fixed rate for a set number of years, after which the rate resets periodically, commonly every six months or once a year, based on a benchmark rate plus a fixed margin. ARMs are often described by two numbers, such as a 5/6 ARM, which has a fixed rate for five years and then adjusts every six months, or a 5/1 ARM, which adjusts every year.
Most US ARMs include caps that limit how much the rate can rise at each adjustment and over the life of the loan, protecting borrowers from extreme increases.

For example, a borrower might take a 5/1 ARM at 5%. After five years, if the benchmark has risen, the rate could reset to 7%, increasing monthly payments significantly. If rates have fallen, payments could go down.

ARMs often start with a lower rate than fixed-rate mortgages, which can make them attractive to buyers who plan to move or refinance before the rate adjusts. The risk is that rates may rise more than expected. Similar products elsewhere are called variable-rate mortgages, and in the United Kingdom include tracker mortgages, which follow the central bank rate, and standard variable rate mortgages, set by the lender.

definition: Adjusted EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, further adjusted to exclude items that management considers unusual, non-recurring or non-cash, such as restructuring costs and share-based compensation.
explanation: Companies report adjusted EBITDA to show what they consider their underlying operating performance. Common adjustments include restructuring and severance costs, acquisition-related expenses, share-based compensation, impairments and gains or losses on asset sales.
For example, a company with EBITDA of 20,000,000 might add back 2,000,000 of restructuring costs and 3,000,000 of share-based compensation, reporting adjusted EBITDA of 25,000,000.
Adjusted EBITDA is widely used in loan agreements, valuations and private equity deals, often as the basis for leverage limits and acquisition prices.

It is not defined by accounting standards, so each company decides what to adjust. This flexibility can make results look better than they are. Costs labelled as one-time sometimes recur every year, and share-based pay is a real cost to shareholders. Regulators require listed companies to reconcile adjusted measures to standard figures. Investors should review each adjustment carefully.

definition: Adjusted gross income (AGI) is a measure of income used in the United States federal tax system: a person's total gross income minus certain specific deductions, called adjustments.
explanation: AGI is a key figure on a US federal tax return. It starts with all taxable income, such as wages, interest, dividends, business profits and capital gains, and then subtracts a defined list of adjustments, such as certain retirement contributions, student loan interest and contributions to health savings accounts.
For example, someone with gross income of 80,000 who makes 6,000 of deductible retirement contributions and has 2,000 of other qualifying adjustments has an AGI of 72,000.

AGI matters because many other tax rules depend on it. It is the starting point for calculating taxable income, after the standard or itemized deductions are subtracted. Eligibility for many credits and deductions, and the ability to contribute to some retirement accounts, shrink or disappear as AGI rises.
Other countries use different terms for similar ideas, such as total income or net income before allowances. The details of what counts as an adjustment are specific to US law and change over time.

definition: An adjusting entry is a journal entry made at the end of an accounting period to update account balances so that revenue and expenses are recorded in the correct period.
explanation: Some financial events happen gradually or are not captured by everyday transactions. Adjusting entries bring the books up to date before the financial statements are prepared.

Common examples include accrued expenses, such as wages earned by staff in the last days of the month but not yet paid. Accrued revenue covers work done but not yet billed. Prepaid expenses, such as insurance paid in advance, need adjusting as each month's cover is used up. Depreciation spreads the cost of equipment across the years it is used.

Suppose a company pays 12,000 for a year of insurance on 1 January. At the end of January, an adjusting entry moves 1,000 from prepaid insurance, an asset, to insurance expense, because one month of cover has been used.

Adjusting entries are required under accrual accounting. Without them, profit in one month could be overstated and in another understated, simply because of when bills were paid. They usually do not involve cash; they move amounts between accounts so each period reflects what really happened.

definition: An adverse opinion is an audit opinion stating that a company's financial statements are not fairly presented, because misstatements are both material and pervasive.
explanation: An adverse opinion is the most severe judgment an auditor can give on financial statements. It means the errors or departures from accounting standards are so significant and widespread that the statements as a whole are misleading.
This differs from a qualified opinion, where a problem is material but limited to a specific area. An adverse opinion indicates that users cannot rely on the financial statements.

For example, an auditor might issue an adverse opinion if a company refuses to consolidate several significant subsidiaries that it controls, so that the group accounts leave out large parts of the business.

Adverse opinions are rare, because companies usually correct problems when auditors raise them, rather than receive such an opinion. For listed companies, an adverse opinion can lead to serious consequences, including action by stock exchanges or regulators, breaches of loan agreements and loss of investor confidence. The auditor's report explains the reasons in a section describing the basis for the adverse opinion.

definition: Adverse selection is a situation in which one party in a transaction has more information than the other, leading to a higher likelihood of attracting the wrong type of participant, such as high-risk customers in insurance or poor-quality goods in a market.
explanation: Adverse selection arises from information asymmetry, when buyers and sellers do not have equal knowledge. It happens before a transaction takes place, unlike moral hazard, which concerns behaviour after an agreement is made.

In health insurance, people who know they are likely to need medical care are more eager to buy insurance than those who expect to stay healthy. If the insurer cannot tell them apart and charges everyone the same price, it will attract more high-risk customers, so claims rise, premiums must increase, and healthy people drop out, worsening the problem.

A famous example is the used car market described by economist George Akerlof. Sellers know whether their car is reliable, but buyers do not. Fearing they might buy a poor-quality car, buyers offer lower prices, which drives sellers of good cars out of the market.

Ways to reduce adverse selection include medical questionnaires and underwriting, warranties, independent inspections, credit checks, and in some cases requiring everyone to participate, as in compulsory insurance schemes.

definition: The after-tax cost of debt is the interest rate a company pays on its borrowing after taking into account the tax savings from deducting interest from taxable profit.
explanation: In many countries, companies can deduct interest payments when calculating taxable profit. This means part of the interest cost is effectively paid by lower taxes. The after-tax cost of debt reflects this saving.

It is calculated by multiplying the pre-tax cost of debt by one minus the tax rate. If a company pays 6% interest and its tax rate is 25%, the after-tax cost of debt is 6% multiplied by 0.75, which is 4.5%.

To see why, imagine the company pays 60,000 of interest on a 1 million loan. Deducting that interest reduces taxable profit by 60,000, saving 15,000 of tax at a 25% rate. The true cost to the company is 45,000, or 4.5% of the loan.

The after-tax cost of debt is used in the weighted average cost of capital. The tax benefit only applies if the company is profitable enough to pay tax and if local rules allow the deduction; some countries limit how much interest can be deducted. This tax advantage is one reason companies use debt in their capital structure.

definition: After-tax return is the return an investor actually keeps from an investment after paying any taxes on the income and gains it produced.
explanation: Taxes can significantly reduce investment returns, so the return that matters most to an investor is often the after-tax figure.

For example, an investment earning 8% in a year, where all of that return is taxed at 25%, gives an after-tax return of 6%. Over many years, this difference compounds into a large gap in final wealth.

The impact of tax depends on the type of return and the investor's situation. Interest, dividends and capital gains may be taxed at different rates. Gains may be taxed only when an investment is sold, allowing tax to be deferred. Investments held in tax-advantaged accounts, such as certain retirement or savings accounts, may grow partly or fully free of tax.

Comparing after-tax returns can change which investment looks best. A tax-exempt bond yielding 3% may give a higher after-tax return than a taxable bond yielding 4% for an investor in a high tax bracket.

Because tax rules and rates differ between countries and individuals, after-tax returns are personal. Fund performance figures are usually reported before tax, so investors need to consider their own tax position.

definition: Agency cost is the cost that arises from conflicts of interest between people who own a business, or have a stake in it, and the people who manage it on their behalf.
explanation: In a company, shareholders are the principals and managers are their agents. Managers may sometimes act in their own interest rather than the shareholders', for example by pursuing expensive acquisitions to build a larger empire, taking excessive perks or avoiding risky but valuable projects to protect their jobs.

Agency costs include the loss of value from such decisions, and the costs of trying to prevent them, such as audits, board oversight, monitoring and performance-related pay. They also include bonding costs, such as managers accepting contracts that tie their pay to performance.

Conflicts can also arise between shareholders and lenders. For example, shareholders of a struggling company may prefer very risky projects, since they gain if the gamble succeeds while lenders bear much of the loss if it fails.

Agency costs were formalised in a well-known 1976 paper by Michael Jensen and William Meckling. Ways to reduce them include linking executive pay to long-term performance, independent boards, active shareholders, loan covenants and, some argue, debt itself, which limits the free cash available to managers.

definition: Aggregate demand is the total demand for all goods and services in an economy at a given overall price level, over a period of time.
explanation: Aggregate demand combines the spending of four groups: households on consumption, businesses on investment, government on goods and services, and foreigners on a country's exports, minus the country's spending on imports.

Changes in aggregate demand drive short-term fluctuations in economic activity. When aggregate demand rises, businesses sell more, increase production and hire more workers. When it falls, output and employment decline.

Many factors influence aggregate demand, including interest rates, consumer and business confidence, household wealth, government spending and taxes, exchange rates and economic conditions abroad. For example, a cut in interest rates makes borrowing cheaper, encouraging households to buy homes and cars and businesses to invest, which increases aggregate demand.

Governments and central banks manage aggregate demand through fiscal and monetary policy. If demand is too weak, unemployment rises; if it is too strong relative to what the economy can produce, inflation tends to rise. The balance between aggregate demand and aggregate supply determines overall output and the price level.

definition: Aggregate supply is the total amount of goods and services that all businesses in an economy are willing and able to produce at a given overall price level, over a period of time.
explanation: Aggregate supply reflects the economy's productive capacity. In the long run, it depends on the quantity and quality of the factors of production: the number of workers and their skills, the stock of capital such as machinery and buildings, natural resources and the technology used to combine them.

In the short run, businesses can increase output somewhat by using existing resources more intensively, for example through overtime. But in the long run, sustained increases in output require growth in productive capacity.

Aggregate supply can be affected by shocks. For example, a sharp rise in oil prices increases production costs across the economy, reducing aggregate supply. This tends to push prices up and output down at the same time, a combination that can lead to stagflation.

Policies aimed at increasing aggregate supply over time are often called supply-side policies. They include investing in education and training, improving infrastructure, encouraging innovation and reducing barriers to business activity.

definition: Algorithmic trading is the use of computer programs to place trades automatically according to pre-set rules, based on factors such as price, timing, volume or mathematical models.
explanation: Algorithms can analyse markets and execute trades far faster and more consistently than humans. They are now responsible for a large share of trading in many major markets.

Algorithmic trading has many uses. Institutional investors use execution algorithms to split large orders into smaller ones over time, reducing their impact on prices. Market makers use algorithms to quote buy and sell prices continuously. Quantitative funds use them to follow trading strategies based on statistical patterns. High-frequency trading, a subset, aims to profit from very small price differences over fractions of a second.
For example, a pension fund wanting to buy 2,000,000 shares might use an algorithm that buys in small amounts throughout the day, matching the market's average price.

Algorithmic trading has improved liquidity and lowered trading costs, but it raises concerns. Programming errors or interactions between algorithms can cause sudden price swings, as in the US flash crash of May 2010. Regulators require firms to test algorithms, apply risk controls and keep records.

definition: An allowance for doubtful accounts is an estimate of how much of a business's accounts receivable will not be collected. It reduces the receivables shown on the balance sheet to the amount the business realistically expects to receive.
explanation: Customers owe the business money, but not all of it will arrive. Rather than waiting until a specific customer fails to pay, the business estimates the likely loss in advance and records it as an allowance, sometimes called a provision.

The allowance sits on the balance sheet as a deduction from accounts receivable. If receivables are 150,000 and the allowance is 7,500, the net amount shown is 142,500, which is the amount the business expects to collect.

Estimates are usually based on past experience and on how overdue each debt is. Older debts are less likely to be paid, so a business might apply a small percentage to invoices under 30 days old and a much larger percentage to those more than 90 days overdue.

When a particular debt is finally confirmed as uncollectable, it is written off against the allowance. This approach follows the matching principle, because the expected loss is recorded in the same period as the sales that caused it.

definition: Alpha is the return an investment earns above or below what would be expected given the risk it took, often measured against a benchmark index.
explanation: Alpha is used to measure the value a fund manager adds. If a fund simply follows the market, its returns will rise and fall with the market. Alpha captures the extra return, positive or negative, beyond what the market exposure alone would explain.

In a simple version, alpha is the fund's return minus the benchmark's return. In a more refined version, the expected return is calculated using the fund's beta through the Capital Asset Pricing Model, and alpha is the difference between the actual and expected return.

For example, a fund with a beta of 1.0 earns 12% in a year when its expected return, based on market performance and its risk, is 9%. Its alpha is 3 percentage points. If it had earned 7%, its alpha would be −2 percentage points.
Positive alpha suggests the manager added value through skill, such as selecting securities or timing decisions. Negative alpha suggests the manager underperformed, possibly after fees.

Research shows that consistently generating positive alpha after fees is difficult, and many active funds fail to do so over long periods, which is one reason for the growth of low-cost index investing.

definition: Alternative data is information used by investors and analysts that comes from sources other than traditional financial data, such as company reports, market prices and economic statistics.
explanation: Investors seek an edge by finding information others do not have or have not yet analysed. Alternative data can provide early or unique insights into company performance, consumer behaviour and economic activity.

Examples include credit and debit card transaction data, satellite images of car parks, shipping routes or crop fields, mobile phone location data, web traffic and app downloads, online reviews, social media sentiment, job postings and product prices scraped from websites.

For example, an investment firm might analyse anonymised card transaction data to estimate a retailer's quarterly sales before the company reports them, or use satellite images of oil storage tanks to estimate global oil inventories.

Alternative data has become widely used by hedge funds and asset managers, but it raises challenges. Data can be expensive, messy and hard to interpret. There are legal and ethical concerns about privacy, consent and whether some data could count as inside information. As more investors use the same data, its advantage tends to diminish.

definition: An American option is an option that can be exercised at any time up to and including its expiration date.
explanation: Like European options, the name refers to the exercise style, not location. American options are traded in many countries.
The extra flexibility of early exercise means an American option is worth at least as much as an otherwise identical European option, and sometimes more.

In practice, it rarely makes sense to exercise an American call option on a share that pays no dividends before expiry, because selling the option usually gives more money than exercising it, as the option still has time value. Early exercise can make sense in some cases, such as exercising a call just before a large dividend is paid or exercising a deep in-the-money put.

For example, a holder of an American put option with a strike of 50 on a share that has fallen to 20 might exercise early to receive 50 per share immediately and invest the money, rather than waiting for expiry.

Most options on individual shares traded on exchanges are American style. Because of the early exercise feature, they are more complex to value than European options, usually requiring numerical methods.

definition: Amortization is the gradual repayment of a loan through regular payments that cover both interest and part of the principal, so that the loan is fully repaid by the end of its term.
explanation: In an amortising loan, every payment is the same size, but what it pays for changes over time. Early payments are mostly interest, because interest is charged on a large balance. As the balance shrinks, less of each payment goes to interest and more goes to reducing the principal.

Take a 200,000 mortgage at 6% over 25 years. The monthly payment is about 1,289. In the first month, interest is 1,000, because 6% a year is 0.5% a month on 200,000, so only about 289 reduces the balance. Near the end of the loan, almost the entire payment goes to principal.

A table showing each payment split into interest and principal, along with the remaining balance, is called an amortization schedule. It is useful for seeing how much of the debt has really been repaid at any point.
This pattern explains why extra payments early in a loan are so effective. Money paid towards principal early reduces the balance on which all future interest is charged.
The same word is also used in accounting for spreading the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life. That meaning is covered under Amortization Expense.

definition: Amortization expense is the portion of an intangible asset's cost, such as a patent, software licence or customer contract, that is charged to the income statement in a period as the asset is used up.
explanation: Amortization works like depreciation, but for intangible assets, which have no physical form. When a company buys an intangible asset with a limited useful life, it spreads the cost over that life rather than recording it all at once.
For example, a company buys a patent for 300,000 that has ten years of legal protection remaining. Using the straight-line method, it records amortization expense of 30,000 a year for ten years.

Not all intangible assets are amortised. Goodwill and some brand names with no foreseeable end to their useful life are not amortised under IFRS and US GAAP for public companies. Instead, they are tested regularly for impairment, a reduction in value.

Like depreciation, amortization is a non-cash expense, so it is added back when calculating operating cash flow. It is also one of the items removed when calculating EBITDA. The word amortization is also used for repaying a loan in regular instalments, which is a separate meaning covered under Foundations & Personal Finance.

definition: An amortization schedule is a table showing every payment on a loan, how much of each payment goes to interest and how much to principal, and the balance remaining after each payment.
explanation: With most loans, every monthly payment is the same size, but what it pays for changes over time. An amortization schedule makes this visible, line by line.

Take a loan of 10,000 at 6% a year, repaid monthly over one year. The payment is about 860.66 a month. In the first month, interest is 50, because 0.5% of 10,000 is 50, so about 810.66 reduces the principal and the balance falls to about 9,189.34. In the second month, interest is charged on that smaller balance, so slightly less goes to interest and slightly more to principal. By the final payment, almost all of it repays principal.
On long loans, such as 25-year mortgages, the pattern is striking: early payments are mostly interest, and the balance falls slowly at first.

Reading an amortization schedule helps borrowers see how much they still owe at any point, how much interest they will pay in total and how much an extra payment would save. Lenders usually provide one, and spreadsheets can create one easily.

definition: Anchoring bias is the tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information encountered, called the anchor, when making judgments and decisions, even when it is not relevant.
explanation: People often use an initial number as a reference point and adjust from it, but usually not enough. Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman showed this effect in experiments where even random numbers influenced people's estimates.

In investing, a common anchor is the price paid for a share. An investor who bought at 50 may refuse to sell while it trades at 35, waiting for it to get back to 50, even though the purchase price has no bearing on the company's future prospects.
Other anchors include a share's recent high, an analyst's first price target or the asking price of a house. In negotiations, the first offer often acts as an anchor that shapes the final outcome.

Anchoring can lead investors to hold losing positions, misjudge value and underreact to new information. Reducing its effect involves asking what an investment is worth based on current information, considering a range of possible values and asking whether one would buy the investment today at the current price.

definition: An angel investor is a wealthy individual who invests their own money in early-stage start-ups, usually in exchange for an ownership stake or convertible securities.
explanation: Angel investors often provide the first outside money a start-up receives, after the founders' own savings and money from friends and family, but before venture capital firms become involved.
Angel investments are typically smaller than venture capital investments. Angels may invest alone or as part of angel groups or syndicates, which pool money and share research.

Many angels are successful entrepreneurs or experienced executives who, besides money, offer advice, industry contacts and mentoring. For example, a former technology executive might invest 50,000 in a promising software start-up and help the founders with hiring and introductions to potential customers.

Angel investing is very risky. Most start-ups fail, and investors may lose their entire investment. Returns usually depend on a small number of successful companies, and money may be tied up for many years before any return is possible.

In many countries, angel investing is limited to people who meet certain wealth or income thresholds, or who are classed as sophisticated investors. Some governments offer tax incentives to encourage investment in early-stage companies.

definition: The annual percentage rate (APR) is the yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage. It includes the interest rate and, in many cases, certain fees, so different loans can be compared more fairly.
explanation: Two loans with the same interest rate can cost different amounts if one charges extra fees. APR aims to roll the main costs into a single yearly percentage so borrowers can compare offers on a like-for-like basis.

For example, Loan A charges 7% interest with no fees. Loan B charges 6.5% interest but adds an arrangement fee. Once the fee is spread across the life of the loan, Loan B's APR might be 7.3%, making it the more expensive choice even though its headline rate is lower.

What APR includes depends on local rules and the type of product. It usually covers interest and compulsory fees for arranging the loan, but may not include optional extras or penalty charges such as late fees.

APR is mainly a borrowing measure. In many places, it does not fully reflect the effect of compounding within the year. A credit card with an APR of 24% that compounds monthly actually costs a little more than 24% a year if the balance is carried. For savings products, the comparable measure is the annual percentage yield, which does include compounding.

definition: The annual percentage yield (APY) is the actual return earned on a savings account or deposit in one year, including the effect of compounding.
explanation: Banks often state a rate together with how often it compounds, such as "6% compounded monthly". Because interest is added each month and then earns interest itself, the amount actually earned over a year is a little more than 6%. APY shows that true one-year figure.
With 6% compounded monthly, the account adds 0.5% each month. After twelve months, a deposit of 1,000 grows to about 1,061.68, not 1,060. The APY is therefore about 6.17%.

APY makes it easy to compare savings accounts with different compounding schedules. An account paying 5.95% compounded daily and one paying 6.00% compounded yearly can be ranked correctly only once both are converted into APY. The account with the higher APY earns more.

APY assumes the rate stays the same all year and that interest is left in the account. In some countries, the same idea goes by a different name, such as the annual equivalent rate (AER) in the United Kingdom. It is the savings-side counterpart of the effective annual rate used for loans.

definition: Annual recurring revenue (ARR) is the yearly value of the subscription or contracted recurring revenue a company expects to receive from its existing customers, based on their current contracts.
explanation: ARR is a key measure for subscription businesses, especially software companies selling annual or multi-year contracts. It shows the predictable, recurring part of revenue, excluding one-time fees such as setup charges or consulting.
For example, a company with 2,000 customers each paying 1,200 a year for a subscription has ARR of 2,400,000.
ARR changes as new customers sign up, existing customers upgrade or downgrade and some customers cancel. Tracking these movements helps companies understand growth and retention.

ARR is not defined by accounting standards, so companies calculate it in different ways. Some include contracted subscriptions that have not yet started, or usage-based revenue. ARR also differs from recognised revenue, which follows accounting rules and timing. Investors value ARR because recurring revenue is more predictable than one-off sales, but they should check how each company defines it.

definition: An annual report is a comprehensive document a company publishes each year describing its activities, strategy, performance and financial position, including its audited financial statements.
explanation: The annual report is a company's main formal communication to shareholders and other stakeholders. Listed companies are generally required to publish one, and many private companies produce them too.

A typical annual report includes a letter from the chair or chief executive; a review of the business and its strategy; an analysis of financial performance by management; information on risks; reports on governance, board members and executive pay; often sustainability or ESG information; the full audited financial statements with notes; and the auditor's report.

For example, an investor reading a company's annual report could learn how revenue grew in each region, what risks management sees ahead, how much the chief executive was paid and what the auditor concluded.

The exact contents depend on local laws and stock exchange rules. In the United States, listed companies file a detailed annual report with the securities regulator on a standard form, and many also produce a more readable glossy version for shareholders.
Annual reports are a key source for analysts and investors. The financial statements and notes provide the hard numbers, while the narrative sections explain management's view of the business.

definition: Annualized return is the average yearly rate of return an investment would need to earn, with compounding, to produce its total return over a period longer or shorter than a year.
explanation: Investments are held for different lengths of time, so their total returns are hard to compare directly. Annualizing converts each return into an equivalent yearly rate.

For example, an investment that grows from 10,000 to 13,310 over three years has a total return of 33.1%. Its annualized return is 10%, because 10,000 growing at 10% a year for three years reaches 13,310. Simply dividing 33.1% by three would give 11%, which overstates the yearly rate because it ignores compounding.
Annualized return is the same idea as the compound annual growth rate. It is the standard way funds report performance over three, five or ten years.
Annualizing returns over periods shorter than a year can be misleading. A 5% gain in one month, annualized, would suggest a return of nearly 80% a year, which is unlikely to continue.

Annualized returns smooth out the path an investment took. Two investments with the same annualized return may have had very different ups and downs along the way, so volatility and drawdowns are also worth considering.

definition: An annuity is a series of equal payments made at regular intervals for a set period, such as monthly loan repayments or yearly pension payments. The word is also used for an insurance product that provides a guaranteed income, often in retirement.
explanation: Many everyday arrangements are annuities in the financial sense. A car loan repaid with 60 equal monthly payments is an annuity. So is a savings plan where you put in the same amount every month, or a pension that pays a fixed sum every year.

Because the payments are spread over time, each one has a different value today. Suppose you will receive 1,000 at the end of each year for five years and money can earn 5% a year. The five payments total 5,000, but their combined value today is only about 4,329, because later payments are worth less than earlier ones. If instead you saved each payment at 5%, you would have about 5,526 after five years.
These calculations explain how loan payments are set. The lender chooses the equal payment that, over the loan term, repays the principal plus interest.

As a retirement product, an annuity is bought from an insurer with a lump sum. In return, the insurer pays a regular income for a set number of years or for life, which protects against the risk of running out of money.

definition: An annuity due is a series of equal payments made at the beginning of each period, such as rent paid at the start of each month.
explanation: The only difference between an annuity due and an ordinary annuity is timing. In an annuity due, the first payment happens immediately, and each later payment comes at the start of its period rather than the end.
Common examples include rent, insurance premiums, many lease payments and subscriptions, which are usually paid in advance.

Because each payment arrives one period earlier, an annuity due is worth more than an equivalent ordinary annuity. Suppose you will receive 1,000 at the start of each year for three years, and money earns 5%. The value today is about 2,859, compared with about 2,723 if the same payments came at the end of each year. The annuity due is worth exactly 5% more, because each payment has one extra period to earn interest.

The same idea applies to saving. If you invest a fixed amount at the start of each month rather than the end, your savings will grow slightly larger over time, because every deposit earns interest for one extra month.

definition: Anti-dilution protection is a provision that protects investors, typically holders of preferred shares in venture capital deals, if a company later issues shares at a lower price than they paid, by adjusting the price at which their shares convert into ordinary shares.
explanation: If a company raises money at a lower valuation than in an earlier round, a down round, earlier investors' stakes become worth less. Anti-dilution protection gives them additional shares to offset part or all of this loss, at the expense of other shareholders, usually founders and employees.

There are two main types. Full ratchet protection resets the investor's conversion price to the new, lower price. Weighted-average protection, which is more common and more moderate, adjusts the price based on both the new price and the number of new shares issued.

For example, investors paid 2.00 per share. The company later issues 5,000,000 new shares at 1.00, when 10,000,000 shares were already outstanding. Under full ratchet, the earlier investors' conversion price falls to 1.00, doubling their shares. Under a broad-based weighted-average formula, it falls to about 1.67.

Anti-dilution protection does not prevent dilution from new shares issued at higher prices, which is normal in growing companies. Founders should understand these terms, since they can significantly affect ownership after a down round.

definition: Anti-money laundering (AML) refers to the laws, regulations and procedures designed to prevent criminals from disguising illegally obtained money as legitimate income.
explanation: Money laundering typically happens in three stages. In placement, illegal cash is introduced into the financial system, for example by depositing it in bank accounts. In layering, the money is moved through complex transactions to hide its origin. In integration, the money re-enters the economy appearing legitimate, for example through property purchases or business investments.

AML rules require banks and many other businesses, including accountants, lawyers, estate agents, casinos and cryptocurrency firms, to take steps to detect and prevent money laundering. These include verifying customers' identities through Know Your Customer checks, monitoring transactions for suspicious activity, keeping records, training staff and reporting suspicious activity to the authorities.
For example, a bank might flag a customer who makes many cash deposits just below the threshold that triggers automatic reporting, a pattern called structuring.

International standards are set by the Financial Action Task Force, an intergovernmental body. Failing to comply with AML rules can lead to very large fines for financial institutions, and in serious cases, criminal charges for individuals.

definition: Appreciation is an increase in the value of a currency compared with other currencies, or more generally an increase in the value of any asset over time.
explanation: In foreign exchange, a currency appreciates when it can buy more of another currency than before. For example, if the exchange rate between the euro and the US dollar moves from 1.10 dollars per euro to 1.21 dollars per euro, the euro has appreciated by 10% against the dollar.

A currency usually appreciates under a floating exchange rate when demand for it rises. This can happen because of higher interest rates attracting foreign investment, strong economic growth, a trade surplus or increased confidence in the country.

Currency appreciation has mixed effects. It makes imports cheaper, which can reduce inflation and benefit consumers and businesses that buy foreign goods. It also makes foreign holidays cheaper. However, it makes a country's exports more expensive for foreign buyers, which can hurt exporters and industries that compete with imports.
The term also applies to other assets. A house, share or piece of art that rises in value has appreciated. The opposite of appreciation is depreciation, a fall in value.

definition: Arbitrage is the practice of profiting from price differences for the same or equivalent assets in different markets, by buying where the price is lower and simultaneously selling where it is higher.
explanation: In its pure form, arbitrage is risk-free: the buying and selling happen at the same time, locking in a profit regardless of future price movements.

For example, if gold trades at 1,900 per ounce in one market and 1,905 in another, a trader could buy in the first market and sell in the second, earning 5 per ounce before transaction costs. Similarly, if a company's shares are listed on two stock exchanges at slightly different prices after adjusting for exchange rates, traders can profit from the gap.

Arbitrage plays an important role in keeping markets efficient. As traders exploit price differences, buying pushes up the lower price and selling pushes down the higher one, until the gap disappears. In modern markets, these opportunities are often tiny and last only fractions of a second, so they are mostly captured by sophisticated firms with fast computers.

Many strategies described as arbitrage involve some risk. Merger arbitrage, for example, involves buying shares of a company being acquired, betting the deal will be completed. Statistical arbitrage uses models to exploit price relationships that usually, but not always, hold.

definition: The arithmetic mean is the sum of a set of values divided by the number of values. It is what most people mean by "the average".
explanation: To find the arithmetic mean, add all the numbers together and divide by how many there are. For the values 3, 5, 5, 7 and 10, the sum is 30 and there are five values, so the mean is 6.
The mean is widely used in finance to summarise data, such as average monthly spending, average sales per store or average annual returns.

It has an important weakness: it is sensitive to extreme values. If one value in a small data set is very large or very small, it can pull the mean far away from what is typical. For example, if nine employees earn 40,000 and one earns 1,000,000, the mean salary is 136,000, which describes nobody in the group. In such cases, the median often gives a better picture.

For investment returns over several periods, the arithmetic mean can also be misleading. If an investment rises 50% one year and falls 50% the next, the arithmetic mean return is 0%, but the investor has actually lost 25% of their money. The geometric mean captures this effect correctly.

definition: The ask price is the lowest price a seller is currently willing to accept for a security. It is also called the offer price.
explanation: The ask is the best price available from sellers at a given moment. If you want to buy a security immediately, the ask price is roughly what you will pay.
For example, if a share's ask price is 50.05, a seller is ready to sell at that price. A market order to buy will normally be filled at or near 50.05.

The ask is normally higher than the bid, the highest price buyers are willing to pay. The gap between them is the bid-ask spread. Market makers and dealers earn part of their income from this gap, buying at the bid and selling at the ask.

When you see a single "price" quoted for a share, it is usually the last price at which a trade happened, which may differ slightly from the current bid and ask. For investors who trade often, or who trade in securities with wide spreads, the difference between bid and ask can become a meaningful cost.

definition: An asset is anything you own or control that has value and is expected to provide a future benefit, such as cash, investments, property, equipment or money others owe you.
explanation: For a person, assets include savings, shares, retirement accounts, a home and a car. For a business, assets include cash, inventory, machinery, buildings and amounts customers still owe it. In accounting, an asset is a resource the business controls as a result of past events and that is expected to bring future economic benefits.

Assets are often grouped by how quickly they can be turned into cash. Current assets, such as cash, inventory and receivables, are expected to be used or converted within about a year. Non-current assets, such as buildings and equipment, are held for longer.

Not all assets produce income. A share that pays dividends or a rental flat that brings in rent generates cash. A car or a personal home usually does not, and a car typically loses value each year. Some people therefore distinguish between assets that grow or pay you and those that mainly cost money to keep.

Assets are one side of the basic accounting relationship: what you own, minus what you owe, equals what is truly yours. That remaining amount is called equity for a business, or net worth for a person.

definition: Asset allocation is the way an investor divides their money among different types of assets, such as shares, bonds, property and cash.
explanation: Different asset types behave differently. Shares have historically offered higher long-term returns but can fall sharply in the short term. Bonds usually offer lower returns but are generally more stable. Cash is the safest but often barely keeps up with inflation. Combining them changes the overall balance of risk and return.

For example, a portfolio of 60% shares and 40% bonds is a common balanced mix. A young investor with decades ahead might choose 90% shares and 10% bonds, while someone close to retirement might prefer 40% shares and 60% bonds to reduce the risk of a large fall just before they need the money.
Many studies suggest that asset allocation explains a large part of the variation in a portfolio's returns over time, more than the choice of individual shares or funds.

The right allocation depends on an investor's goals, time horizon and ability to cope with losses. Because markets move, a portfolio's allocation drifts over time, so investors periodically rebalance to bring it back to their target.

definition: Asset location is choosing which types of investment to hold in which types of account, such as taxable, tax-deferred and tax-free accounts, to reduce the total tax paid.
explanation: Asset allocation decides what mix of investments to hold. Asset location decides where to hold them. Because different accounts are taxed differently, and different investments produce different kinds of taxable income, the placement can affect the after-tax return of the whole portfolio.

A common approach is to hold investments that produce a lot of taxable income each year, such as bonds or real estate investment trusts, inside tax-sheltered accounts, and investments that are already tax-efficient, such as broad share index funds held for the long term, in taxable accounts.

For example, an investor wanting 60% shares and 40% bonds overall might hold all the bonds in a retirement account and most of the shares in a taxable account, rather than splitting each account 60/40.

The benefit depends on tax rates, account sizes and expected returns, and it is usually modest but meaningful over many years. Asset location can make rebalancing more complicated, and it should not distort the overall investment mix the investor has chosen.

definition: An asset sale is a transaction in which a buyer purchases specific assets of a business, and often takes on selected liabilities, rather than buying the company that owns them.
explanation: In an asset sale, the buyer chooses which assets and liabilities to acquire, such as equipment, property, inventory, contracts, intellectual property and customer relationships. The seller company remains in existence and keeps any assets and liabilities not sold.
For example, a buyer might acquire a manufacturing business's factory, machinery, brand and customer contracts, while leaving behind its old lawsuits and tax liabilities with the seller.

Buyers often prefer asset sales because they can avoid unknown or unwanted liabilities, and in some tax systems they can increase the tax value of the acquired assets, leading to larger future tax deductions.

Sellers often prefer share sales, which are usually simpler and may be more tax-efficient for them. Asset sales can also be more complex, because individual contracts, permits and licences may need to be transferred, often requiring consent from third parties, and employees may need to be transferred under employment laws.

definition: Asset turnover is revenue divided by total assets, showing how much sales a company generates for each unit of assets it owns.
explanation: Asset turnover measures efficiency. A company that produces a lot of revenue from relatively few assets has high asset turnover; one that needs large amounts of assets to generate sales has low turnover.
