For example, an acquirer offering 45 in cash per share for a target with 20,000,000 shares pays 900,000,000 in total. Target shareholders know exactly what they will receive.

The acquirer may fund cash consideration from its existing cash, new borrowing or proceeds from issuing shares to other investors. Cash deals can signal the acquirer's confidence that the target is worth more than the price, since it keeps all future gains and bears all the risks.

For target shareholders, cash provides certainty but usually creates a taxable event, since selling shares for cash may trigger capital gains tax. For the acquirer, cash deals avoid diluting existing shareholders but can increase debt and reduce financial flexibility. Many deals combine cash and stock consideration to balance these factors.

definition: The cash conversion cycle is the number of days it takes a business to turn money spent on inventory back into cash from customers, after allowing for the time it takes to pay its suppliers.
explanation: The cash conversion cycle combines three measures. Days inventory outstanding is how long stock is held before being sold. Days sales outstanding is how long customers take to pay. Days payable outstanding is how long the business takes to pay its suppliers. The cycle equals the first two added together, minus the third.

For example, a company holds inventory for 73 days, collects from customers in 73 days and pays its suppliers in 36.5 days. Its cash conversion cycle is 109.5 days. That is how long, on average, its own cash is tied up in operations.

A shorter cycle means the business needs less cash to fund its operations. Some businesses, such as large retailers and online platforms, have negative cycles: they collect money from customers before they have to pay suppliers, effectively using suppliers' money to fund their operations.

A lengthening cycle can be a warning sign, suggesting slow-moving inventory, customers paying later or the business paying suppliers faster than before. Managing the cash conversion cycle is a key part of working capital management and can free up significant amounts of cash.

definition: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that can be quickly converted into a known amount of cash and carry very little risk of changes in value.
explanation: On the balance sheet, cash and cash equivalents are usually shown together, because both are effectively available to spend. Cash includes notes, coins and bank deposits available on demand. Cash equivalents are investments that are almost as good as cash.

To qualify, an investment generally must mature within about three months of the date the company acquires it, and must be readily convertible into cash with an insignificant risk of a change in value. Examples include treasury bills, money market funds, short-term bank deposits and high-quality commercial paper.
For example, a company with 2 million in its bank accounts and 3 million in treasury bills maturing in 60 days might report cash and cash equivalents of 5 million.
Investments that do not meet these tests, such as shares, longer-term bonds or deposits with a one-year term, are usually classified as short-term or long-term investments instead.
Cash and cash equivalents is a key figure for judging a company's liquidity. The cash flow statement explains how this total changed during the period.

definition: A cash flow forecast is an estimate of the cash a business expects to receive and pay out over a future period, usually week by week or month by month.
explanation: A cash flow forecast helps a business see whether it will have enough cash to meet its obligations. It lists expected receipts, such as customer payments, loans and asset sales, and expected payments, such as wages, rent, supplier bills, taxes and loan repayments.

For each period, the forecast starts with the opening cash balance, adds expected receipts, subtracts expected payments and arrives at a closing balance, which becomes the next period's opening balance.

Suppose a business expects to start June with 20,000, receive 45,000 from customers and pay 52,000 in costs. It would end June with 13,000. If July's forecast shows the balance going negative, the business can act in advance: chasing customers, delaying spending or arranging finance.

Cash flow forecasts are especially important for small and growing businesses, which can run out of cash even while profitable. They are only as good as their assumptions, so they are usually updated regularly as actual results come in.

definition: Cash flow from financing is the section of the cash flow statement that shows cash moving between a company and its lenders and owners, such as borrowing, repaying debt, issuing shares and paying dividends.
explanation: Financing activities show how a company raises money and how it returns money to those who fund it. Cash comes in when the company takes out loans, issues bonds or sells new shares. Cash goes out when it repays debt, pays dividends or buys back its own shares.
For example, a company that borrows 10 million, repays 4 million of older loans and pays 3 million in dividends has a net cash inflow from financing of 3 million.

The pattern of financing cash flows tells a story. A young, fast-growing company may show large inflows as it raises money to fund expansion. A mature, profitable company often shows outflows as it pays dividends, buys back shares and reduces debt.

Reading financing cash flows together with operating and investing cash flows shows where a company's cash really comes from. A business that relies on constant borrowing to fund day-to-day operations deserves closer attention.

definition: Cash flow from investing is the section of the cash flow statement that shows cash spent on, or received from, long-term assets and investments.
explanation: Investing activities include buying and selling property, plant and equipment, buying and selling other businesses, and buying and selling investments such as shares and bonds of other companies.

For a growing business, cash flow from investing is usually negative, because the company is spending money on new equipment, buildings or acquisitions. For example, a company might spend 8 million on new machinery and receive 1 million from selling old vehicles, giving net cash used in investing activities of 7 million.

A negative figure is not necessarily bad. It often means the company is investing in its future. A positive figure can mean the company is selling assets, which might be a sensible clear-out of unneeded property or a sign it needs cash.

Analysts compare investing cash flows with operating cash flows. A company whose operations generate enough cash to fund its investments is in a strong position. One that must borrow or raise new equity to keep investing is more dependent on outside funding.

definition: The cash flow statement shows how much cash came into and went out of a business during a period, grouped into operating, investing and financing activities.
explanation: Profit and cash are not the same. A company can report a profit and still run short of cash, or report a loss while its cash grows. The cash flow statement shows the actual movement of money.

It is divided into three parts. Operating activities cover cash from the core business, such as receipts from customers and payments to suppliers and staff. Investing activities cover buying and selling long-term assets, such as equipment or other businesses. Financing activities cover borrowing, repaying debt, issuing shares and paying dividends.
For example, a company might generate 800,000 from operations, spend 500,000 on new equipment and repay 200,000 of loans. Its cash would increase by 100,000 over the period.

Investors pay close attention to operating cash flow, because it shows whether the business itself produces cash. A company that consistently relies on borrowing or selling assets to cover operating shortfalls may be in trouble, even if its income statement looks healthy.

definition: Cash management is the process of collecting, holding, spending and investing a business's cash efficiently, so that it always has enough to meet its needs while making good use of any surplus.
explanation: Even profitable businesses can fail if they run out of cash. Cash management focuses on the timing and control of cash flows.

Key activities include speeding up collections from customers, managing payments to suppliers so they are made on time but not unnecessarily early, forecasting cash needs, maintaining an appropriate cash buffer, arranging credit lines for shortfalls and investing surplus cash in safe, liquid instruments.

For example, a business might offer customers a small discount for paying early, move from paper invoices to electronic payments to receive money faster, and use a cash pooling arrangement so that surplus cash in one bank account automatically covers a shortfall in another.

Good cash management reduces borrowing costs, earns interest on surpluses and lowers the risk of financial distress. For small businesses, it may involve simple weekly cash forecasts and close attention to invoices. For large companies, it is part of the treasury function and uses sophisticated banking systems.

definition: The cash ratio is cash and cash equivalents, sometimes including short-term investments, divided by current liabilities. It is the most conservative measure of a company's ability to meet short-term obligations.
explanation: The cash ratio asks a strict question: if the company had to pay all its short-term obligations right now, using only cash and near-cash assets, could it do so? It ignores receivables and inventory, which take time to convert into cash.
For example, a company with cash and cash equivalents of 120,000 and current liabilities of 250,000 has a cash ratio of 0.48. It could pay about half its short-term obligations immediately from cash.

Few healthy companies have a cash ratio above 1, because holding that much cash is usually inefficient. Cash earns little return, and most businesses can rely on collecting receivables and selling inventory to meet bills as they fall due.

The cash ratio is most useful in times of stress, for example when assessing whether a company could survive a sudden drop in sales or a freeze in credit markets. Lenders and credit analysts sometimes focus on it for companies in difficulty.
Comparing the cash ratio with the current and quick ratios shows how much of a company's liquidity depends on cash, receivables and inventory respectively.

definition: A cash reserve is money deliberately set aside and kept easily accessible to cover unexpected costs, shortfalls in income or short-term needs.
explanation: A cash reserve is a safety cushion. Rather than spending all available cash or investing it in assets that may be slow or costly to sell, a person or business keeps a portion ready for use at short notice.

For households, the most familiar cash reserve is an emergency fund, used for events such as job loss, car repairs or medical bills. For businesses, a cash reserve helps cover payroll, supplier payments and loan repayments during slow periods, delays in customer payments or sudden problems.

The right size depends on how predictable income and costs are. A business with steady monthly sales of 100,000 and costs of 90,000 might keep enough to cover two to three months of costs, or 180,000 to 270,000. A business with seasonal or unpredictable sales would usually hold more.

The trade-off is return. Money held in reserve usually sits in a bank account or very safe short-term investments that pay little interest. The security it provides comes at the cost of the higher return the money might earn elsewhere.

definition: Cash-basis accounting records income only when cash is received and expenses only when cash is paid out.
explanation: Cash-basis accounting works like a personal bank statement. Money in is income, money out is an expense, and the timing of the cash decides the period in which each item is recorded.

If a freelancer finishes a 3,000 job in December but is paid in January, the 3,000 is recorded as January income. If they buy software in December but pay for it in January, the cost is a January expense.
The method is simple and shows clearly how much cash the business has. It is common for small businesses, sole traders and individuals, and some tax systems allow very small businesses to use it.

Its weakness is that it can give a misleading picture of performance. A business could look very profitable in a month when several customers happened to pay old invoices, and unprofitable in a month when it paid a large annual bill. Because income and expenses are not matched to when they were earned or incurred, larger businesses and most companies reporting to investors must use accrual accounting instead.

definition: A catastrophe bond is a type of bond, usually issued for an insurer or reinsurer, that pays investors a high interest rate but can lose some or all of its principal if a specified disaster, such as a major hurricane or earthquake, occurs.
explanation: Catastrophe bonds, often called cat bonds, transfer the risk of large natural disasters from insurers to investors in capital markets. The money raised is held in a secure account. If no qualifying disaster occurs during the bond's life, investors receive interest and their principal back. If a qualifying disaster occurs, part or all of the principal is used to pay the insurer's claims.
Triggers vary. Some pay out based on the insurer's actual losses, some on industry-wide losses, and others on physical measures, such as earthquake magnitude or wind speed at a specific location.

For example, an insurer might issue a three-year catastrophe bond covering hurricane losses in a particular region above a certain level. Investors receive a high yield, but would lose their principal if a severe hurricane caused losses above the trigger.

Catastrophe bonds attract investors because disaster risk is largely unrelated to financial market movements, offering diversification. The market has grown significantly since the 1990s. Investors face the risk of large, sudden losses, and climate change makes estimating disaster risk more uncertain.

definition: A central bank is the public institution that manages a country's or region's currency, money supply and interest rates, and oversees the stability of the banking system.
explanation: Examples include the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan and the Reserve Bank of India. Most countries have one.

Central banks have several key roles. They conduct monetary policy, usually by setting a key interest rate, to keep inflation low and stable and to support economic activity. They issue banknotes. They act as the bank for commercial banks, holding their reserves and lending to them when needed. In a financial crisis, they can act as a lender of last resort, providing emergency funding to stop panic spreading through the banking system. Many also supervise banks to ensure they are safe.

For example, if inflation is running well above target, a central bank may raise its policy rate. This makes borrowing more expensive throughout the economy, slows spending and helps bring inflation down.

Many central banks are independent from day-to-day political control. The idea is that independence allows them to make difficult decisions, such as raising interest rates, based on long-term economic goals rather than short-term political pressures.

definition: A central bank digital currency (CBDC) is a digital form of a country's official currency, issued and backed by its central bank.
explanation: Today, most money used by the public is either physical cash, issued by the central bank, or bank deposits, created by commercial banks. A CBDC would be digital money that is a direct liability of the central bank, just like cash, but in electronic form.

Central banks are exploring CBDCs for several reasons: to provide a safe digital alternative as cash use declines, to improve payment efficiency, to support financial inclusion, to maintain control over money in a world of private cryptocurrencies and stablecoins, and to improve cross-border payments.

Several countries have launched CBDCs, including the Bahamas, Jamaica and Nigeria, while China has carried out large-scale trials of its digital yuan. The European Central Bank has been preparing a possible digital euro, and many other central banks are researching the idea.

CBDCs raise important questions. Critics worry about privacy, since a central bank could potentially see detailed payment data, and about the effect on commercial banks if people move large amounts of deposits into CBDCs, especially during a crisis. Designs being considered include limits on individual holdings and privacy protections.

definition: Central bank independence is the degree to which a central bank can set monetary policy, such as interest rates, free from political interference by the government.
explanation: Governments may be tempted to keep interest rates low before elections or to finance spending by creating money, which can lead to high inflation. Giving central banks independence aims to protect monetary policy from these short-term pressures.

Independence typically involves a clear legal mandate, such as price stability; long, fixed terms for central bank leaders, who cannot easily be dismissed; control over policy tools; and restrictions on lending directly to the government.
For example, the Bank of England was given operational independence to set interest rates in 1997, with the government setting the inflation target and the bank deciding how to achieve it.

Research suggests that countries with more independent central banks have tended to have lower and more stable inflation. Independence comes with accountability, such as publishing decisions, explaining them and appearing before legislatures. Debates continue about how much independence is appropriate, especially as central banks have taken on broader roles since 2008.

definition: A central counterparty (CCP) is a clearing house that steps in between the two sides of a trade, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, and guaranteeing that trades will be completed even if one party defaults.
explanation: Without a central counterparty, each trader is exposed to the risk that the party on the other side fails to pay or deliver. A CCP replaces many bilateral exposures with a single exposure to the CCP, a process called novation.

CCPs manage risk in several ways. They require members to post initial margin when they open positions and variation margin as prices change. They maintain default funds, contributed by members, and their own capital to absorb losses. If a member defaults, the CCP uses these resources, in a set order called the default waterfall, to cover losses.
For example, if a trader holding a large futures position goes bankrupt, the CCP closes or transfers the position, using the trader's margin to cover any loss, so that other traders are not affected.

After the 2008 financial crisis, regulators required many standardised over-the-counter derivatives to be cleared through CCPs. This has reduced counterparty risk, but concentrated it in a small number of CCPs, which are now regulated as critical financial infrastructure.

definition: The central limit theorem is a principle of statistics stating that the average of a large number of independent random values tends to follow a normal distribution, regardless of the shape of the original distribution.
explanation: The central limit theorem explains why the normal distribution appears so often in statistics. Even if individual observations follow an unusual distribution, the averages of large samples of them will be approximately normally distributed, as long as certain conditions are met.

For example, the outcome of rolling a single die is evenly spread from 1 to 6, which is not a bell shape at all. But if you roll 30 dice many times and record the average each time, those averages will form a pattern very close to a bell-shaped normal distribution, centred on 3.5.

The theorem is the basis for many statistical methods, such as confidence intervals and hypothesis tests, which rely on sample averages being approximately normal. It allows analysts to draw conclusions about a whole population from a sample.

In finance, it is sometimes used to justify modelling returns over longer periods as roughly normal, since they are made up of many smaller daily returns. However, the theorem relies on assumptions, such as independent observations without extremely fat tails, which do not always hold in financial markets.

definition: A certificate of deposit (CD) is a type of time deposit offered by banks and credit unions that pays a fixed interest rate for a fixed term, such as six months, one year or five years.
explanation: A CD works much like other time deposits: you deposit a sum of money for a set period and earn a guaranteed rate of interest. The term is especially common in the United States.

CDs usually pay higher interest than regular savings accounts, with longer terms often paying higher rates. In exchange, the money is locked up until the CD matures. Withdrawing early typically means paying a penalty, often a few months' worth of interest.
For example, a five-year CD of 5,000 paying 4% a year, compounded annually, would be worth about 6,083 at maturity.

Some investors use a strategy called laddering, splitting money across CDs that mature at different times, such as one, two, three, four and five years. As each CD matures, the money can be spent or reinvested, providing regular access to funds while still earning higher long-term rates.

CDs from insured banks are covered by deposit insurance up to the applicable limit. Some brokered CDs can be sold before maturity in a secondary market, but their price may be lower than the amount invested if interest rates have risen.

definition: A change in accounting estimate is an adjustment to an amount in the financial statements that was based on judgment, made because new information or developments show the earlier estimate needs revising.
explanation: Many figures in accounts rely on estimates, such as the useful life of equipment, the amount of customer debts that will not be paid, warranty costs and the value of inventory. As circumstances change, estimates are updated.
A change in estimate is applied from the current period onwards. Earlier years are not restated, because the original estimate was reasonable based on the information available at the time.

For example, a company bought a machine for 100,000 expecting a ten-year life, depreciating it at 10,000 a year. After four years, with 60,000 left to depreciate, it decides the machine will last only three more years. From now on, it depreciates 20,000 a year.

This treatment differs from a change in accounting policy, which is usually applied to earlier years as well, and from the correction of a prior-period error, which requires restating past figures. Companies must disclose significant changes in estimates. Frequent or convenient changes in estimates can be a warning sign of earnings management.

definition: A change of control is a transaction or event in which ownership or control of a company passes to a different person or group, such as when it is acquired or a new shareholder gains a majority stake.
explanation: Many contracts include change-of-control clauses that give rights to the other party if ownership changes. These clauses can significantly affect acquisitions.

Common examples include loan agreements, which may allow lenders to demand repayment; bond terms, which may give bondholders the right to sell their bonds back to the company at a premium; commercial contracts, which may allow customers or suppliers to terminate; licences that may require consent; and executive employment contracts, which may trigger large payments if executives leave after a takeover.
For example, a company's bank loan might allow the bank to demand full repayment if the company is acquired. A buyer must then arrange new financing as part of the deal.

Buyers review change-of-control provisions carefully during due diligence, since they can affect the cost and structure of a deal. Change of control is also relevant in regulation, since acquiring control of banks, insurers and some other businesses may require regulatory approval.

definition: Chapter 11 is a section of the United States Bankruptcy Code that allows a struggling company to continue operating while it reorganises its debts and business under court supervision.
explanation: Under Chapter 11, a company can seek protection from its creditors while it develops a plan to restructure. An automatic stay stops most creditors from collecting debts or seizing assets during the process. Management usually remains in control, as a debtor in possession.

The company proposes a reorganisation plan, which may reduce debts, convert debt into equity, close unprofitable operations or sell assets. Creditors vote on the plan by class, and the court can approve it even if some classes object, under certain conditions, a process called a cramdown.

For example, an airline in Chapter 11 might keep flying while it renegotiates aircraft leases, labour contracts and debts, then emerge from bankruptcy with a stronger balance sheet. Several major US airlines and carmakers have used Chapter 11.

Chapter 11 can save viable businesses, but it is expensive and time-consuming, and shareholders are often wiped out. It differs from Chapter 7, under which a company is liquidated. Other countries have their own processes, such as administration and restructuring plans in the United Kingdom.

definition: A chargeback is a reversal of a card payment, initiated by the cardholder's bank, usually after the cardholder disputes a transaction because of fraud, non-delivery or faulty goods.
explanation: If a customer pays by card and something goes wrong, such as goods never arriving, being significantly different from what was described, or a payment being taken without permission, they can ask their card issuer to reverse the transaction.

The card issuer investigates using rules set by the card network, such as Visa or Mastercard. If the claim is valid, the money is taken back from the merchant's bank and returned to the customer. The merchant can dispute the chargeback by providing evidence, such as proof of delivery.
For example, a customer who orders a jacket online that never arrives, and who cannot get a response from the seller, might contact their bank and request a chargeback.

Chargeback is a scheme run by the card networks, not a legal right, and there are usually time limits for making a claim, often around 120 days. It applies to both debit and credit cards. In some countries, credit card purchases also have separate legal protections; for example, in the United Kingdom, Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act makes the card provider jointly liable for purchases between 100 and 30,000. Merchants usually pay fees for each chargeback, and frequent chargebacks can lead to losing the ability to accept cards.

definition: A charge-off is a debt that a lender has written off as unlikely to be collected, usually after the borrower has missed payments for several months. The term is used mainly in the United States.
explanation: In the United States, lenders typically charge off credit card debts after around 180 days of missed payments, and many instalment loans, such as personal loans, after around 120 days. The lender records the debt as a loss in its accounts, but the borrower still legally owes the money.

After a charge-off, the lender may continue trying to collect the debt itself, pass it to a collection agency or sell it to a debt buyer for a fraction of its value. The charge-off is recorded on the borrower's credit report and generally remains there for seven years from the original missed payment, significantly lowering their credit score.

For example, a person who stops paying a credit card with a balance of 4,000 may find that, after six months, the account is charged off and later sold to a debt collection company, which then contacts them to recover the money.

The equivalent idea in the United Kingdom and many other countries is a default, where the account is formally marked as defaulted on the credit file after several months of missed payments. A default usually stays on a UK credit file for six years.

definition: A charitable deduction is a reduction in taxable income allowed for donations made to qualifying charities.
explanation: Many tax systems encourage giving by letting donors reduce their taxable income by the amount given, within limits. The charity must usually be registered or approved by the tax authority.

For example, a taxpayer whose top rate of income tax is 30% gives 1,000 to a qualifying charity and deducts it. Their taxable income falls by 1,000, saving 300 in tax. The donation's real cost to them is 700.

In the United States, charitable donations have mainly been deductible for taxpayers who itemize, with limits based on income and the type of gift; from 2026, taxpayers who take the standard deduction can also deduct a limited amount of cash gifts. Gifts of appreciated assets, such as shares held for more than a year, can be especially tax-efficient, because the donor may avoid capital gains tax and still deduct the market value.

Other countries use different methods. In the United Kingdom, Gift Aid lets charities reclaim basic-rate tax on donations, while higher-rate taxpayers can claim extra relief. Records, such as receipts, are usually needed to support the deduction.

definition: A chart of accounts is a complete, organised list of all the accounts a business uses to record its transactions, usually grouped by type and given reference numbers.
explanation: Every transaction must be recorded in a specific account, such as cash, sales, rent expense or bank loan. The chart of accounts is the master list of those accounts, a bit like the table of contents for a company's books.

Accounts are usually grouped in the order they appear in the financial statements: assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses. Each account gets a number, often with the first digit showing its group. For example, accounts beginning with 1 might be assets, so 1000 could be cash and 1200 accounts receivable, while accounts beginning with 5 might be expenses, such as 5100 for rent.

A well-designed chart of accounts makes it easy to record transactions consistently and to produce useful reports. It should be detailed enough to show what managers need, such as separate accounts for each type of expense, but not so detailed that recording becomes confusing.
Businesses in the same industry often use similar charts of accounts, and some countries require a standard national structure.

definition: A check is a written order from an account holder instructing their bank to pay a specified amount from their account to a named person or organisation. It is spelled cheque in British English.
explanation: A check includes the date, the name of the payee, the amount in words and figures, and the account holder's signature. The payee deposits the check at their bank, which collects the money from the payer's bank through a clearing process.

Checks were once one of the main ways to pay bills and transfer money. Their use has declined sharply in most countries as electronic payments, cards and mobile transfers have become widespread. They remain more common in the United States than in many other countries, for example for rent and some business payments.
For example, a tenant might write a check for 1,200 to their landlord, who deposits it by taking a photo using a banking app, a process called mobile check deposit.

Checks carry risks. A check can bounce if there is not enough money in the account, and check fraud, including forged and altered checks, remains a problem. Payments by check are also slower than most electronic methods. Some countries are phasing out checks entirely.

definition: A checking account is a bank account used for everyday transactions, such as receiving pay, paying bills, making card payments and withdrawing cash.
explanation: A checking account is designed for convenience and frequent use. Money can be deposited and withdrawn at any time, and most accounts come with a debit card, online banking, mobile payments and the ability to set up regular payments.

The name comes from cheques, also spelled checks, which were traditionally used to pay from these accounts. Cheques are now used much less, but the name remains in the United States and some other countries. In the United Kingdom and many other countries, the same type of account is called a current account.

Checking accounts usually pay little or no interest. Some charge monthly fees, which may be waived if you keep a minimum balance or have your salary paid in. Some offer an overdraft facility, allowing you to spend more than your balance up to a limit, usually at a cost.

For example, a person might have their 3,000 monthly salary paid into their checking account, pay rent and bills from it by automatic payment and use the debit card for daily spending. Keeping track of the balance helps avoid overdraft fees.

definition: The churn rate is the percentage of customers who stop using a company's product or service during a given period.
explanation: Churn rate is calculated by dividing the number of customers lost during a period by the number of customers at the start of that period.
For example, if a streaming service starts the month with 20,000 subscribers and 600 cancel during the month, its monthly churn rate is 3%.

Churn is a critical measure for subscription businesses, telecoms providers, software companies and banks. Even a small monthly churn rate adds up. A monthly churn of 3% means the business loses roughly 30% of its customers over a year, so it must keep winning new customers just to stand still.

Reducing churn is often cheaper than winning new customers. Businesses analyse why customers leave, such as price, poor service, better alternatives or lack of use, and respond with improvements, loyalty rewards or better onboarding.

Churn can also be measured in revenue rather than customers. Revenue churn shows the share of recurring revenue lost from cancellations and downgrades, which can differ from customer churn if larger customers are more or less likely to leave.

definition: A circuit breaker is a rule that temporarily halts trading on a stock exchange, or in a particular security, when prices fall or rise sharply within a short time.
explanation: Circuit breakers are designed to prevent panic selling and give investors time to absorb information and reconsider their decisions during extreme market movements.

Market-wide circuit breakers pause trading on an entire exchange if a major index falls by certain percentages in a single day. For example, under rules used in some markets, trading might pause for 15 minutes if the index falls 7%, pause again at 13% and close for the rest of the day at 20%. The exact thresholds and durations vary between exchanges.

Single-stock circuit breakers, sometimes called trading halts or volatility pauses, stop trading in an individual share if its price moves too far, too fast, often within a set band around a reference price.
Circuit breakers were widely introduced after the 1987 stock market crash and have been refined since, including after sudden "flash crashes" caused by automated trading.

Supporters argue that they calm markets and prevent disorderly trading. Critics suggest they can sometimes increase anxiety, as traders rush to sell before a halt is triggered. Either way, they are a standard feature of modern stock exchanges.

definition: A circular reference is a situation in a spreadsheet or financial model where a formula depends, directly or indirectly, on its own result.
explanation: Spreadsheets normally calculate in a sequence, with each formula using results that have already been calculated. A circular reference breaks this, because a cell's value depends on itself.

In financial models, circular references often arise intentionally. A common example involves interest: interest expense depends on the average debt balance, the debt balance depends on how much cash is available to repay it, and available cash depends on interest expense.
For example, in a leveraged buyout model, the amount of debt repaid each year affects interest, which affects net income and cash flow, which in turn affects the amount of debt repaid.

Spreadsheets can solve intentional circular references through iterative calculation, repeatedly recalculating until the values settle. However, circular references can make models unstable, slow and hard to check, and errors can spread unnoticed. Many modellers avoid them by calculating interest on opening balances, or include a switch to turn the circularity off. Unintended circular references usually indicate a mistake.

definition: A claim reserve is the amount of money an insurer sets aside to pay claims that have occurred but have not yet been fully settled, including claims that have been reported and those not yet reported.
explanation: Insurance claims are often paid long after the event that caused them. Settling claims, especially for injuries or liability, can take years. Insurers must estimate how much they will eventually pay and record this as a liability.

Claim reserves typically include reported claims not yet settled, estimated from information about each case; incurred but not reported claims, for events that have happened but have not yet been reported; and the costs of handling and settling claims.
For example, after a major storm, an insurer might set aside 50,000,000 for claims already reported and a further 15,000,000 for claims it expects policyholders to report in the coming months.

Claim reserves are usually the largest liability on a general insurer's balance sheet. Estimating them requires actuarial judgment, using past patterns of claims. If reserves prove too low, the insurer must strengthen them, reducing profits; if they prove too high, the release boosts profits. Regulators and auditors examine reserves closely.

definition: A claim is a formal request made by a policyholder to an insurer for payment or other benefits under the terms of an insurance policy, following a covered loss or event.
explanation: When something happens that is covered by an insurance policy, such as a car accident, house fire, theft, illness or death, the policyholder or beneficiary submits a claim. The insurer then assesses whether the loss is covered and how much it should pay.

The claims process typically involves notifying the insurer promptly, providing details and evidence, such as photographs, receipts, police reports or medical records, and cooperating with any investigation. For larger claims, the insurer may send a loss adjuster to assess the damage.
For example, after a storm damages a roof, a homeowner contacts their insurer, sends photographs and repair quotes, and receives payment for the repairs minus their policy excess or deductible.

The payment may be reduced or refused if the loss falls under an exclusion, exceeds the policy limit, or if the policyholder did not disclose important information when buying the policy. Policyholders who disagree with a claims decision can usually complain to the insurer and, in many countries, escalate the dispute to an ombudsman or regulator. For insurers, claims are their largest cost, and managing them efficiently and fairly is central to their business.

definition: Classical economics is a school of economic thought, developed in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, which holds that free markets tend to reach full employment on their own, with flexible prices and wages balancing supply and demand.
explanation: Classical economists, including Adam Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill, laid the foundations of modern economics. Smith's 1776 book The Wealth of Nations described how individuals pursuing their own interests in competitive markets can benefit society, an idea often summarised as the invisible hand.

Key classical ideas include the benefits of specialization and free trade, the role of competition in setting prices, and the belief that markets are self-correcting. If there is unemployment, wages fall until employers hire the available workers. Government intervention in the economy should therefore be limited.
For example, a classical economist would expect a fall in demand to lead to lower prices and wages, restoring full employment without government action.

Classical economics was challenged by the Great Depression, which led to Keynesian economics. Many classical ideas were later revived and developed in new classical and other market-oriented schools of thought.

definition: A clawback is a provision that allows money already paid to be taken back, such as requiring a fund manager to return excess carried interest or requiring executives to repay bonuses after misconduct or misstated results.
explanation: In private equity, carried interest may be paid to the manager on early profitable investments. If later investments perform poorly and the fund as a whole does not meet the agreed return, a clawback requires the manager to return the excess, so that it does not receive more than its agreed share of overall profits.

For example, a manager receives 10,000,000 in carried interest from early successful deals, but later losses mean it was entitled to only 6,000,000 over the whole fund. A clawback requires it to return 4,000,000 to investors.

In companies, clawback policies allow boards to recover bonuses or incentive pay from executives if financial results are later restated or if executives are found to have engaged in misconduct. In the United States, stock exchange rules adopted under the Dodd-Frank Act require listed companies to have policies to recover incentive pay after accounting restatements.
The term is also used in other contexts, such as governments recovering funds from businesses that fail to meet grant conditions.

definition: Clearing is the process, after a trade is agreed, of confirming its details, calculating what each party owes and managing the risk that one side fails to complete the trade before settlement takes place.
explanation: Between the moment a trade is agreed and the moment it settles, when cash and securities actually change hands, several steps must happen. Clearing covers this period. It involves matching and confirming trade details, netting trades so that each party pays or receives only the net amount, and managing the risk of a party defaulting.

In many markets, clearing is carried out by a central counterparty, which becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. This means each trader faces the central counterparty rather than each other, which reduces counterparty risk.
For example, a broker that buys and sells many shares in a single day might owe only a small net amount after clearing, rather than settling every trade separately.

Clearing makes markets safer and more efficient. After the 2008 financial crisis, regulators required many standard derivatives that were previously traded privately to be cleared centrally. Clearing is followed by settlement, the final transfer of securities and cash.

definition: A clearing house is an organisation that sits between buyers and sellers in financial markets, confirming and processing trades, and in many cases guaranteeing their completion if one party defaults.
explanation: When large numbers of trades take place, clearing houses make settlement more efficient and safer. They match and confirm trade details, calculate how much each participant owes or is owed, net trades so only the final amounts need to be paid, and arrange settlement.

Many clearing houses also act as central counterparties, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer. This means each participant's risk is with the clearing house rather than with many different trading partners.
For example, on a futures exchange, the clearing house collects margin from traders each day based on their gains and losses, so that losses are covered before they can build up.

Clearing houses exist for shares, bonds, derivatives, foreign exchange and payments, such as cheque and bank transfer clearing. Because they concentrate risk, clearing houses must have strong risk management, including margin requirements, default funds contributed by members and plans for handling the failure of a member.

definition: A closed-end fund is an investment fund that issues a fixed number of shares, which then trade on a stock exchange at market prices that can differ from the value of the fund's investments.
explanation: A closed-end fund raises money through an initial offering and then invests it. After that, investors who want to buy or sell shares trade them with other investors on the stock exchange, rather than with the fund itself. The fund does not normally create or redeem shares.

Because the share price is set by supply and demand, it often differs from the fund's net asset value. When the price is below net asset value, the fund trades at a discount; when above, at a premium.
For example, a closed-end fund with a net asset value of 10 per share might trade at 9, a 10% discount, giving buyers access to its investments at less than their market value.

Closed-end funds are well suited to less liquid investments, such as private companies, property or infrastructure, because the manager does not need to sell assets to meet withdrawals. Many can borrow to increase returns. Investment trusts in the United Kingdom are a well-known form of closed-end fund.

definition: A closing entry is a journal entry made at the end of an accounting period to move the balances of revenue, expense and dividend accounts into retained earnings, resetting those accounts to zero for the next period.
explanation: Revenue and expense accounts measure performance for a single period, such as a year. Once the period ends and the financial statements are prepared, these accounts need to start again from zero, so the next period's results are measured separately.

Closing entries do this. They transfer the year's total revenue and total expenses into retained earnings, the part of equity that holds profits kept in the business. Any dividends declared during the year are also closed into retained earnings.
For example, if a business had revenue of 400,000 and expenses of 340,000 during the year, closing entries reduce both accounts to zero and add the profit of 60,000 to retained earnings.

Accounts that close each period are called temporary accounts. Asset, liability and equity accounts are permanent accounts: their balances carry forward from one period to the next. In modern accounting software, closing entries are usually generated automatically at year-end.

definition: The coefficient of determination, written R-squared, is a measure of how much of the variation in a dependent variable is explained by a regression model. It ranges from 0 to 1.
explanation: R-squared shows how well a regression line fits the data. An R-squared of 0 means the model explains none of the variation; an R-squared of 1 means it explains all of it.

For simple linear regression, R-squared equals the square of the correlation coefficient. If two funds' returns have a correlation of about 0.92, the R-squared is about 0.85, meaning about 85% of the variation in one fund's returns can be explained by the other's.

In investing, R-squared is often used to show how closely a fund follows its benchmark. A fund with an R-squared of 0.95 against an index moves very much in line with that index. A low R-squared suggests the fund's performance is driven by other factors.

A high R-squared does not mean a model is correct or useful for prediction. It can be high by coincidence, especially with trending data, and adding more variables to a model always increases R-squared, even if they add no real explanatory power. Adjusted R-squared corrects for this by penalising extra variables. A low R-squared can still be meaningful in fields where outcomes are naturally noisy, such as share price movements.

definition: Cohort analysis is a method of studying groups of customers who share a common starting point, such as the month they signed up, to see how their behaviour, such as retention or spending, changes over time.
explanation: Looking at all customers together can hide important patterns. Cohort analysis separates customers by when they joined, so each group's behaviour can be tracked and compared.

For example, an app company might find that 40% of customers who joined in January are still active after six months, while 55% of those who joined in June are still active after six months. This suggests that recent product improvements have increased retention.

Cohort analysis is widely used by subscription businesses, online retailers, mobile apps and lenders. Common measures include retention rates, revenue per customer over time, repeat purchase rates and default rates for groups of loans issued in the same period.

It helps businesses judge whether growth is healthy. Total revenue can rise because many new customers are joining, even while each cohort is leaving quickly. Cohort analysis reveals this. It also shows the effects of changes in marketing, pricing or product features on new customers.

definition: Coinsurance is the percentage of medical costs that a person with health insurance pays after meeting their deductible, with the insurer paying the remaining percentage.
explanation: Coinsurance is a way of sharing costs between the insurer and the insured person. It is usually expressed as a split, such as 80/20, meaning the insurer pays 80% of covered costs and the patient pays 20%.
For example, a patient with a 20% coinsurance requirement who has already met their deductible receives a hospital bill of 1,000. The patient pays 200 and the insurer pays 800.

Coinsurance usually applies after the deductible has been paid. It continues until the patient reaches the plan's out-of-pocket maximum, after which the insurer typically pays 100% of covered costs for the rest of the year.

Unlike a copayment, which is a fixed amount, coinsurance rises with the cost of care. This can make large medical bills expensive for patients, which is why the out-of-pocket maximum is an important protection.

In property insurance, the term coinsurance has a different meaning. It refers to a clause requiring the policyholder to insure the property for a minimum percentage of its value, often 80% or more. If they insure it for less, any claim payment may be reduced in proportion.

definition: A collar is an options strategy that protects an existing holding against large losses by buying a put option and paying for it, partly or fully, by selling a call option, which limits potential gains.
explanation: A collar sets both a floor and a ceiling on the value of an investment. The put option sets the floor, giving the right to sell at a set price if the share falls. The call option sets the ceiling, obliging the investor to sell at a set price if the share rises above it.

For example, an investor owns shares trading at 50. They buy a put option with an exercise price of 45 and sell a call option with an exercise price of 60. If the share price falls to 35, the put lets them sell at 45, limiting the loss. If the share price rises to 70, they must sell at 60, giving up gains above that level. Between 45 and 60, the investor simply gains or loses along with the share.
If the premium received from selling the call equals the cost of buying the put, the collar costs nothing upfront, and is called a zero-cost collar.

Collars are used by investors who want to protect large gains, by executives holding concentrated positions in their company's shares, and by companies hedging commodity prices or currency risk. The trade-off is giving up potential upside in exchange for protection.

definition: Collateral is an asset that a borrower pledges to a lender as security for a loan. If the loan is not repaid, the lender can take the asset and sell it.
explanation: Collateral reduces the lender's risk. If the borrower defaults, the lender can recover some or all of the money by selling the pledged asset. In return, the borrower usually gets a lower interest rate or a larger loan than would otherwise be possible.

Many kinds of assets can serve as collateral. A house secures a mortgage. A car secures a car loan. Businesses may pledge equipment, inventory, property or amounts owed by customers. Some loans are secured by savings or investments.

Lenders usually lend less than the full value of the collateral to protect themselves if its value falls. For example, a bank might lend up to 80% of a property's value, so a home worth 250,000 could support a mortgage of up to 200,000. This gap gives the lender a cushion if prices drop.
For borrowers, the key point is that collateral is at risk. Missing payments on a secured loan can mean losing the asset, so it should only be pledged for borrowing that is clearly affordable.

definition: A collateralized debt obligation (CDO) is a structured investment that pools debt instruments, such as bonds, loans or mortgage-backed securities, and divides the resulting cash flows into tranches with different levels of risk and return.
explanation: A CDO is created by a special purpose vehicle that buys a portfolio of debt and funds the purchase by issuing notes to investors. Payments from the underlying debts flow to investors through a waterfall: senior tranches are paid first and are the safest, while junior tranches absorb losses first but offer higher returns.
CDOs allowed banks and investors to repackage risk, offering highly rated securities to investors who wanted safety and riskier tranches to those seeking higher yields.

Before the 2008 financial crisis, many CDOs were built from subprime mortgage-backed securities, and some were built from tranches of other CDOs. Many senior tranches received top credit ratings. When US house prices fell and mortgage defaults rose, losses spread far beyond what models predicted, and many highly rated CDO tranches suffered heavy losses.

For example, an investor holding a AAA-rated CDO tranche backed by subprime mortgage securities could have lost much of its value. CDOs backed by mortgages largely disappeared after the crisis, although related structures, such as collateralized loan obligations, remain widely used.

definition: A collateralized loan obligation (CLO) is a structured investment that pools leveraged loans to companies and divides the cash flows from them into tranches with different levels of risk and return.
explanation: A CLO is a type of collateralized debt obligation backed by a diversified portfolio of senior secured loans, typically to companies with below-investment-grade credit ratings, often owned by private equity firms. A CLO manager selects and actively manages the loans.

The CLO issues notes in tranches. Interest and principal from the loans flow to investors in order, with senior tranches paid first. Junior tranches and the equity tranche absorb losses first but receive higher returns.
For example, a CLO might hold 400 loans worth 500,000,000 in total, issuing AAA-rated notes making up about 60% of its funding, lower-rated notes for the next layers and equity at the bottom.

CLOs are major buyers of leveraged loans, providing much of the funding for leveraged buyouts. Unlike mortgage-backed CDOs, CLOs performed relatively well during the 2008 financial crisis, with very few losses on senior tranches. They include protections such as tests that divert cash to senior investors if loan quality deteriorates. Junior tranches and equity can still suffer significant losses in recessions.

definition: A collection account is an entry on a credit report, used mainly in the United States, showing that an unpaid debt has been passed to a collection agency or sold to a debt buyer.
explanation: When a borrower falls far behind on payments, the original creditor may stop trying to collect the debt itself. It may hire a collection agency to recover the money on its behalf or sell the debt outright. Once this happens, a collection account may appear on the borrower's credit report.

Collection accounts can come from many types of unpaid bills, including credit cards, medical bills, utility bills, phone contracts and personal loans. For example, an unpaid phone bill of 300 might be sent to a collection agency, which then reports the debt to the credit bureaus.

In the United States, a collection account typically remains on a credit report for seven years from the date of the first missed payment, even if the debt is later paid. Paying it off is still generally beneficial, as newer scoring models may ignore paid collections. US law, including the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, limits how collectors can contact and treat consumers.
In the United Kingdom and many other countries, the comparable situation is a defaulted account being passed to a debt collection agency, with the default recorded on the credit file.

definition: Combined leverage measures how sensitive a company's earnings per share are to changes in sales, taking account of both operating leverage and financial leverage.
explanation: Operating leverage arises from fixed operating costs: a change in sales leads to a larger percentage change in operating profit. Financial leverage arises from fixed interest costs: a change in operating profit leads to a larger percentage change in earnings for shareholders. Combined leverage brings the two together.

The degree of combined leverage is the degree of operating leverage multiplied by the degree of financial leverage. For example, if a company's degree of operating leverage is 4 and its degree of financial leverage is 2, its degree of combined leverage is 8. A 5% rise in sales would increase earnings per share by about 40%, and a 5% fall would reduce them by about 40%.

High combined leverage means profits swing sharply with sales, increasing both potential rewards and risks. Companies with high operating leverage, such as manufacturers with large fixed costs, often choose lower debt to limit their total risk.
These measures apply around a given level of sales and change as sales change, so they are best used as approximations.

definition: The combined ratio is a measure of an insurer's underwriting profitability, calculated as the sum of its claims and expenses divided by the premiums it earns, expressed as a percentage.
explanation: The combined ratio adds together the loss ratio, claims as a share of premiums, and the expense ratio, operating costs as a share of premiums.

For example, an insurer with a loss ratio of 68% and an expense ratio of 29% has a combined ratio of 97%. For every 100 of premiums, it spends 97 on claims and expenses, making an underwriting profit of 3.
A combined ratio below 100% means the insurer is making a profit from its insurance activities. Above 100% means it is paying out more than it earns in premiums, an underwriting loss.

Insurers also earn investment income from premiums held before claims are paid, so an insurer can still be profitable overall with a combined ratio somewhat above 100%, especially when interest rates are high. However, a consistently high combined ratio is a warning sign. Investors compare combined ratios across insurers and over time, keeping in mind that large catastrophes can push them sharply higher in a single year.

definition: A commercial bank is a bank that takes deposits and makes loans to individuals and businesses, providing everyday banking services such as current accounts, savings accounts, loans and payments.
explanation: Commercial banks are the type of bank most people deal with. They earn money mainly by lending at higher interest rates than they pay on deposits, and from fees for services such as account maintenance, card payments and foreign exchange.
Their customers range from individuals with savings accounts and mortgages to small businesses needing working capital loans and large companies requiring complex financing.
For example, a commercial bank might take deposits from thousands of local households and use that money to lend to a business expanding its factory, earning interest on the loan.

The term is often used to distinguish these deposit-taking, lending banks from investment banks, which focus on helping companies raise money in financial markets, advising on mergers and trading securities. Many large banking groups do both, through separate divisions.
note: Commercial banking refers to the business activity of taking deposits and making loans. It is sometimes used more narrowly to mean banking services for businesses, as opposed to retail banking for individuals.

definition: Commercial paper is a short-term, unsecured debt instrument issued by large companies and financial institutions to raise money for immediate needs, such as payroll or stock purchases.
explanation: Commercial paper typically matures within a few days to several months, rarely more than a year. It is usually issued at a discount to its face value, so the investor's return comes from receiving the full face value at maturity.

For example, a company might issue commercial paper with a face value of 1,000,000, maturing in 90 days, selling it to investors for 990,000. At maturity, investors receive 1,000,000, a return of 10,000.

Because commercial paper is unsecured, only companies with strong credit ratings can issue it at attractive rates. Buyers include money market funds, other companies and institutional investors looking for safe, short-term places to put cash.

Commercial paper is often cheaper than bank loans for highly rated companies. However, the market can dry up during periods of financial stress, as happened during the 2008 financial crisis and in early 2020, when central banks intervened to support it. Companies issuing commercial paper often maintain backup credit lines with banks in case they cannot roll over their paper when it matures.

definition: A commodity derivative is a financial contract whose value depends on the price of a commodity, such as oil, natural gas, metals or agricultural products.
explanation: Commodity derivatives include futures, forwards, options and swaps. They allow producers, consumers and investors to manage or take on exposure to commodity prices without necessarily handling the physical goods.

Producers use them to lock in selling prices, protecting against falls. Consumers lock in buying prices, protecting against rises. For example, an airline might buy oil futures or swaps to fix the price of a portion of its future fuel purchases, while a farmer might sell wheat futures to lock in a price before harvest.

Investors and speculators use commodity derivatives to gain exposure to commodity prices, diversify portfolios or profit from expected price movements. Many commodity funds hold futures rather than physical commodities.

Commodity derivatives are traded on exchanges, such as major futures exchanges in Chicago, New York and London, and over the counter. Prices can be very volatile, affected by weather, geopolitical events, supply disruptions and economic growth. Positions often involve leverage, magnifying gains and losses.

definition: Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) is the highest-quality form of bank capital, made up mainly of ordinary shares and retained earnings, after deductions for items such as goodwill, and is used to absorb losses while a bank continues operating.
explanation: Under the Basel framework, bank capital is divided into tiers by quality. CET1 is the core, because it is permanent, has no obligation to pay dividends and is the first to absorb losses.

The key measure is the CET1 ratio, which compares CET1 capital with the bank's risk-weighted assets. For example, a bank with 12,000,000,000 of CET1 capital and 100,000,000,000 of risk-weighted assets has a CET1 ratio of 12%.

Under Basel III, banks must maintain a minimum CET1 ratio of 4.5%, plus a capital conservation buffer of 2.5%, giving 7% in total. Larger and systemically important banks face additional buffers, and national regulators may add further requirements based on stress tests or economic conditions.

The CET1 ratio is one of the most closely watched measures of a bank's financial strength. A bank that falls below its required buffers faces restrictions on paying dividends, buying back shares and paying bonuses until it rebuilds its capital.

definition: A common resource is a good that is rivalrous, meaning one person's use reduces what is available to others, but non-excludable, meaning it is hard to stop people from using it. Examples include ocean fish, groundwater and clean air.
explanation: Because no one can easily be prevented from using a common resource, and each person's use leaves less for others, these resources are at risk of being overused. This problem is known as the tragedy of the commons.

Consider a lake where anyone can fish. Each fisher gains by catching as many fish as possible. But if everyone does this, the fish population collapses and everyone loses. Each person bears only a small part of the cost of overfishing, while gaining the full benefit of their own catch.
Other examples include overgrazing on shared land, overuse of groundwater and pollution of the atmosphere.

Solutions usually involve some form of rules or ownership. Governments may set quotas, such as limits on fishing catches, charge fees or taxes for use, issue tradable permits or assign property rights. Communities can also manage shared resources successfully through local rules and cooperation. The goal is to make users take account of the cost their use imposes on others.

definition: Common stock is the standard type of company ownership. It gives holders voting rights and a share of profits, but they are paid last if the company is wound up.
explanation: Most shares issued and traded on stock markets are common stock. Holders typically get one vote per share on major decisions, such as electing the board of directors, and may receive dividends when the company chooses to pay them.

Common stockholders have the most to gain if a company does well, because they own whatever value remains after all other claims are paid. If profits grow, the share price can rise substantially. They also bear the most risk. Dividends are not guaranteed, and in a bankruptcy, common stockholders are paid only after lenders, bondholders and preferred stockholders, often receiving nothing.
For example, if a company is sold for 500 million and owes 400 million to lenders and 50 million to preferred stockholders, common stockholders share the remaining 50 million.
Common stock differs from preferred stock, which usually pays a fixed dividend and has priority over common stock but typically has no voting rights.
note: Ordinary share is the term used in the United Kingdom and many other countries for common stock. The two mean the same thing.

definition: Common-size analysis expresses every line of a financial statement as a percentage of a single base figure, such as revenue for the income statement or total assets for the balance sheet.
explanation: Common-size statements remove the effect of size, so companies of very different scale, or the same company in different years, can be compared directly.

On a common-size income statement, revenue is set at 100% and every other line is shown as a percentage of it. For example, if revenue is 2 million and cost of goods sold is 1.2 million, cost of goods sold is 60% of revenue, leaving a gross margin of 40%. If operating expenses are 500,000, they are 25%, and operating income is 15%.

On a common-size balance sheet, each asset, liability and equity item is shown as a percentage of total assets. This reveals, for instance, how much of a company's assets are tied up in inventory or how much of its funding comes from debt.
Comparing common-size statements of two competitors might show that one spends 30% of revenue on marketing while the other spends 18%, or that one carries far more inventory relative to its size.
Common-size analysis is closely related to vertical analysis. Both focus on the structure of the statements rather than on changes over time.

definition: Comparable company analysis is a valuation method that estimates a company's value by comparing it with similar publicly traded companies, using valuation multiples such as price-to-earnings or EV/EBITDA.
explanation: The idea is that similar businesses should be valued in similar ways. If comparable companies are valued at around ten times their EBITDA, a company with similar characteristics might be worth roughly ten times its own EBITDA.

The process involves choosing a group of comparable companies, often called a peer group, based on factors such as industry, size, growth, profitability and geography. Their market values are then compared with financial measures to calculate multiples. Finally, those multiples are applied to the target company's figures.

For example, if a group of similar software companies trades at an average of 8 times EV/Revenue and the target company has revenue of 50 million, its enterprise value might be estimated at about 400 million.

The method is quick and grounded in actual market prices. Its weaknesses are that truly comparable companies can be hard to find, and if the whole market is overvalued or undervalued, the result will be too. Analysts therefore usually use it alongside other methods, such as discounted cash flow analysis.
note: Trading comparables, often called trading comps, is another name for comparable company analysis. The word "trading" refers to the fact that the peer companies' shares trade publicly.

definition: Comparative advantage is the ability of a country, business or person to produce a good or service at a lower opportunity cost than others, meaning they give up less of other things to produce it.
explanation: The idea, developed by economist David Ricardo in the early nineteenth century, explains why trade can benefit everyone involved, even when one party is better at producing everything.

For example, suppose Country A can produce either 10 cars or 20 tonnes of wheat with the same resources, while Country B can produce either 2 cars or 10 tonnes of wheat. Country A is better at producing both. But for Country A, each car costs 2 tonnes of wheat, while for Country B, each car costs 5 tonnes. Country A has a comparative advantage in cars, and Country B, where a tonne of wheat costs only a fifth of a car instead of half a car, has a comparative advantage in wheat.
If each country specialises in what it produces at the lowest opportunity cost and they trade, total output increases and both can end up with more than they could produce alone.

Comparative advantage is a foundation of the case for free trade. In practice, the gains from trade are not always evenly distributed within countries, and some workers and industries may lose out when trade increases.

definition: Competition policy is the set of laws and enforcement actions designed to keep markets competitive, by preventing practices such as cartels, abuse of market dominance and mergers that would significantly reduce competition.
explanation: Competitive markets tend to deliver lower prices, better quality and more innovation for consumers. Competition policy protects these benefits by stopping businesses from restricting competition.

Its main areas include banning cartels, in which competitors agree to fix prices, share markets or rig bids; preventing dominant companies from abusing their position, for example by excluding rivals unfairly; reviewing mergers and acquisitions, and blocking or imposing conditions on those that would harm competition; and, in some regions, controlling government subsidies to businesses.
For example, a competition authority might block a merger between the two largest suppliers in a market, or fine companies that secretly agreed to keep prices high.

In the United States, competition law is called antitrust law, based on laws such as the Sherman Act of 1890. In the European Union, it is enforced by the European Commission, and most countries have their own competition authorities. Applying competition rules to large digital platforms has become a major focus.
note: Antitrust is the term used in the United States for competition policy and law.

definition: A competitive advantage is a feature or capability that allows a business to outperform its rivals, for example by offering better value, charging higher prices or operating at lower cost.
explanation: In a competitive market, profits tend to attract rivals, who compete them away. A competitive advantage helps a business protect its profits.

Advantages can come from many sources. A business might have lower costs because of scale, efficient processes or access to cheap resources. It might offer a better or more distinctive product, through quality, design, technology or brand reputation. It might have a strong location, valuable patents, exclusive contracts, a loyal customer base or a network that rivals cannot easily copy.

For example, a large supermarket chain can negotiate lower prices from suppliers because it buys in enormous quantities, allowing it to offer lower prices than smaller rivals while still making a profit.

The most valuable competitive advantages are sustainable: hard for competitors to copy or overcome over long periods. Temporary advantages, such as a new product feature that rivals soon match, may not provide lasting benefits. Investors pay close attention to whether a company's advantage is likely to last, because it strongly affects long-term profitability.

definition: A complementary good is a product that is typically used together with another, so that demand for one depends on demand for the other, such as printers and ink or cars and petrol.
explanation: When two goods are complements, a rise in the price of one tends to reduce demand for the other. If cars become more expensive, fewer people buy them, which also reduces demand for petrol, tyres and car insurance. This gives complementary goods a negative cross-price elasticity.
Other examples include smartphones and apps, coffee machines and coffee pods, tennis rackets and tennis balls, and flights and hotel rooms.

Businesses often use complements in their pricing strategies. A company may sell a games console at a low price, even at a loss, to build a large base of customers who will then buy profitable games. Printer manufacturers have often sold printers cheaply and earned more from ink cartridges.
Understanding complements also helps businesses predict demand. A rise in new home sales, for example, is likely to increase demand for furniture, appliances and home improvement products.

definition: Completion accounts are financial statements prepared shortly after an acquisition completes, showing the business's actual cash, debt and working capital at the completion date, used to calculate the final purchase price.
explanation: In acquisitions using completion accounts, the price paid at completion is based on estimates. Completion accounts determine the actual figures, and the price is adjusted up or down accordingly.

Usually, the buyer prepares draft completion accounts within a set period after completion, often 60 to 90 days. The seller reviews them and can dispute items. Disagreements that cannot be resolved are often referred to an independent accountant.
For example, the estimated price assumed cash of 5,000,000, but completion accounts show cash of 5,600,000. The buyer pays the seller an additional 600,000.

Completion accounts give buyers protection, because they pay for what they actually receive. However, they create uncertainty for sellers about the final price, take time to prepare and can lead to disputes over accounting policies. The agreement should define clearly how each item is calculated. In the United States, the same approach is usually described as a closing balance sheet with a purchase price adjustment.

definition: The compound annual growth rate (CAGR) is the steady yearly growth rate that would take a value from its starting point to its ending point over a number of years, assuming growth compounds each year.
explanation: Real growth is rarely smooth. A company's revenue might jump 20% one year and only 2% the next. CAGR smooths out these ups and downs into a single average annual rate that accounts for compounding.

For example, if revenue grows from 100 million to 150 million over four years, the total increase is 50%. Dividing by four would suggest 12.5% a year, but that ignores compounding. The CAGR is about 10.7%, because 100 million growing at 10.7% a year for four years reaches 150 million.

CAGR is widely used to compare the growth of companies, investments, markets or economies over the same period. An investment that grew from 10,000 to about 16,100 over five years has a CAGR of about 10%.

CAGR hides the path taken. Two investments with the same CAGR may have had very different ups and downs along the way. It also depends heavily on the start and end points chosen, so it is worth checking the period used.

definition: Compound interest is interest calculated on your original money and on the interest it has already earned, so your balance grows a little faster each period.
explanation: Interest is added to your balance at regular intervals, and the next round of interest is calculated on that new, larger balance. Simple interest, by contrast, only ever pays on the original amount.

Suppose you save 100 at 10% a year. In the first year you earn 10 and have 110. In the second year you earn 11 and have 121. In the third year you earn 12.10 and have 133.10. The rate stays at 10%, but the interest you earn grows every year because each year starts from a bigger balance.

Compounding works faster with a higher interest rate, with more frequent compounding, such as monthly instead of yearly, and, most of all, with more time. The effect looks small in the first few years but becomes the main source of growth over decades.
Compounding also works against borrowers. When interest on a loan or credit card is not paid off, it is added to the debt, and you are then charged interest on that interest too.

definition: Compounding frequency is how often interest is calculated and added to a balance, such as yearly, quarterly, monthly or daily.
explanation: When interest compounds, it is added to the balance and then starts earning interest itself. The more often this happens, the sooner each bit of interest begins earning more, so the balance grows slightly faster.

Take 10,000 at a stated rate of 12% a year. With yearly compounding, interest is added once and the balance after one year is 11,200. With monthly compounding, 1% is added each month, and the balance after a year is about 11,268. With daily compounding, it is about 11,275.
