It typically covers the target market and customer segments, the value proposition and messaging, pricing and packaging, sales channels, such as direct sales, online self-service, partners or retailers, and marketing tactics to generate demand.

For example, a software company might decide to target mid-sized manufacturers, offer a free trial, sell through an online sign-up for small customers and a sales team for larger accounts, and generate leads through industry events and online content.

GTM strategies are used for new companies, new products and expansion into new markets. A good strategy helps keep customer acquisition costs under control and speeds up growth. Companies often test and adjust their GTM approach as they learn which channels and messages work best.

definition: A government bond is a bond issued by a national government to borrow money, paying regular interest and repaying the face value at maturity.
explanation: Governments issue bonds to fund spending that is not covered by taxes, such as infrastructure, public services or budget deficits. Investors lend money to the government by buying these bonds.

Bonds issued by financially stable governments in their own currency are generally considered among the safest investments, because such governments are very unlikely to fail to pay. For that reason, the yields on these bonds are often used as the risk-free rate in financial calculations. Examples include US Treasury securities, UK gilts and German government bonds.

Not all government bonds are equally safe. Governments with large debts, weak economies or political instability, or those that borrow in a foreign currency, may have to pay much higher interest rates to attract investors, and some have defaulted in the past.

Government bond yields are an important signal in financial markets. They influence mortgage rates, corporate borrowing costs and the valuation of shares. The difference between yields on short-term and long-term government bonds forms the yield curve, which is closely watched as an indicator of economic expectations.
note: A sovereign bond means the same as a government bond issued by a national government. The term "sovereign" is often used when discussing a country's creditworthiness or bonds issued in foreign currencies.

definition: Government debt is the total amount of money a government owes to its creditors, accumulated from past budget deficits.
explanation: Governments borrow by issuing bonds and other securities, which are bought by domestic and foreign investors, banks, pension funds, insurance companies and central banks. Government debt is also called public debt, national debt or sovereign debt.

Debt builds up over time. Each year's budget deficit adds to the total, while a surplus can reduce it. For example, a government that runs a deficit of 50 billion every year for ten years will add around 500 billion to its debt, plus the interest owed.

Government debt allows governments to fund spending without immediately raising taxes, smooth out the effects of recessions and invest in long-term projects. Governments that borrow in their own currency and have strong institutions can often sustain high levels of debt.

High debt has potential drawbacks. Interest payments take up a growing share of the budget, leaving less for other spending. If investors lose confidence, borrowing costs can rise sharply, leading to a debt crisis. Debt levels are usually assessed relative to the size of the economy, using the debt-to-GDP ratio.

definition: A government grant is assistance from a government, in the form of money or other resources, given to a business in return for meeting certain conditions, such as investing in a region, creating jobs or carrying out research.
explanation: Governments offer grants to encourage activities that they want more of, such as building factories in disadvantaged areas, training workers, developing green technology or carrying out research. Grants differ from loans because they usually do not need to be repaid, as long as the conditions are met.

Under IFRS, a grant is recognised only when there is reasonable assurance that the company will meet the conditions and receive it. It is then recognised in profit over the periods in which the related costs are recognised, rather than all at once.

For example, a company receives a grant of 1,000,000 towards a machine with a ten-year life. It recognises grant income of 100,000 a year, matching the depreciation on the machine, either as income or by reducing the asset's cost.

If conditions are breached, the grant may have to be repaid, and the company must record a liability. US GAAP has no single standard for grants to businesses, although newer disclosure requirements apply, and many companies follow approaches similar to IFRS.

definition: Government spending is the money spent by national, regional and local governments on goods, services, investment and transfers, such as healthcare, education, defence, infrastructure, pensions and welfare.
explanation: Government spending can be divided into several categories. Purchases of goods and services, such as salaries for teachers and soldiers and spending on equipment, count directly in GDP. Public investment, such as roads, schools and hospitals, adds to the country's capital. Transfer payments, such as pensions and unemployment benefits, redistribute income but do not count directly in GDP. Interest on government debt is another major item.
For example, a government might spend a large share of its budget on social protection, health and education, with smaller amounts on defence, transport and public order.
Government spending is a key part of fiscal policy. Increasing spending can support demand during recessions, while cutting spending can help reduce deficits.

The level of government spending as a share of GDP varies widely between countries, reflecting different choices about the role of the state. Debates about spending often focus on its efficiency, how it is financed and its effects on growth and inequality.

definition: A grace period is a set length of time after a payment is due, or after a purchase is made, during which no interest or penalty is charged.
explanation: On many credit cards, the grace period is the time between the end of a billing cycle and the payment due date. If you pay the full statement balance by the due date, you are not charged interest on purchases made during that cycle. This can give you several weeks of interest-free borrowing on everyday purchases.

The grace period usually applies only if the full balance is paid. If you carry part of the balance into the next month, interest is often charged and the grace period may be lost on new purchases until the balance is cleared. Cash withdrawals on credit cards usually have no grace period at all.

Loans and bills can also have grace periods. A loan agreement might allow payment up to ten days after the due date before a late fee is added. Student loans in some countries have a grace period after graduation before repayments begin.
Grace periods are helpful, but they are not extensions without consequences in every case. It is always worth checking exactly how long the period lasts and what conditions apply.

definition: Grant income is the amount of a government or other grant that a business or organisation recognises as income in a particular period.
explanation: Grants are usually not recognised as income as soon as the cash arrives. Instead, under accounting standards such as IFRS, grant income is matched with the costs the grant is intended to cover.

Grants related to income, such as a grant towards training costs or wages, are recognised over the period in which those costs are incurred. Grants related to assets, such as a grant towards buying equipment, are recognised over the asset's useful life, either as income or by reducing depreciation.

For example, a company receives a grant of 60,000 to cover the wages of three apprentices for one year. It recognises grant income of 5,000 a month as the wages are paid, rather than 60,000 when the money arrives.

Grant income is especially important for charities, universities and research organisations, which often depend heavily on grants. These organisations may follow their own accounting rules, distinguishing restricted grants, which must be spent on specific purposes, from unrestricted ones.

definition: The Greeks are a set of measures, named after Greek letters, that show how sensitive an option's price is to changes in factors such as the underlying asset's price, time, volatility and interest rates.
explanation: Option prices change for several reasons at once. The Greeks break these down, helping traders understand and manage the risks in their positions.

Delta measures how much an option's price changes when the underlying asset's price changes by one unit. Gamma measures how much delta itself changes as the asset's price moves. Theta measures how much an option's value declines as each day passes, known as time decay. Vega measures how much the option's price changes when implied volatility changes by one percentage point. Rho measures sensitivity to changes in interest rates.

For example, an option with a delta of 0.5, a theta of −0.04 and a vega of 0.10 would be expected to rise by about 0.50 if the share price rises by 1, lose about 0.04 in value each day if nothing else changes, and gain about 0.10 if implied volatility rises by one percentage point.

Professional traders use the Greeks to hedge their positions, for example keeping a portfolio's overall delta close to zero so that it is not exposed to small movements in the underlying asset's price. The Greeks are estimates that change constantly as market conditions change.

definition: Greenwashing is making misleading or exaggerated claims about how environmentally friendly a company, product or investment is.
explanation: As demand for sustainable products and investments has grown, so has the temptation to overstate green credentials. Greenwashing can involve vague claims such as eco-friendly without evidence, highlighting a small green initiative while ignoring a much larger environmental impact, or labelling investment funds as sustainable when their holdings differ little from conventional funds.
For example, a fund marketed as focused on climate solutions might hold large positions in companies with high carbon emissions and little evidence of transition plans.
Greenwashing misleads consumers and investors, and undermines trust in genuine sustainable efforts.

Regulators in several regions have introduced rules to tackle it. These include rules on how sustainable investment funds can be labelled and what they must disclose in the European Union and the United Kingdom, and enforcement actions against firms that misrepresented their environmental practices. Investors can reduce the risk of being misled by checking a fund's actual holdings, its stated methods and independent assessments.

definition: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country over a period, usually a quarter or a year. It is the most widely used measure of the size of an economy.
explanation: GDP adds up everything an economy produces, from cars and houses to haircuts and software, counting only final products to avoid double counting. The flour sold to a baker is not counted separately; its value is included in the price of the bread.

GDP can be measured in three ways that should give the same answer: by adding up production across industries, by adding up spending on final goods and services, and by adding up incomes earned. The spending approach is the most familiar: consumer spending, plus business investment, plus government spending, plus exports minus imports.

GDP growth is reported as a percentage. If an economy's output rises from 2,000 billion to 2,050 billion in a year, nominal GDP has grown by 2.5%. Economists usually focus on real GDP, which removes the effect of inflation, to see whether the economy is actually producing more.

GDP per person is often used to compare living standards across countries. However, GDP has limits: it does not capture unpaid work, inequality, environmental damage or wellbeing, so it is best used alongside other measures.

definition: Gross income is total income before any taxes or deductions are taken out. For an employee, it is the full salary and other pay agreed with the employer.
explanation: Gross income is the starting figure in almost every income calculation. If a job is advertised at 50,000 a year, that is gross income. The amount that actually reaches your bank account will be lower, because income tax, social security contributions and sometimes pension contributions are deducted first.

For an employee, gross income usually includes basic pay, overtime, bonuses, commissions and some taxable benefits. Someone earning a salary of 48,000 plus a bonus of 4,000 has gross employment income of 52,000 for the year.

For a business, the phrase "gross income" can mean something slightly different. It is often used for revenue minus the cost of goods sold, which accountants usually call gross profit. Always check which meaning is intended.

Lenders often ask for gross income when deciding how much you can borrow, and many affordability ratios, such as debt-to-income, are calculated using it. Budgeting, however, is better done on net income, because that is the money you actually have to spend.

definition: Gross margin is gross profit expressed as a percentage of revenue. It shows how much of each unit of sales is left after paying the direct costs of the goods or services sold.
explanation: Gross margin is calculated by dividing gross profit by revenue. If a company sells products for 1,000,000 and their direct cost is 650,000, its gross profit is 350,000 and its gross margin is 35%. In other words, for every 100 of sales, 35 is left to pay for overheads and contribute to profit.

Gross margins vary widely between industries. Software companies often have very high gross margins, because extra copies cost little to produce. Supermarkets usually have low gross margins but make up for it with high sales volumes.

Changes in gross margin over time are revealing. A falling margin can signal rising costs, price competition or a shift towards lower-margin products. A rising margin can indicate stronger pricing power or better production efficiency.
In everyday conversation, "gross margin" is sometimes used to mean the gross profit amount rather than the percentage, so it is worth checking which is meant.

definition: Gross merchandise value is the total value of goods or services sold through a marketplace or platform over a period, before deducting fees, discounts, returns or other costs.
explanation: Gross merchandise value, often shortened to GMV, is widely used by online marketplaces, e-commerce platforms, travel booking sites and delivery apps to show the scale of activity happening on their platform.

It is important to understand that GMV is not the company's revenue. A marketplace usually keeps only a small share of each transaction as fees or commissions. For example, if a marketplace processes 500 million of sales in a year and charges an average commission of 12%, its GMV is 500 million but its revenue is about 60 million.
The share of GMV that a platform keeps as revenue is sometimes called the take rate. In this example, the take rate is 12%.

GMV is useful for tracking a platform's growth and market share. However, because it is much larger than revenue and does not reflect profitability, it can make a business look bigger than it really is. Investors therefore look at GMV alongside revenue, take rate, profitability and customer measures to judge the health of a marketplace business.

definition: Gross national product (GNP) is the total value of goods and services produced by a country's residents and businesses, whether located at home or abroad, over a period.
explanation: Gross domestic product measures production within a country's borders, regardless of who owns the businesses or workers involved. GNP instead focuses on ownership: it measures production by a country's residents, wherever it takes place.

GNP can be calculated as GDP plus income earned by residents from abroad, such as profits from overseas investments and wages earned by residents working abroad, minus income paid to foreign residents from domestic production.
For example, if a country's GDP is 2,000, its residents earn 50 from abroad and foreign investors earn 80 from the country, its GNP is 1,970.

For most large economies, GDP and GNP are close. The difference can be large for countries with major foreign investment or many workers abroad. Ireland, for instance, hosts many multinational companies, so its GDP is much larger than the income retained by residents. Today, most statistical agencies publish gross national income, which is essentially the same concept, and GDP has become the more widely used headline measure.

definition: Gross profit is the money left from revenue after subtracting the direct cost of the goods or services sold.
explanation: Gross profit shows how much a business earns from its core product before paying for overheads such as rent, salaries, marketing and administration. It is calculated as revenue minus cost of goods sold.

For example, a clothing retailer with sales of 800,000 and cost of goods sold of 480,000 has a gross profit of 320,000. That 320,000 must then cover all its other costs, such as staff, shop rent and advertising, with anything left over becoming operating profit.

Gross profit is a useful measure of how efficiently a business produces or buys what it sells, and how much pricing power it has. If suppliers raise prices and the business cannot pass them on, gross profit shrinks.

Because absolute amounts are hard to compare between businesses of different sizes, gross profit is often expressed as a percentage of revenue, called gross margin. In this example, the gross margin is 40%.

definition: Gross revenue retention (GRR) is the percentage of recurring revenue a company keeps from its existing customers over a period after downgrades and cancellations, ignoring any expansion revenue.
explanation: GRR measures how well a company holds on to the revenue it already has. Because upgrades and expansion are excluded, it can never exceed 100%.
It is calculated by taking recurring revenue from existing customers at the start of the period, subtracting revenue lost from downgrades and cancellations, and dividing by the starting revenue.

For example, a company starts the year with 10,000,000 of annual recurring revenue. It loses 500,000 through downgrades and 700,000 through cancellations. Its GRR is 8.8 million divided by 10 million, or 88%.

GRR complements net revenue retention. A company may have strong NRR because a few customers expanded a lot, while still losing many others. GRR reveals this underlying loss. A high GRR suggests customers find the product essential and are unlikely to leave. It is particularly important for judging the stability of a subscription business's revenue base.

definition: A growing annuity is a series of cash flows paid at regular intervals for a fixed number of periods, with each payment increasing at a constant rate.
explanation: A growing annuity is similar to an ordinary annuity, which pays the same amount each period, except that the payments grow over time. It is useful for valuing cash flows that are expected to rise with inflation or business growth for a set period.
For example, an investment pays 100 at the end of the first year, with payments growing at 3% a year for ten years. With a discount rate of 8%, the present value of these payments is about 755.

Growing annuities are used in many financial calculations, including valuing pensions that increase with inflation, leases with rising rents, salaries in personal financial planning and the forecast-period cash flows of a business that is expected to grow steadily.

A growing annuity can also be thought of as the difference between two growing perpetuities: one starting now, and one starting at the end of the annuity's life. This is why the formulas are closely related. As with growing perpetuities, the result is sensitive to the assumptions about both the discount rate and the growth rate.

definition: A growing perpetuity is a series of cash flows that continues forever and increases at a constant rate each period.
explanation: A growing perpetuity is a theoretical concept, since nothing truly lasts forever, but it is extremely useful in valuation. Its present value has a simple solution: the first cash flow divided by the difference between the discount rate and the growth rate.
For example, if an investment will pay 100 next year, growing by 3% a year forever, and the appropriate discount rate is 8%, its present value is 100 divided by 5%, or 2,000.

The growing perpetuity is the basis of the Gordon growth model, which values shares as a stream of dividends growing at a constant rate. It is also used to calculate the terminal value in a discounted cash flow model, representing the value of all cash flows beyond the forecast period.

The formula only works when the growth rate is lower than the discount rate. Results are very sensitive to both inputs. In the example above, raising the growth rate from 3% to 4% increases the value from 2,000 to 2,500. For this reason, analysts usually use conservative long-term growth rates, often close to expected inflation or long-term economic growth.

definition: Growth capex is capital spending aimed at expanding a company's capacity, entering new markets or adding new products and capabilities, rather than just maintaining existing operations.
explanation: Growth capex is investment in the future. It includes building new factories, opening new stores, adding production lines, buying additional equipment to serve more customers and investing in new technology platforms.
For example, a coffee chain that spends 50 million opening 100 new stores is making growth capex. Replacing espresso machines in existing stores would be maintenance capex.

Growth capex reduces free cash flow in the short term, but it is expected to generate higher revenues and profits later. Fast-growing companies often have high growth capex and low or negative free cash flow, even if their underlying businesses are healthy.

Investors try to separate growth capex from maintenance capex to understand a company's true earning power. A company with large free cash flow after maintenance capex, but low free cash flow after growth capex, may be investing heavily for future growth rather than struggling.

The value of growth capex depends on the returns it generates. Investments that earn more than the company's cost of capital create value, while those that earn less destroy it, even if they make the company bigger.

definition: Growth equity is a type of private equity investment in established, growing companies that need capital to expand, typically in exchange for a minority ownership stake.
explanation: Growth equity sits between venture capital and traditional buyouts. The companies are usually more mature than typical venture-backed start-ups, often with significant revenue and proven business models, and sometimes already profitable. But unlike buyouts, growth equity investors usually do not take full control or use large amounts of debt.
Companies use growth equity to expand into new markets, develop new products, make acquisitions or allow early shareholders and founders to sell part of their stakes.
For example, a profitable software company growing quickly might sell a 25% stake to a growth equity firm to fund international expansion, while its founders keep control.

Growth equity is generally considered less risky than venture capital, because the companies are more established, but it offers higher growth potential than many buyouts of mature businesses. Investors typically seek protections such as board representation and certain rights over major decisions.
Growth equity investors aim to exit within several years, through a sale of the company, a stock market listing or a sale of their stake to another investor.

definition: Growth investing is an investment strategy focused on buying shares of companies expected to grow their revenues and earnings faster than average, even if their shares look expensive by traditional measures.
explanation: Growth investors are willing to pay high prices relative to current earnings because they expect strong future growth to justify the valuation. They look for companies with expanding markets, innovative products, competitive advantages and strong management.

Typical growth investments include companies in technology, healthcare and consumer sectors that are gaining market share quickly. Many reinvest most of their profits, so they pay little or no dividends.
For example, a growth investor might buy shares in a software company trading at 60 times earnings because its revenue is growing 35% a year and it is expected to dominate a large market.

Growth investing can deliver exceptional returns when investors correctly identify companies that sustain rapid growth for many years. But it carries significant risks. High valuations leave little room for disappointment, so if growth slows, share prices can fall sharply. Growth stocks are also often more sensitive to rising interest rates.
Growth investing is often contrasted with value investing. Historically, each style has outperformed the other for long periods, and many investors hold a mix of both.

definition: A growth stock is a share in a company expected to grow its sales and earnings faster than the overall market, often valued at a high price relative to its current profits.
explanation: Growth companies typically reinvest most of their profits into expansion, research and new products, rather than paying dividends. Investors buy them expecting that rapid future growth will lead to rising share prices.

Growth stocks are often found in technology, healthcare and other innovative sectors, although any company with strong expansion prospects can be one. They usually have high price-to-earnings and price-to-sales ratios, because investors are paying for expected future profits rather than current ones.
For example, a company growing revenue at 30% a year might trade at 50 times its earnings, while a mature company growing at 3% might trade at 12 times earnings.

Growth stocks can deliver large returns if the company meets or exceeds expectations. But they can be volatile and especially sensitive to changes in interest rates, because much of their value depends on profits expected far in the future. If growth slows or expectations fall, their share prices can drop sharply.
Growth stocks are often contrasted with value stocks, which trade at lower prices relative to their current earnings or assets.

definition: A guarantor is a person or organisation that promises to repay a debt if the main borrower fails to do so.
explanation: A guarantor provides a backstop for the lender. They do not usually make the regular payments, but if the borrower defaults, the lender can turn to the guarantor to recover the money. Guarantors are common for rental agreements, student loans, small business loans and loans to people with limited credit history.

The difference from a cosigner is mainly one of timing and role. A cosigner is typically a joint borrower, equally responsible from the start. A guarantor is usually called upon only after the borrower has failed to pay. In practice, the exact responsibilities depend on the contract and on local law, so the wording of the agreement matters.
In business, company owners are often asked to provide a personal guarantee for a company loan. This means that if the business cannot repay, the owner's personal assets may be at risk.
Becoming a guarantor is a serious commitment. A guarantor should understand the full amount they could be asked to pay, for how long the guarantee lasts and whether it can be ended.

definition: A hard landing is when efforts to slow an overheating economy, usually by raising interest rates, lead to a sharp slowdown or recession, with falling output and rising unemployment.
explanation: When central banks raise interest rates to fight inflation, they aim to cool demand gradually. If they tighten too much, or if other shocks occur at the same time, the economy may slow more sharply than intended.
A hard landing typically involves falling output, rising unemployment, declining business investment and weaker consumer spending. It may bring inflation down, but at a significant cost.

For example, in the early 1980s, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates to very high levels to defeat double-digit inflation. Inflation fell dramatically, but the economy suffered a deep recession with unemployment above 10%.

The term is also used for rapidly growing economies that slow abruptly, for example if a property or credit boom ends suddenly. The risk of a hard landing is one reason central banks often prefer to raise interest rates gradually and communicate their plans clearly, giving households and businesses time to adjust.

definition: The harmonic mean is a type of average calculated by dividing the number of values by the sum of their reciprocals. It is useful for averaging rates and ratios.
explanation: The harmonic mean gives the correct average in situations where values are rates, such as speeds, prices per unit or ratios, and the quantity being held constant is the one in the numerator.

A simple example is travel speed. If you drive 120 kilometres to a city at 60 kilometres per hour and return the same distance at 40 kilometres per hour, your average speed is not 50. The trip there takes 2 hours and the trip back 3 hours, so you travel 240 kilometres in 5 hours, an average of 48 kilometres per hour. That is the harmonic mean of 60 and 40.

In finance, the harmonic mean is used when averaging valuation multiples, such as price-to-earnings ratios across a group of companies, because it reduces the influence of very high multiples. It also applies to pound-cost or dollar-cost averaging: if you invest the same amount of money at regular intervals, the average price you pay per share is the harmonic mean of the prices, which is lower than their arithmetic mean.
For any set of positive values that are not all equal, the harmonic mean is lower than the geometric mean, which is lower than the arithmetic mean.

definition: A headcount forecast is a plan of how many employees a business expects to have over a future period, by team or role, and what they will cost.
explanation: Staff are often a company's largest expense, especially in service and technology businesses. A headcount forecast shows how many people will be employed each month, when new hires will start and what salaries, benefits and taxes will add up to.

The forecast usually starts with current staff, then adds planned hires and expected departures. Each role is assigned a start date and an annual cost, including salary, employer taxes, benefits and other related costs such as equipment.
For example, a company planning to hire five engineers in March at a total annual cost of 90,000 each would add about 37,500 a month to staff costs from March onwards.

Headcount forecasts link directly to revenue plans, because more sales often require more staff, and to cash flow forecasts, because wages must be paid every month. They also help managers plan recruitment, office space and training. Because hiring often takes longer than expected, comparing planned with actual headcount is a regular part of financial reviews.

definition: Health insurance is insurance that pays for some or all of the cost of medical care, such as doctors' visits, hospital stays, surgery and medicines, in exchange for regular premiums.
explanation: Health insurance protects people from the high and unpredictable costs of illness and injury. How it works varies greatly between countries.

In many countries, including the United Kingdom, Canada and most of Europe, governments provide or fund healthcare for all residents through taxes or compulsory social insurance, and private health insurance is optional, often used for faster access or extra services. In the United States, many people get private health insurance through their employer, while government programmes such as Medicare and Medicaid cover older people and those on low incomes.

Private health insurance policies usually involve several cost-sharing features. The policyholder pays a premium, and may also pay a deductible before cover begins, a fixed copayment for certain services, and a percentage of costs called coinsurance. Many policies, particularly in the United States, include an out-of-pocket maximum that caps the total amount the policyholder pays in a year.

For example, a policy might cover most hospital costs after the policyholder pays a deductible of 1,000. Policies differ widely in which doctors and hospitals are included, which treatments are covered and what exclusions apply.

definition: Hedging is taking a position in one investment or contract to reduce the risk of losses in another, much like buying insurance against an unfavourable price movement.
explanation: A hedge works by offsetting risk. If the main position loses value, the hedge gains value, or at least limits the loss.

Businesses hedge to make their costs and revenues more predictable. An airline might buy fuel futures to lock in the price of jet fuel for the coming year. If fuel prices rise, the airline pays more for fuel but gains on the futures, so its overall cost stays roughly the same. An exporter expecting payment in a foreign currency might use a forward contract to fix the exchange rate in advance.
Investors also hedge. Someone holding shares worth 50,000 might buy put options that rise in value if the shares fall, limiting their potential loss.

For example, a European company due to receive 1 million US dollars in six months could agree a forward exchange rate of 1.10 dollars per euro today. Whatever happens to the exchange rate, it will receive about 909,000 euros.

Hedging has costs, such as option premiums or fees, and it usually limits potential gains as well as losses. If prices move favourably, the hedger gives up some of the benefit. The aim of hedging is not to make money but to reduce uncertainty.

definition: Herding is the tendency of investors to follow what other investors are doing, rather than relying on their own analysis, which can push prices further and faster than fundamentals justify.
explanation: People often feel safer doing what others do, especially when they are uncertain. In markets, this can lead investors to buy because prices are rising and others are buying, or sell because others are selling.

For example, during a speculative boom in a popular technology or asset, many investors buy simply because prices keep rising and stories of others' gains spread, rather than because they have studied the investment. When sentiment turns, the same tendency can trigger panic selling.

Herding can contribute to bubbles and crashes, and to momentum in prices. It can affect professional investors too, since fund managers may fear underperforming their peers more than they fear being wrong together.

Not all herding is irrational; following others can make sense when they may have better information. But blindly following the crowd can lead to buying near peaks and selling near lows. Having a clear investment plan, diversifying and avoiding decisions driven by headlines or social media can help reduce the influence of herding.

definition: Historical cost is the accounting practice of recording an asset at the price originally paid for it, rather than at its current market value.
explanation: When a company buys a building, machine or piece of land, it records the asset at the amount it actually paid, including costs needed to get it ready for use, such as delivery and installation. That figure stays as the starting point in the accounts, even if the asset's market value later rises or falls.
For example, a company that bought land for 500,000 twenty years ago may still show it at 500,000, even though similar land nearby now sells for 2 million.

Historical cost has a big advantage: it is objective and easy to verify, because it is backed by an invoice or contract. It does not depend on estimates or opinions about what an asset might be worth today.

Its weakness is that it can become out of date. Balance sheets based on historical cost may understate the value of long-held assets, especially property, and do not reflect inflation. That is why accounting standards allow or require fair value for some assets, such as many financial investments, and require write-downs when an asset's value falls below its recorded amount.

definition: Historical volatility is a measure of how much an asset's price has actually fluctuated over a past period, usually calculated as the annualized standard deviation of its returns.
explanation: Historical volatility looks backwards. It is calculated from past price data, typically daily returns over a period such as 30, 90 or 252 trading days, and is usually expressed as an annual percentage.

To annualize daily volatility, analysts commonly multiply it by the square root of the number of trading days in a year, often taken as 252. For example, a share whose daily returns have a standard deviation of 1% has an annualized historical volatility of about 16%.

Higher historical volatility means the asset's price has moved more, which indicates higher risk. Government bonds typically have low volatility, broad stock market indices moderate volatility, and individual shares, commodities and cryptocurrencies often much higher volatility.

Historical volatility is used in risk management, portfolio construction and option pricing. Traders often compare it with implied volatility. If implied volatility is much higher than historical volatility, options may look expensive relative to how much the asset has typically moved, although the market may be anticipating an event that past data does not reflect. Past volatility is not a guarantee of future volatility, which can change suddenly.

definition: A holding period is the length of time an investor owns an investment, from the date of purchase to the date of sale.
explanation: The holding period matters for measuring returns and for tax. Returns are often compared over a holding period, and longer returns are usually converted to an annual rate so they can be compared fairly.

In many tax systems, the holding period determines how gains are taxed. In the United States, for example, gains on assets held for more than one year are generally taxed at lower long-term capital gains rates than those held for a year or less. Some countries offer reduced rates or exemptions after longer holding periods.
For example, an investor who buys shares on 1 March and sells them on 1 September of the following year has a holding period of 18 months.

Holding periods also matter in other rules, such as the minimum holding period for dividends to qualify for favourable tax treatment, and in fund rules that may charge fees for selling within a short time. An investor's intended holding period, or investment horizon, affects which investments are suitable.

definition: Home equity is the part of a home's value that the owner owns outright. It equals the current market value of the home minus the amount still owed on any mortgage or other loans secured against it.
explanation: When you buy a home with a mortgage, your equity starts with your down payment. It then grows in two ways: as you repay the mortgage principal, and as the home's value rises.

For example, if your home is worth 350,000 and you owe 210,000 on your mortgage, your home equity is 140,000. If the home rises in value to 380,000 and you repay another 10,000 of the loan, your equity grows to 180,000.
Equity can also fall. If house prices drop, equity shrinks, and if the home's value falls below the amount owed, the owner has negative equity, which can make it hard to sell or remortgage.

Homeowners can borrow against their equity through products such as a home equity loan or home equity line of credit. This can provide money for renovations or other needs, but it increases the debt secured on the home, so failing to repay could put the home at risk. For many households, home equity is their largest single source of wealth.

definition: A home equity line of credit (HELOC) is a revolving credit line, common in the United States, secured on a borrower's home, which allows them to borrow, repay and borrow again up to a set limit based on the equity in the property.
explanation: A HELOC works more like a credit card than a traditional loan. Instead of receiving a lump sum, the homeowner is given a credit limit and can draw money as needed, paying interest only on the amount actually borrowed.

HELOCs usually have two phases. During the draw period, often around ten years, the borrower can take out money and may only have to pay interest. During the repayment period that follows, they can no longer borrow and must repay both principal and interest, which can significantly increase monthly payments.
For example, a homeowner might open a HELOC with a limit of 50,000 and draw 15,000 to pay for a kitchen renovation, paying interest only on that 15,000.

HELOC interest rates are usually variable, so payments can rise if interest rates increase. As with home equity loans, the home serves as collateral, so failure to repay could lead to foreclosure. Products like HELOCs are less common outside North America. In the United Kingdom, flexible borrowing against a home is more often arranged through offset or flexible mortgages, or by remortgaging.

definition: A home equity loan is a loan, common in the United States, that allows a homeowner to borrow a lump sum against the equity in their home, which is the difference between the property's value and the amount still owed on the mortgage.
explanation: A home equity loan is sometimes called a second mortgage, because it is secured on the home in addition to the main mortgage. The borrower receives the money upfront and repays it over a fixed term, usually at a fixed interest rate.

Lenders typically allow borrowing up to a percentage of the home's value, minus the existing mortgage. For example, if a home is worth 400,000, the existing mortgage is 250,000 and the lender allows total borrowing of up to 80% of the home's value, the homeowner could borrow up to 70,000.

Because the loan is secured on the home, interest rates are usually lower than for unsecured loans such as personal loans or credit cards. People often use home equity loans for home improvements, education costs or consolidating more expensive debts.

The key risk is that the home is collateral. If the borrower cannot repay, they could lose their home. In the United Kingdom and some other countries, similar borrowing is often arranged as a further advance from the existing mortgage lender, by remortgaging, or as a secured loan, sometimes called a second-charge mortgage.

definition: Horizontal analysis compares financial statement figures across two or more periods to show how each item has changed over time, in amounts and in percentages.
explanation: Horizontal analysis reads financial statements across the years, line by line. For each item, it calculates the change from one period to the next, often as a percentage of the earlier figure.

For example, if revenue rose from 1.8 million last year to 2.07 million this year, it grew by 270,000, or 15%. If operating expenses rose by 25% over the same period, the analysis highlights that costs are growing faster than sales, which may squeeze profits.

Horizontal analysis can also use a base year. Every year's figures are expressed as a percentage of the base year, making long-term trends easy to see. If revenue is 100 in the base year and 140 five years later, it has grown by 40% over the period.
This type of analysis is useful for spotting trends, unusual movements and potential problems, such as receivables growing much faster than sales, which could mean customers are paying more slowly.
Horizontal analysis complements vertical analysis. Horizontal analysis looks at change over time, while vertical analysis looks at the structure of the statements in a single period.

definition: Human capital is the knowledge, skills, health, experience and abilities that people possess, which make them productive and allow them to earn income.
explanation: Just as physical capital, such as machinery and buildings, helps produce goods and services, human capital makes workers more productive. It can be increased through education, training, work experience and good health.

The concept was developed by economists such as Gary Becker and Theodore Schultz in the mid-twentieth century. It explains why individuals and governments invest in education and why more skilled workers tend to earn higher wages.
For example, a person who spends several years training as an engineer increases their human capital, expecting higher lifetime earnings in return for the time and cost of study.

At the national level, human capital is a major driver of economic growth and innovation. Countries invest in schools, universities, healthcare and training programmes to strengthen it. In personal finance, human capital is often viewed as a person's most valuable asset early in life, which is one reason younger people can sometimes take more investment risk with their savings.

definition: A hurdle rate is the minimum rate of return a company requires before it will approve an investment or project.
explanation: A company has limited money and many possible uses for it. The hurdle rate sets the bar a project must clear to be worth doing. If a project's expected return is below the hurdle rate, it is rejected.

The hurdle rate is usually based on the company's cost of capital, since a project that earns less than the cost of its funding would destroy value. Many companies add an extra margin for risk. A safe project, such as replacing old equipment, might have a hurdle rate close to the cost of capital, while a risky venture into a new market might need to clear a much higher rate.

For example, a company with a cost of capital of 8% might set a hurdle rate of 10% for normal projects and 15% for high-risk ones. A project with an expected internal rate of return of 12% would be approved under the first rate but rejected under the second.
Setting the hurdle rate too low risks approving poor investments, while setting it too high can cause a company to pass up good opportunities.

definition: Hyperinflation is extremely rapid and out-of-control inflation, in which prices rise so quickly that money loses its value very fast, often defined as prices rising by more than 50% in a single month.
explanation: At 50% a month, prices would rise by nearly 13,000% over a year. In the worst historical episodes, prices have doubled within days or even hours.

Hyperinflation usually occurs when a government finances large spending by creating money, often during war, political upheaval or economic collapse, when it cannot raise enough through taxes or borrowing. As more money chases the same or fewer goods, prices soar. People then try to spend money as quickly as possible before it loses value, which drives prices even higher.
Well-known examples include Germany in the early 1920s, Hungary after the Second World War, Zimbabwe in the late 2000s and Venezuela in the late 2010s.

The effects are devastating. Savings become worthless, fixed incomes and pensions collapse in value, businesses struggle to set prices and people may turn to foreign currencies or barter. Ending hyperinflation typically requires major reforms, such as a new currency, strict limits on money creation and restoring confidence in the government's finances.

definition: A hypothesis test is a statistical method for using sample data to decide whether there is enough evidence to reject an assumption about a population, called the null hypothesis.
explanation: A hypothesis test starts with two competing statements. The null hypothesis usually states that there is no effect or no difference, for example, that a new trading strategy performs no better than the market. The alternative hypothesis states that there is an effect, for example, that the strategy does perform better.

Data are collected and a test statistic is calculated. This is then used to find a p-value: the probability of seeing results at least as extreme if the null hypothesis were true. If the p-value is below a chosen threshold, called the significance level and often set at 5%, the null hypothesis is rejected in favour of the alternative.

For example, a bank might test whether a new marketing campaign increased average account balances. If the p-value is 0.02, it rejects the null hypothesis of no change and concludes there is evidence of an increase.

Hypothesis tests can be wrong in two ways. A false positive rejects a true null hypothesis, finding an effect that is not real. A false negative fails to reject a false null hypothesis, missing a real effect. Choosing the significance level and sample size involves balancing these risks.

definition: An IBAN, or International Bank Account Number, is a standard international format for identifying a bank account, used to make cross-border payments more accurate and efficient.
explanation: Different countries use different formats for bank account numbers, which can lead to errors in international payments. The IBAN standardises the format, including a country code, check digits and the domestic account details.

An IBAN can be up to 34 characters long. It starts with a two-letter country code, followed by two check digits that help detect typing errors, and then the domestic bank and account information. For example, an IBAN might begin with DE for Germany or FR for France.

IBANs are used throughout Europe, including all countries in the Single Euro Payments Area, and in many countries in the Middle East, North Africa and elsewhere. They are often used together with a SWIFT or BIC code, which identifies the bank.

The United States, Canada and Australia do not use IBANs for domestic accounts, relying instead on their own systems, such as routing numbers in the United States. Payments to these countries require different details.

definition: Identity theft is the use of someone else's personal information, such as their name, identity number or bank details, without permission, usually to commit fraud or obtain money, credit or services.
explanation: Criminals obtain personal information through data breaches, phishing emails, stolen post, fake websites or by buying stolen details online. They then use the information to impersonate the victim.

With stolen details, a fraudster might open credit cards or loans in the victim's name, access their bank accounts, file false tax returns to claim refunds, make purchases or take out phone contracts. Victims may not notice until they find unfamiliar transactions, receive bills for accounts they never opened or are refused credit because of debts they did not take on.
For example, someone might discover that a loan of 8,000 was taken out in their name after their details were stolen in a data breach, damaging their credit score.

Ways to reduce the risk include using strong, unique passwords, enabling two-factor authentication, shredding documents with personal details, being wary of unexpected requests for information, checking bank statements and credit reports regularly and, where available, placing a credit freeze. Acting quickly by contacting banks, credit bureaus and the authorities helps limit the damage.

definition: The if-converted method is a way of calculating diluted earnings per share that assumes convertible securities, such as convertible bonds or preferred shares, were converted into ordinary shares at the start of the period.
explanation: Convertible securities can become ordinary shares, diluting existing shareholders. The if-converted method shows what earnings per share would be if conversion had happened.
Two adjustments are made. The extra shares from conversion are added to the share count. And because converted bonds no longer pay interest, the after-tax interest saved is added back to earnings.

For example, a company has net income of 40,000,000 and 20,000,000 shares, giving basic earnings per share of 2.00. It also has convertible bonds of 100,000,000 paying 5% interest, convertible into 4,000,000 shares. If converted, it saves 5,000,000 of interest, or 3,750,000 after 25% tax. Diluted earnings per share is 43,750,000 divided by 24,000,000, or about 1.82.
The convertibles are included only if they reduce earnings per share. If including them would increase it, they are excluded as anti-dilutive. The method is required under both IFRS and US GAAP.

definition: An immediate annuity is an insurance contract in which a person pays a lump sum to an insurer in exchange for regular income payments that begin straight away, often for the rest of their life.
explanation: Immediate annuities are commonly bought by people at or near retirement to turn part of their savings into a guaranteed income. Payments typically begin within a month to a year of purchase.

For example, a 65-year-old might use 200,000 to buy an immediate lifetime annuity paying a fixed monthly income for as long as they live. The exact amount depends on their age, health, interest rates at the time and the features chosen.

Options can include payments that continue to a spouse after death, a guaranteed minimum payment period, and payments that increase each year to help offset inflation, which reduces the starting income.

The main advantage is protection against outliving savings, known as longevity risk. Disadvantages include giving up access to the lump sum, the possibility of dying early and receiving less than was paid, and, for fixed payments, loss of purchasing power over time. Annuity rates are higher when interest rates are high and for older buyers. In the United Kingdom and some other countries, people in poor health may qualify for enhanced annuities with higher payments.

definition: Impact investing is investing with the intention of generating measurable positive social or environmental outcomes alongside a financial return.
explanation: Impact investors seek to make a difference through their investments, such as providing affordable housing, expanding renewable energy, improving healthcare access or supporting small businesses in underserved communities.

Two features distinguish impact investing from broader approaches. First, the intention to create positive impact is central, not a side effect. Second, impact is measured and reported, using specific indicators such as homes built, emissions avoided or people served.
For example, an impact fund might lend to small businesses in low-income areas, aiming to earn a modest return while tracking jobs created and incomes improved.

Expected financial returns vary. Some impact investors seek market-rate returns, while others accept lower returns to achieve greater impact. Impact investing is common in private markets, such as private equity, private debt and venture capital, but also includes certain bonds, such as green and social bonds. Measuring and verifying impact consistently remains a challenge.

definition: Impairment is a reduction in the recorded value of an asset when its recoverable amount falls below the value shown on the balance sheet.
explanation: Assets are recorded at cost, less any depreciation or amortization. Sometimes, however, something happens that makes an asset worth much less than its book value. A factory may become unprofitable, technology may become obsolete or an acquired business may perform far worse than expected. When this happens, the asset is impaired.

Accounting rules require companies to test assets for impairment when there are signs of a problem, and to test goodwill and certain other intangibles at least once a year. If the asset's recoverable amount, broadly the higher of what it could be sold for and the value of the cash it will generate, is below its book value, the difference is recorded as an impairment loss.

For example, if a company paid 50 million for a business, recorded as goodwill and other assets, and that business is now worth only 30 million, the company may record an impairment loss of 20 million.
Impairment losses reduce profit and asset values. Large impairments often signal that a past acquisition or investment did not work out as planned.

definition: Implied volatility is the level of future volatility in an asset's price that is implied by the current market price of its options.
explanation: Option prices depend on several factors, including the asset's current price, the exercise price, the time until expiry, interest rates and how much the asset's price is expected to move. All except the last can be observed directly. Implied volatility is found by working backwards from the option's market price, using an option pricing model, to calculate the level of volatility the market must be assuming.

Higher implied volatility means the market expects larger price swings, which makes options more expensive. For example, a share's options might show implied volatility of 20% in calm times, rising to 50% ahead of a major announcement, such as earnings results or a court decision, when a large price move is expected.
Implied volatility is forward-looking, reflecting market expectations, whereas historical volatility measures how much prices actually moved in the past.

Implied volatility is widely used by options traders to judge whether options are cheap or expensive. Indices of implied volatility, such as the VIX, which is based on options on the US S&P 500 index, are often called fear gauges, because they tend to rise sharply when markets fall and investors seek protection.

definition: The impossible trinity is the principle that a country cannot have all three of the following at the same time: a fixed exchange rate, free movement of capital across its borders, and an independent monetary policy.
explanation: The idea, also called the trilemma, comes from work by economists Robert Mundell and Marcus Fleming in the 1960s. A country can choose any two of the three goals, but not all three.

With a fixed exchange rate and free capital movement, a country must follow the interest rates of the country it is pegged to, otherwise money would flow in or out and break the peg. Hong Kong, which pegs its dollar to the US dollar and allows free capital flows, broadly follows US interest rates.
With free capital movement and an independent monetary policy, the country must let its exchange rate float, as the United States, the euro area and the United Kingdom do.
With a fixed exchange rate and independent monetary policy, the country must restrict capital flows, as China has done to a significant extent.
The trinity helps explain why countries choose different exchange rate systems and why some currency pegs have collapsed when countries tried to pursue all three goals at once.

definition: Income is money a person or business receives over a period of time, such as a salary, business profits, interest, rent or dividends.
explanation: Income is a flow: it is measured over a period, such as a month or a year. This makes it different from wealth, which is a stock measured at a single moment. Someone can have a high income but little wealth if they spend everything they earn, or high wealth but little income if their assets produce no cash.

Income can come from many sources. Earned income comes from working, such as wages, salaries, tips and self-employment profits. Investment income comes from what you own, such as interest on savings, dividends from shares or rent from property. Some people also receive transfer income, such as pensions or government benefits.

It is important to know which income figure is being discussed. Gross income is the total before anything is taken out. Net income, often called take-home pay, is what remains after taxes and other deductions. A person earning 4,000 a month before tax might receive only about 3,200 in their bank account once tax and contributions are deducted.
Lenders, landlords and tax authorities all look at income, because it shows how much money is regularly available to pay bills, debts and taxes.

definition: Income elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in consumers' incomes.
explanation: It compares the percentage change in quantity demanded with the percentage change in income. The result shows how a product's sales are likely to change as people become richer or poorer.

If income rises by 10% and demand for a product rises by 5%, its income elasticity is 0.5. It is a normal good, because demand rises with income, and a necessity, because demand rises less than proportionally. If demand rises by 20%, the elasticity is 2, which is typical of luxury goods such as foreign holidays or fine dining.

If demand falls when income rises, the income elasticity is negative and the product is an inferior good. For example, if incomes rise 10% and demand for a basic, low-cost brand falls by 5%, the income elasticity is −0.5. People switch to more expensive alternatives as they can afford them.

Businesses use income elasticity to anticipate how sales will change through economic booms and recessions. Companies selling luxury goods tend to see bigger swings in sales than those selling everyday necessities.

definition: Income inequality is the extent to which income is distributed unevenly among individuals or households in a population.
explanation: In any economy, some people earn more than others. Income inequality measures how large these differences are. It is often measured using the Gini coefficient, the share of income going to the top 1% or 10% of earners, or ratios comparing the incomes of the richest and poorest groups.
For example, if the top 10% of households receive 40% of a country's total income while the bottom half receive 20%, income is distributed quite unequally.

Inequality is influenced by many factors, including education and skills, technology, globalisation, the strength of trade unions, tax and benefit systems, and the returns earned on wealth. Taxes and government transfers usually reduce inequality significantly, so measures before and after taxes and benefits can differ greatly.

Income inequality differs from wealth inequality, which looks at the distribution of assets and is usually much greater. Economists debate how inequality affects growth, social mobility and political stability, and what policies best address it.

definition: An income statement is a financial statement that shows a business's revenue, expenses and resulting profit or loss over a period, such as a quarter or a year.
explanation: Unlike the balance sheet, which is a snapshot at one date, the income statement covers a period of time. It shows how well the business performed during that period.

It usually starts with revenue, the money earned from sales. Cost of goods sold is subtracted to give gross profit. Operating expenses, such as wages, rent and marketing, are then subtracted to give operating income. Finally, interest and taxes are deducted to arrive at net income, the bottom line.
For example, a company with revenue of 1,000,000, cost of goods sold of 600,000, operating expenses of 250,000, interest of 20,000 and tax of 30,000 reports net income of 100,000.

The income statement is prepared on an accrual basis, so profit is not the same as cash. A company can show a profit while running low on cash if customers have not paid yet. Investors read the income statement alongside the cash flow statement to get the full picture.
note: The income statement is also called the profit and loss statement, or P&L. The names are interchangeable.

definition: Income tax expense is the total tax charge a company records in its income statement for a period, including both tax payable now and changes in deferred tax.
explanation: Income tax expense is deducted from pretax income to arrive at net income. It is not always the same as the tax the company actually pays in cash that year.

It has two parts. Current tax is the tax payable on the period's taxable profit under tax law. Deferred tax reflects tax that will be payable or recoverable in future periods because of timing differences between accounting and tax rules.
For example, a company might owe current tax of 800,000 for the year and also record a deferred tax charge of 100,000, giving total income tax expense of 900,000.
Dividing income tax expense by pretax income gives the effective tax rate. If pretax income is 3.6 million and income tax expense is 900,000, the effective tax rate is 25%.

The notes to the financial statements usually explain the difference between the effective rate and the statutory rate, listing reasons such as tax credits, non-deductible expenses, profits earned in countries with different rates and changes in tax law. Analysts read this reconciliation to understand whether a company's tax rate is likely to persist.

definition: Incremental cash flow is the additional cash a company expects to receive or pay out as a direct result of undertaking a specific project or decision, compared with not doing it.
explanation: When evaluating an investment, the key question is how the company's future cash flows will change if it goes ahead. Only cash flows that would not happen otherwise should be counted.

Incremental cash flows include the initial investment, extra revenues, extra operating costs, changes in working capital, taxes and any cash received when the project ends, such as from selling equipment.

For example, a company launching a new product expects it to bring in 500,000 a year in sales, but it will also reduce sales of an existing product by 100,000. The incremental revenue is 400,000, not 500,000.

Some cash flows should be excluded. Sunk costs, such as money already spent on research, are irrelevant because they cannot be recovered. Fixed overheads that will continue regardless of the decision should not be counted. Opportunity costs, such as income from renting out a building the project will now use, should be included.
Incremental cash flows form the basis of capital budgeting tools such as net present value and internal rate of return. Getting them right is essential for making sound investment decisions.

definition: An incremental cost is the additional cost incurred as a result of a decision, such as producing more units, accepting an order or launching a project.
explanation: Incremental cost focuses on the change in total costs caused by a particular choice. It compares total costs with the decision and without it.

For example, a factory currently producing 10,000 units has total costs of 120,000. If producing 11,000 units would raise total costs to 124,000, the incremental cost of the extra 1,000 units is 4,000, or 4 per unit. If a customer offers to buy those 1,000 units for 6 each, the order adds 2,000 of profit.

Incremental costs often include extra materials, labour and energy, and sometimes additional fixed costs if the decision requires more space or equipment. Costs that would be incurred anyway are excluded.

Incremental cost is closely related to marginal cost. Marginal cost usually refers to the cost of one additional unit, while incremental cost can refer to the cost of any additional batch, project or decision.
Comparing incremental costs with incremental revenues is a core part of business decision-making, used for pricing special orders, deciding whether to expand production and choosing between projects.

definition: Incurred but not reported (IBNR) refers to insurance claims for events that have already happened but have not yet been reported to the insurer, for which the insurer must set aside an estimated reserve.
explanation: Some losses are reported long after they occur. A person injured in an accident may not file a claim for months. Liability claims, such as those for illness caused by exposure to harmful substances, may emerge years later.

Insurers must estimate these future claims for events that have already happened and include them in their liabilities. IBNR reserves are usually estimated by actuaries using historical patterns of how claims develop over time.

For example, at the end of a year, an insurer might estimate that, based on past experience, a further 20,000,000 of claims will be reported for accidents that occurred during the year, and record this as an IBNR reserve.

IBNR reserves can be a large part of an insurer's liabilities, especially for long-tail business, such as liability and workers' compensation insurance, where claims take years to emerge and settle. Because they rely on estimates, they involve significant judgment, and changes to IBNR estimates can materially affect an insurer's reported profits.

definition: The indemnity principle is the insurance principle that a policyholder should be restored to the same financial position after a loss as they were in immediately before it, but should not profit from the loss.
explanation: Insurance is meant to compensate for losses, not to provide a gain. The indemnity principle ensures that payouts reflect the actual loss suffered, up to the policy limit.

This principle underpins several insurance rules. Insurers pay only for the actual loss, not more. If a policyholder has insurance with several insurers for the same risk, they cannot claim the full loss from each, and the insurers share the cost, a principle called contribution. After paying a claim, the insurer can recover the amount from a third party responsible for the loss, known as subrogation.
For example, if a car insured for 20,000 is worth 12,000 when it is written off in an accident, the insurer typically pays 12,000, its actual value, not 20,000.

The indemnity principle applies mainly to property and liability insurance. It does not apply in the same way to life insurance or certain personal accident policies, which pay agreed amounts, since the value of a life cannot be measured precisely. Some property policies offer new-for-old cover, which goes beyond strict indemnity by an agreed amount.

definition: An index fund is an investment fund that aims to match the performance of a specific market index by holding all, or a representative sample, of the securities in that index.
explanation: Rather than trying to pick winning investments, an index fund simply mirrors an index, such as a broad stock market index, a bond index or a sector index. Its returns closely follow the index, minus a small fee.

Index funds can be mutual funds or exchange-traded funds. Because they do not require teams of analysts selecting investments or frequent trading, they typically have much lower fees than actively managed funds.

For example, an index fund tracking an index of the 500 largest US companies holds shares in all those companies in proportion to their weights in the index. If the index rises 10% in a year, the fund rises by close to 10%, less its fee.

Index funds offer broad diversification, low costs, transparency and simplicity. The idea was popularised by John Bogle, founder of Vanguard, who launched one of the first index funds available to individual investors in the 1970s.

The trade-off is that index fund investors receive the market's full ups and downs and cannot outperform the index. They also hold every company in the index, regardless of whether it looks expensive or risky.

definition: An index number is a figure that shows how a value has changed relative to a base period, which is usually set equal to 100.
explanation: Index numbers make it easy to compare changes over time, especially for quantities measured in different units or combining many items.
For example, if the average price of a basket of goods was 50 in the base year and is 55 today, the price index is 110, showing a 10% increase since the base year.

Many important economic statistics are expressed as index numbers. The Consumer Price Index measures changes in the cost of living. Stock market indices, such as major benchmark indices around the world, track the combined value of groups of shares. Index numbers are also used for house prices, wages, production and many other measures.

Index numbers can be simple, tracking a single item, or composite, combining many items. Composite indices assign weights to their components, reflecting their importance. For example, a consumer price index gives more weight to housing and food than to items that make up a small share of household spending.

Index numbers show relative change, not absolute values. An index of 120 means a 20% rise from the base, but says nothing about the actual price level. Comparing two index values directly shows the percentage change between them.

definition: An indirect cost is a cost that supports several products, services or activities and cannot be traced directly to any single one of them, such as factory rent, utilities or administrative salaries.
explanation: Indirect costs are necessary to run the business but are shared. A factory's electricity powers machines making many different products; the accounts team supports the whole company.
For example, a company making chairs and tables cannot say exactly how much of the factory's 10,000 monthly rent belongs to chairs and how much to tables. The rent is an indirect cost.

To work out the full cost of a product, businesses allocate indirect costs using a reasonable basis, such as machine hours, labour hours, floor space or sales value. If chairs use 60% of machine hours, they might be assigned 60% of the factory's indirect costs.

The allocation method can significantly affect how profitable each product appears. Poor allocation may make a profitable product look unprofitable, or the reverse, leading to bad decisions. Activity-based costing is one approach that tries to allocate indirect costs more accurately by linking them to the activities that actually drive them.
Indirect costs are often fixed, but not always. Collectively, indirect costs are often called overhead.

definition: An individual retirement account (IRA) is a tax-advantaged personal retirement account in the United States that individuals can open themselves, separate from any employer plan.
explanation: IRAs let people save for retirement with tax benefits, whether or not they have a workplace plan. They are opened with banks, brokers or fund companies, and can hold a wide range of investments.

There are two main types. A traditional IRA may allow contributions to be deducted from taxable income, depending on income and workplace plan coverage; investments grow tax-deferred, and withdrawals are taxed as income. A Roth IRA takes contributions from taxed income, but qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
For example, someone who leaves a job may roll their old employer plan into an IRA, gaining more investment choice while keeping the tax benefits.

IRAs have annual contribution limits, set by law and adjusted over time. Withdrawals before age 59 and a half usually face a 10% penalty plus tax, with some exceptions. Traditional IRAs require minimum withdrawals from a set age. Similar personal pension accounts in other countries include self-invested personal pensions in the United Kingdom and registered retirement savings plans in Canada.

definition: Industrial production is a measure of the output of a country's factories, mines and utilities, usually published monthly as an index.
explanation: Industrial production tracks the physical volume of goods produced in the manufacturing, mining, and electricity and gas sectors. It is one of the most timely indicators of economic activity, since it is published monthly, while GDP is usually published quarterly.
For example, if a country's industrial production index rises from 100 to 103 over a year, output in these sectors has grown by 3%.

Industrial production is closely watched because these sectors are sensitive to the business cycle. Factory output often falls early in recessions and recovers early in expansions, making it a useful coincident indicator.

In many developed economies, industry now makes up a smaller share of output than services, so industrial production gives only a partial picture of the economy. It remains important for understanding manufacturing-heavy economies and for tracking global trade and supply chains. In the United States, the Federal Reserve publishes the index alongside a measure of capacity utilization.

definition: An inferior good is a product for which demand falls when consumers' incomes rise and increases when incomes fall.
explanation: "Inferior" does not mean poor quality. It means that people tend to buy less of the product as they become better off, usually because they switch to more expensive alternatives they prefer.

Common examples include supermarket own-brand basics, instant noodles, second-hand clothes and long-distance bus travel. When incomes rise, people may switch to branded products, fresher food, new clothes or train and air travel. When incomes fall, they switch back.
Inferior goods have a negative income elasticity of demand. For example, if incomes rise by 10% and demand for a budget brand falls by 4%, its income elasticity is −0.4.
Businesses that sell inferior goods may see sales rise during recessions, as more people look for cheaper options. Discount retailers, for example, often gain customers when the economy weakens.

Whether a good is inferior depends on the people and the situation. Public transport may be an inferior good in one city, where people switch to cars as they get richer, and a normal good in another, where it is fast and convenient.

definition: Inflation is the general rise in the prices of goods and services over time. As prices rise, each unit of money buys less.
explanation: Inflation does not mean that every price goes up at once. Some prices rise, some fall and some stay the same. Inflation describes the average direction across the whole economy, usually measured by tracking the cost of a typical basket of goods and services, such as the Consumer Price Index.
Inflation is usually expressed as a yearly percentage. If the basket cost 1,000 last year and costs 1,040 this year, inflation is 4%.

Prices can rise for different reasons. When people and businesses want to buy more than the economy can produce, sellers raise prices; this is often called demand-pull inflation. When costs such as energy, raw materials or wages rise, businesses pass them on to customers; this is cost-push inflation. Expectations matter too: if people expect prices to rise, they may ask for higher wages and buy sooner, which can push prices up further.
