Most central banks aim for low and stable inflation, often around 2% a year. Very high inflation damages savings and makes planning difficult. Falling prices, called deflation, can also be harmful, because people delay spending while they wait for prices to drop.

definition: Inflation expectations are the rates of inflation that households, businesses and investors expect to see in the future.
explanation: Expectations about inflation matter because they influence behaviour today. If workers expect prices to rise by 5% next year, they are likely to ask for wage increases of at least that much. If businesses expect their costs to rise, they may raise prices in advance. In this way, expectations of high inflation can help create high inflation.

Central banks pay close attention to inflation expectations. When expectations are anchored, meaning people trust that inflation will return to the central bank's target over time, temporary price shocks are less likely to turn into persistent inflation.

Inflation expectations are measured in several ways. Surveys ask households, businesses and professional forecasters what they expect. Financial markets also provide estimates, for example by comparing yields on ordinary government bonds with yields on inflation-linked bonds.

For example, if a ten-year government bond yields 4% and a ten-year inflation-linked bond yields 1.5%, the difference of 2.5 percentage points suggests investors expect inflation to average roughly 2.5% a year over the next decade.

definition: Inflation risk is the risk that rising prices will reduce the real value of an investment's returns or of money saved, so that it buys less in the future.
explanation: Inflation erodes purchasing power. An investment that pays a fixed amount in money terms becomes less valuable in real terms when prices rise.

For example, a bond paying a fixed 3% a year delivers a real return of about −2% in a year when inflation is 5%. The investor receives the promised interest but can buy less with their total wealth than before.

Inflation risk is highest for investments with fixed payments over long periods, such as long-term bonds, fixed annuities and cash held for many years. It is also a major concern for retirees whose income does not rise with prices.

Some investments offer protection. Inflation-linked bonds adjust their payments in line with an inflation index. Shares, property and some commodities have tended to keep pace with or outgrow inflation over long periods, although not reliably in every period.

Inflation risk is often underestimated because its effects are gradual. Even moderate inflation of 3% a year roughly halves purchasing power over about 23 years. For long-term goals, planning in real terms, after inflation, gives a more accurate picture.

definition: Inflation targeting is a monetary policy framework in which a central bank publicly commits to keeping inflation at or near a specific numerical target, and sets interest rates with that goal in mind.
explanation: Under inflation targeting, the central bank announces a target, often 2% a year, and uses its policy tools, mainly interest rates, to steer inflation towards it over the medium term.

New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting in 1990. Many central banks, including those of the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and the euro area, now use inflation targets or similar frameworks. The US Federal Reserve also has a 2% inflation goal alongside its aim of maximum employment.

For example, if inflation rises to 5%, a central bank targeting 2% would typically raise interest rates to slow demand and bring inflation back down. If inflation falls well below target, it would cut rates.

A clear target helps anchor inflation expectations. If people and businesses believe the central bank will deliver low, stable inflation, they are less likely to push up wages and prices excessively. Critics note that focusing heavily on inflation may sometimes come at the cost of employment or financial stability, which is why many frameworks allow some flexibility.

definition: Information asymmetry is a situation in which one party in a transaction or relationship has more or better information than the other.
explanation: Information asymmetry is common in finance. Company managers know more about their business than outside investors. Borrowers know more about their ability to repay than lenders. Sellers of used goods know more about their condition than buyers.

It can lead to two main problems. Adverse selection occurs before a transaction, when the less-informed party risks attracting the wrong type of counterparty, such as an insurer attracting mostly high-risk customers. Moral hazard occurs after a transaction, when one party changes its behaviour in ways the other cannot observe.

For example, when a company announces it will issue new shares, investors may suspect managers believe the shares are overvalued, since managers know more about the company's prospects. As a result, the share price often falls.

Many financial practices exist partly to reduce information asymmetry, including audited financial statements, credit ratings, disclosure rules, due diligence, warranties and signalling actions such as paying dividends. It is central to theories such as the pecking order theory and signalling theory.

definition: The information ratio measures a portfolio's return above its benchmark for each unit of tracking error, showing how consistently a manager has outperformed.
explanation: Active fund managers aim to beat their benchmark, but outperformance that comes with large, erratic deviations from the benchmark is less impressive than steady outperformance. The information ratio captures this.

It is calculated by dividing the portfolio's active return, its return minus the benchmark's return, by its tracking error, the standard deviation of that difference. For example, a fund that beats its benchmark by an average of 2% a year with a tracking error of 4% has an information ratio of 0.5.

A higher information ratio indicates more consistent skill in adding value relative to the benchmark. As a rough guide, ratios of around 0.5 are often considered good and those near 1 exceptional over long periods, though these are rules of thumb.

The information ratio differs from the Sharpe ratio, which compares return with the risk-free rate rather than a benchmark. Like other performance measures, it depends on the period studied and the benchmark chosen, and past results may not continue.

definition: Inheritance tax is a tax on money or property received from someone who has died. Depending on the country, it is charged either on the heir who receives the assets or on the deceased person's estate as a whole.
explanation: Countries tax wealth passed on at death in different ways. Some charge tax on the heir, often with rates and allowances that depend on how closely related the heir was to the deceased. Children may pay little or nothing, while distant relatives or unrelated people pay more. Others, such as the United States, use an estate tax, charged on the whole estate before it is shared out.

The United Kingdom calls its tax inheritance tax, but it works more like an estate tax: it is charged on the estate above a tax-free threshold, with exemptions such as transfers to a spouse or civil partner and gifts to charity.
For example, under a system with a tax-free threshold of 300,000 and a rate of 40%, an estate worth 500,000 would pay 40% of 200,000, or 80,000, if no other reliefs applied.
Some countries have no tax on death at all. Rules on gifts made during a person's lifetime are often linked to inheritance tax, to stop people avoiding it by giving assets away shortly before death.

definition: Initial margin is the amount of money or collateral an investor must deposit with a broker or clearing house when opening a leveraged position, such as a futures contract or a margin purchase of shares.
explanation: Initial margin acts as a security deposit, protecting the broker or clearing house against losses if the price moves against the investor and they fail to pay.

For example, to open a futures contract worth 100,000, an exchange might require initial margin of 10,000. The investor controls a position worth ten times their deposit, so a 10% move in the contract's value would equal the entire margin.

Initial margin requirements are set by exchanges, clearing houses and brokers, often within limits set by regulators. They are usually higher for more volatile assets, because larger price swings mean larger potential losses. Requirements can be raised during periods of market turbulence.

When buying shares on margin, initial margin is the portion of the purchase price the investor must pay with their own money, while the broker lends the rest. In the United States, regulations generally require initial margin of at least 50% for share purchases.
Once a position is open, the account must stay above a lower level called the maintenance margin. If losses push it below that level, the investor receives a margin call and must add funds.

definition: An initial public offering (IPO) is the first time a private company sells its shares to the public, after which its shares can be traded on a stock exchange.
explanation: Companies go public through an IPO to raise money for growth, to give early investors and founders a way to sell some of their holdings and to raise their profile. Once listed, the company can more easily raise further money in the future.

The process usually involves investment banks, which help prepare detailed documents describing the business, its finances and its risks, advise on the share price and find investors. The company must meet the exchange's listing requirements and the rules of securities regulators.

For example, a company might sell 20 million shares at 25 each in its IPO, raising 500 million. On its first day of trading, the share price may rise above or fall below the IPO price, depending on demand.

Going public brings obligations. Listed companies must publish regular financial reports, follow governance rules and face scrutiny from investors and the media. Some companies choose to stay private to avoid these demands. IPO investments can be volatile, and newly listed shares do not always perform well in the long run.

definition: Inorganic growth is growth a business achieves by buying or merging with other companies, rather than by expanding its existing operations.
explanation: Instead of building new products or winning customers one by one, a company can grow quickly by acquiring another business that already has customers, products, staff and revenue.
For example, a company with revenue of 200 million that buys a competitor with revenue of 50 million immediately increases its revenue by 25%, even if its own business did not grow at all.
Inorganic growth can bring speed, access to new markets or technologies, and cost savings from combining operations. It can also remove a competitor or fill gaps in a product range.

It carries risks. Acquisitions are often expensive, and buyers frequently pay a large premium over the target's market value. Integrating two businesses, with different systems and cultures, can be difficult. If the expected benefits do not appear, the buyer may later need to write down the value of the acquisition. This is why investors look at organic growth separately to judge how the underlying business is really doing.

definition: Insider trading is buying or selling a company's securities while in possession of material information about the company that is not yet public, which is illegal in most countries.
explanation: Material information is information a reasonable investor would consider important, such as upcoming earnings results, a planned takeover, a major contract or a failed drug trial. Using such information to trade before it is public gives an unfair advantage and undermines trust in markets.

Insider trading laws apply not only to company directors and employees but also to anyone who receives confidential information, such as lawyers, bankers, consultants, friends and relatives, and to those who pass on tips.
For example, an employee who learns their company is about to be acquired at a large premium, and buys shares before the announcement, is engaging in illegal insider trading.

Legal insider trading also exists. Directors and employees can buy and sell their company's shares, provided they do not use inside information, follow company trading windows and report their trades as required. Many executives use pre-arranged trading plans to avoid suspicion. Penalties for illegal insider trading can include large fines and prison sentences.

definition: Insolvency is the financial state in which a person or company cannot pay its debts as they fall due, or its liabilities exceed its assets.
explanation: There are two main tests of insolvency. Cash-flow insolvency means being unable to pay debts when they are due, even if the business owns valuable assets. Balance-sheet insolvency means total liabilities are greater than total assets.

For example, a company might own buildings worth millions but be unable to pay suppliers and employees because it has run out of cash. It is cash-flow insolvent, even though it may be solvent on its balance sheet.

Insolvency is a financial condition, while bankruptcy is a legal process. In many countries, including the United Kingdom, bankruptcy applies to individuals, while insolvent companies go through processes such as administration, liquidation or company voluntary arrangements. In the United States, bankruptcy applies to both individuals and companies.

Directors of companies approaching insolvency often have legal duties to consider the interests of creditors, and may face personal liability if they continue trading when there is no reasonable prospect of avoiding insolvency. Insolvency does not always mean the end of a business. Some companies are rescued through restructuring or sale, while others are wound up and their assets sold to repay creditors.

definition: An instalment loan is a loan for a fixed amount that is repaid in regular, scheduled payments over a set period until the balance reaches zero.
explanation: With an instalment loan, you receive the full amount up front and then repay it in equal, regular instalments, usually monthly. Each payment covers interest and part of the principal. Mortgages, car loans, student loans and most personal loans work this way.
For example, borrowing 25,000 at 6% over five years means 60 monthly payments of about 483. After the last payment, the loan is fully repaid.

Instalment loans differ from revolving credit, such as credit cards. With revolving credit, you can borrow, repay and borrow again up to a limit, and payments vary. With an instalment loan, the amount, term and payment are set from the start, and repaid money cannot be borrowed again without a new loan.

The fixed structure makes instalment loans predictable and easier to budget for. Making payments on time also builds a positive credit history. The main things to compare between offers are the interest rate or APR, the term, any fees and whether early repayment is allowed without penalty.

definition: An institutional investor is an organisation that invests large sums of money on behalf of others, such as a pension fund, insurance company, mutual fund, endowment or sovereign wealth fund.
explanation: Institutional investors manage money collected from many individuals or held for specific purposes. A pension fund invests contributions to pay future retirement benefits; an insurer invests premiums to pay future claims; a university endowment invests donations to support its activities.

Because of their size, institutional investors own a large share of the shares and bonds traded in major markets. Their decisions can significantly influence prices, and their votes at shareholder meetings can shape company policies.
For example, a large pension fund might hold shares in thousands of companies worldwide, with a single holding worth hundreds of millions.

Institutional investors often have advantages over individual investors, including access to professional research, lower trading costs, the ability to invest in private markets and greater bargaining power with fund managers and companies.

They are usually subject to regulation and are often treated as sophisticated investors, meaning some consumer protection rules designed for individuals do not apply to them. Many institutional investors also have long investment horizons, which allows them to hold less liquid assets, such as infrastructure and private equity.

definition: Insurable interest is the requirement that a person buying insurance must stand to suffer a genuine financial loss if the insured event happens.
explanation: Insurance is meant to compensate for real losses, not to allow people to gamble on events that do not affect them. Insurable interest ensures that the policyholder has a legitimate stake in what is being insured.

For example, a homeowner has an insurable interest in their house, because they would lose money if it burned down. A stranger with no connection to the house does not, and could not take out a valid insurance policy on it. A bank that has lent money secured on the house also has an insurable interest, up to the amount of its loan.

In life insurance, people are generally considered to have an insurable interest in their own lives and in the lives of their spouses or partners. Businesses may have an insurable interest in key employees, and creditors in their debtors. The exact rules vary by country.

Insurable interest also reduces moral hazard. If people could insure property or lives in which they had no stake, they might have an incentive to cause the loss. For property insurance, insurable interest usually must exist at the time of the loss; for life insurance, it is usually required when the policy is taken out.

definition: An insurance agent is a person or business licensed to sell insurance policies on behalf of one or more insurance companies, acting as the insurer's representative.
explanation: Insurance agents help customers choose and buy insurance policies, explain coverage, collect premiums and sometimes assist with claims. They are usually paid commissions by the insurers whose products they sell.

There are two main types. Captive or tied agents represent a single insurance company and sell only its products. Independent agents represent several insurers and can offer a wider range of products, although still only from the companies they have agreements with.

For example, a family looking for home and car insurance might visit a captive agent for a large insurer, who offers that insurer's policies, or an independent agent, who compares policies from several insurers.

The key difference from an insurance broker is whom they represent. Agents legally represent the insurer, while brokers typically represent the customer and search the wider market. In practice, the distinction varies by country and the terms are sometimes used loosely. Agents must usually be licensed and follow rules on disclosure and conduct.

definition: An insurance broker is an intermediary who helps clients find and buy insurance, acting on behalf of the client rather than the insurance company.
explanation: Insurance brokers compare policies from multiple insurers to find cover that suits their clients' needs and budget. They can also advise on how much cover is needed, explain policy terms and exclusions, and help with making claims.

Brokers are particularly valuable for complex insurance needs, such as large businesses, specialist industries, high-value homes or unusual risks, where policies need to be tailored and negotiated. For example, a construction company might use a broker to arrange liability, property, vehicle and employee insurance from several insurers in one coordinated programme.

Brokers differ from insurance agents. Agents typically represent one or more insurance companies and sell their products, while brokers represent the client and can search the wider market. The exact legal distinctions vary between countries.

Brokers are usually paid through commission from the insurer, a fee from the client or both. Because commission could create a conflict of interest, regulations in many countries require brokers to disclose how they are paid and to act in their clients' best interests. Online comparison websites have taken over much of the simple personal insurance market, but brokers remain important for business and specialist cover.

definition: An insurance policy is a contract in which an insurer agrees to pay for specified losses or events in exchange for regular payments, called premiums, from the policyholder.
explanation: Insurance works by pooling risk. Many people pay premiums into a common pool, and the insurer uses that money to pay the claims of the few who suffer losses. Each policyholder exchanges a small, certain cost for protection against a large, uncertain one.

A policy sets out what is covered, such as damage to a car, illness or death; what is excluded; how much the insurer will pay at most, called the limit; and how much the policyholder must pay themselves before cover begins, called the deductible or excess.
For example, a homeowner might pay a premium of 600 a year for a policy that covers up to 300,000 of damage to their house from fire, storms or theft.
Premiums depend on how likely and how large a claim is expected to be. A young driver with a powerful car usually pays more for car insurance than an experienced driver with a small car.

Common types include health, life, car, home, travel, disability and business insurance. Reading the policy carefully matters, because exclusions and conditions determine what will actually be paid when a claim is made.

definition: An insurer is a company that provides insurance, agreeing to compensate policyholders for specified losses in exchange for regular payments called premiums.
explanation: Insurers collect premiums from many customers and use that money to pay claims from the relatively small number who suffer losses. This allows individuals and businesses to protect themselves against financial risks they could not afford to bear alone.

Insurers specialise in different types of cover. Life insurers provide life insurance, annuities and some pension products. General insurers, also called property and casualty or non-life insurers, cover homes, cars, businesses, travel and liability. Health insurers cover medical costs.

Insurers earn money in two main ways: from underwriting, if premiums exceed claims and expenses, and from investing the premiums they hold before claims are paid. For example, an insurer might collect premiums at the start of the year and invest them in bonds, earning income until the money is needed to pay claims.

Because insurers make promises that may need to be kept many years into the future, they are closely regulated. Rules require them to hold enough capital and reserves to pay expected claims, and to manage risks carefully. Many insurers also buy reinsurance to protect themselves against very large losses.

definition: An intangible asset is a valuable resource that has no physical form, such as a patent, trademark, copyright, software, customer list or brand.
explanation: Not all valuable things can be touched. A company's brand, the rights to an invention or a database of loyal customers can be worth a great deal, sometimes more than its buildings and machinery. These are intangible assets.

In accounting, intangible assets are recorded on the balance sheet when they are bought from someone else or acquired as part of buying a business. For example, if a company pays 2 million for a competitor's software and customer contracts, those items are recorded as intangible assets.

Internally created intangibles are harder to record. Most costs of building a brand or doing research are expensed as they are incurred, so a company's own brand often does not appear on its balance sheet at all, even if it is extremely valuable.
Intangible assets with a limited life, such as a patent, are amortised over that life. Those with no foreseeable end, such as goodwill, are not amortised but are tested regularly for impairment.

definition: Intellectual property is creations of the mind, such as inventions, designs, brand names, artistic works and confidential know-how, that the law allows owners to protect and control.
explanation: Intellectual property, often called IP, gives creators and businesses exclusive rights to use and benefit from their ideas for a period of time. This encourages innovation and creativity, because people can earn a return on their work.

The main types are patents, which protect inventions; trademarks, which protect brand names, logos and slogans; copyright, which protects original creative works such as books, music, films and software; design rights, which protect the appearance of products; and trade secrets, which protect confidential business information.
For example, a pharmaceutical company can patent a new medicine, giving it the exclusive right to sell it for a number of years and recover its research costs.

Intellectual property can be extremely valuable. For many technology, media and consumer companies, IP is worth more than their physical assets. It can be used directly, licensed to others for royalties or sold. Protecting IP often involves registering it, monitoring for infringement and taking legal action when necessary. Rules and protection periods differ between types of IP and between countries.

definition: The interbank market is the market in which banks lend money to and borrow money from each other, usually for very short periods, often overnight.
explanation: Banks' cash positions change constantly as customers deposit and withdraw money and make payments. At the end of each day, some banks have more cash than they need, while others are short. The interbank market allows them to lend and borrow among themselves to balance their positions.
Interbank loans can be unsecured, based on trust in the borrowing bank, or secured, through repurchase agreements in which the borrower provides collateral such as government bonds.
For example, a bank with surplus reserves at the end of the day might lend 100 million overnight to another bank that needs to meet its reserve requirements, earning interest for one night.

Interest rates in the interbank market are closely watched because they reflect banks' funding costs and confidence in the banking system. During the 2008 financial crisis, banks became reluctant to lend to each other, interbank rates rose sharply and lending dried up, forcing central banks to step in. Benchmark rates based on overnight transactions, such as SOFR in the United States, SONIA in the United Kingdom and €STR in the euro area, are used to price many financial products.

definition: An interchange fee is a fee paid by a merchant's bank to a cardholder's bank each time a card payment is made, set by the card network and usually calculated as a percentage of the transaction plus a small fixed amount.
explanation: When a customer pays by card, several parties are involved: the customer, the merchant, the customer's bank that issued the card, the merchant's bank that processes card payments, and the card network, such as Visa or Mastercard. The interchange fee is paid by the merchant's bank to the card issuer.

The merchant's bank passes this cost on to the merchant, as part of the total fee the merchant pays for accepting cards. This total is often called the merchant service charge or merchant discount rate.
For example, on a 100 purchase with an interchange fee of 1.5%, the card issuer receives 1.50. The merchant pays this plus other processing and network fees.

Interchange fees help pay for card issuers' costs, fraud protection, interest-free periods and rewards programmes such as cashback and air miles. However, merchants often pass the costs on to all customers through higher prices. Because of concerns about high fees, several regions have capped interchange fees. For example, the European Union limits them to 0.2% for consumer debit cards and 0.3% for consumer credit cards.

definition: An intercompany transaction is a transaction between two companies in the same group, such as a sale of goods, a loan, a service charge or a dividend between a parent and its subsidiary.
explanation: Groups often trade within themselves. A manufacturing subsidiary may sell products to a sales subsidiary in another country, a parent may lend money to a subsidiary, or a central services company may charge other group companies for IT and finance support.

In the separate accounts of each company, these transactions are recorded like any other. But in the consolidated accounts, which present the group as a single business, they must be removed, because a group cannot make a sale to itself or owe money to itself.

For example, if one subsidiary sells goods to another for 500,000, the group's consolidated revenue and costs must both be reduced by 500,000, and any profit still sitting in unsold inventory must be removed.

Intercompany transactions require careful tracking and matching between group companies, which can be a major task during the financial close. Across borders, their prices also determine where profits are taxed, so they must follow transfer pricing rules.

definition: Interest is the cost of borrowing money, or the reward for lending or saving it. It is usually expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed or saved.
explanation: When you borrow, interest is the price you pay for using someone else's money. When you save or lend, interest is what you earn for letting someone else use yours. A bank pays interest on savings because it lends that money to other customers at a higher rate.
Interest is usually set as an annual percentage, called the interest rate. If you borrow 10,000 at 6% a year, you pay about 600 in interest over a year if the full amount remains outstanding.

There are two main ways interest is calculated. Simple interest is charged only on the original amount. Compound interest is charged on the original amount plus any interest already added, which makes balances grow faster over time.

Interest rates reflect several things: how risky the borrower is, how long the money is borrowed for, expected inflation and the general level of rates set by the central bank. When central banks raise rates, borrowing becomes more expensive and saving becomes more rewarding.

definition: The interest coverage ratio is a company's operating profit, usually EBIT, divided by its interest expense. It shows how many times over the company can pay its interest from its earnings.
explanation: This ratio measures how comfortably a company can meet the interest payments on its debt. A higher ratio means a bigger cushion before interest payments become a strain.
For example, a company with EBIT of 400,000 and interest expense of 50,000 has an interest coverage ratio of 8. Its operating profit is eight times its interest bill.

A ratio below about 1.5 is often seen as a warning sign, because a modest fall in profits could leave the company unable to cover its interest. A ratio below 1 means operating profit does not cover interest at all, so the company must use cash reserves, sell assets or borrow more.
Some versions use EBITDA instead of EBIT in the numerator, giving a higher figure because depreciation and amortization are excluded.

Lenders and credit rating agencies use interest coverage to assess credit risk, and many loan agreements include a minimum required ratio. The ratio is particularly important when interest rates are rising, since higher rates increase interest expense and can quickly erode coverage for companies with large amounts of floating-rate debt.

definition: Interest expense is the cost a company incurs for borrowed money during a period, such as interest on loans, bonds and lease liabilities.
explanation: When a company borrows, it must pay interest to its lenders. Interest expense records that cost in the income statement for the period in which it accrues, whether or not it has been paid yet.
For example, a company with a 2 million loan at 6% a year incurs about 120,000 of interest expense annually.

Interest expense usually appears below operating income on the income statement, because it reflects how the business is financed rather than how well it operates. Subtracting it from operating income, along with any other non-operating items, gives profit before tax.
In many tax systems, interest expense is deductible, which reduces taxable profit, although some countries limit how much interest can be deducted.

Analysts watch interest expense closely. Rising interest expense can signal growing debt or higher interest rates, and it reduces the profit left for shareholders. Comparing operating income with interest expense, through the interest coverage ratio, shows how comfortably a company can meet its interest payments.

definition: Interest income is the money a company or individual earns from lending money or holding interest-bearing assets, such as bank deposits, bonds and loans.
explanation: Interest income is the opposite of interest expense. When a company keeps cash in interest-bearing accounts, holds bonds or lends money to others, it earns interest, which is recorded as income in the period it is earned.
For example, a company with 5 million in deposits earning 4% a year would record about 200,000 of interest income.

For most non-financial companies, interest income is a small, non-operating item, shown separately from revenue from their main business. It is often reported net of interest expense as "net finance costs" or "net interest".

For banks and other lenders, interest income is the core of the business. It is their main source of revenue, and the difference between interest income and interest expense, called net interest income, is a key measure of their performance.

For individuals, interest income includes interest on savings accounts and bonds. In many countries it is taxable, although some accounts or allowances let people earn a certain amount of interest tax-free.

definition: An interest rate is the percentage charged on borrowed money, or paid on saved money, over a period of time, usually a year.
explanation: An interest rate turns the cost of borrowing into a simple percentage. If a loan has an interest rate of 8% a year, borrowing 1,000 for a year costs about 80 in interest.

Interest rates vary widely. A government savings product might pay 3%, a mortgage might charge 5%, a car loan 8% and a credit card more than 20%. The differences reflect risk, loan length, whether the loan is secured by an asset and the lender's costs and profit.

Across an economy, interest rates are influenced by the central bank, which sets a key policy rate. When the central bank raises its rate to fight inflation, banks usually raise the rates they charge borrowers and pay savers. When it cuts rates to support the economy, borrowing becomes cheaper.

When comparing interest rates, it helps to check what the rate includes. Some rates include fees and the effect of compounding, while others do not. Terms such as APR and APY exist so that borrowers and savers can compare products on a fair basis.

definition: An interest rate cap is a derivative contract that pays the holder when a floating interest rate rises above a set level, called the cap rate, protecting borrowers against rising interest costs.
explanation: A cap works like insurance on a floating-rate loan. The borrower pays an upfront premium. Then, at each payment date, if the reference rate is above the cap rate, the seller of the cap pays the difference on the notional amount for that period. If the rate stays below the cap, nothing is paid.

For example, a company with a 20,000,000 floating-rate loan buys a cap at 5%. If the reference rate rises to 6.5% for a quarter, the cap pays 1.5% on 20,000,000 for a quarter of a year, or 75,000, offsetting the extra interest.

A cap is made up of a series of individual options, called caplets, one for each interest period. Its price depends on the cap rate, the length of the cap, current rates and expected interest rate volatility.

Caps let borrowers benefit from low rates while limiting the cost if rates rise sharply. Lenders sometimes require borrowers with floating-rate debt, such as in property or leveraged buyouts, to buy caps. Combining a cap with a floor creates a collar, which reduces the cost.

definition: An interest rate floor is a derivative contract that pays the holder when a floating interest rate falls below a set level, called the floor rate, protecting lenders and investors against falling interest income.
explanation: A floor is the mirror image of a cap. The buyer pays a premium, and at each payment date, if the reference rate is below the floor rate, the seller pays the difference on the notional amount for that period.

For example, an investor holding 20,000,000 of floating-rate assets buys a floor at 2%. If the reference rate falls to 1.25% for a quarter, the floor pays 0.75% on 20,000,000 for a quarter of a year, or 37,500.
A floor is made up of a series of individual options called floorlets. Floors are used by banks, investors and lenders who earn floating-rate income and want protection if rates fall.

Many floating-rate loans also include a built-in floor, which sets a minimum interest rate the borrower must pay, often by setting a minimum level for the benchmark rate. Combining a bought cap with a sold floor creates an interest rate collar, which reduces the cost of protection but limits the benefit if rates fall.

definition: Interest rate parity is the principle that the difference in interest rates between two countries should be offset by the difference between the forward exchange rate and the spot exchange rate, so that investors cannot earn risk-free profits by moving money between currencies.
explanation: If one currency offers higher interest rates than another, investors might be tempted to move money into it. Interest rate parity says that, when currency risk is hedged with a forward contract, the extra interest is cancelled out by a less favourable forward rate.

For example, suppose one euro buys 1.10 US dollars today, US interest rates are 5% and euro interest rates are 3% for one year. Covered interest rate parity implies a one-year forward rate of about 1.1214 dollars per euro. An investor who converts dollars into euros, earns 3% and converts back at the forward rate ends up with the same amount as one who simply earns 5% in dollars.

This version, covered interest rate parity, generally holds closely in normal markets because of arbitrage, although small deviations have appeared since 2008. Uncovered interest rate parity, which assumes expected future exchange rates offset interest differences without hedging, often fails in practice, which is why carry trades, borrowing in low-rate currencies to invest in high-rate ones, can be profitable for long periods, but also risky.

definition: Interest rate risk is the risk that changes in interest rates will reduce the value of an investment or increase the cost of borrowing.
explanation: For bond investors, the main form of interest rate risk is that bond prices fall when interest rates rise. Existing bonds paying a fixed rate become less attractive compared with new bonds paying higher rates, so their prices drop.

The size of the effect depends mainly on a bond's duration. As a rough guide, a bond with a duration of 7 will fall in price by about 7% if interest rates rise by one percentage point. Longer-term bonds are therefore more exposed to interest rate risk than short-term ones.

For example, an investor holding a ten-year government bond may see its market value fall noticeably if rates rise, even though the government is certain to repay at maturity. If the investor holds the bond until it matures, they will still receive the full face value.

Interest rate risk also affects borrowers. Those with variable-rate loans face higher payments when rates rise. Banks face interest rate risk when the rates on their loans and deposits adjust at different times.
Investors manage this risk by choosing bonds with shorter durations, spreading maturities over time or using financial contracts such as interest rate swaps.

definition: The interest rate spread is the difference between the average interest rate a bank charges on loans and the average rate it pays on deposits and other borrowing.
explanation: The spread is a basic measure of how much a bank earns from its lending activity. If a bank charges an average of 6% on loans and pays an average of 2.5% on deposits, its interest rate spread is 3.5 percentage points.
The spread must cover the bank's operating costs, such as staff, branches and technology, the cost of loans that are not repaid and the bank's profit.

The interest rate spread is similar to, but not the same as, the net interest margin. The spread compares two average rates. The net interest margin compares net interest income with interest-earning assets, so it also reflects how much of the bank's funding comes from sources that pay little or no interest, such as current accounts and equity.

Spreads vary by country and by type of lending. Credit cards and unsecured loans have wide spreads because they are riskier. Mortgages usually have narrower spreads. Changes in competition, central bank rates and economic conditions all affect spreads.

definition: An interest rate swap is a contract in which two parties agree to exchange interest payments on a notional principal amount, typically with one paying a fixed rate and the other paying a floating rate.
explanation: Interest rate swaps are used to manage exposure to changes in interest rates. The notional principal is not exchanged; only the difference between the interest payments is usually paid.

For example, a company has a 10 million loan with a floating interest rate. Worried that rates will rise, it enters a swap agreeing to pay a fixed rate of 4% and receive the floating rate. If the floating rate is 3.5% in a year, the company pays the net difference of 0.5%, or 50,000, to the swap counterparty. If the floating rate rises to 5%, it receives 100,000. Combined with its floating-rate loan, the company has effectively locked in a cost of 4%.

Banks use swaps to manage the mismatch between their fixed-rate loans and floating-rate deposits. Investors use them to adjust the interest rate sensitivity of their portfolios. Speculators use them to bet on interest rate movements.

Floating rates in swaps are linked to benchmarks such as SOFR in the United States, SONIA in the United Kingdom and €STR in the euro area, which have replaced the older LIBOR benchmarks, now discontinued. Interest rate swaps are the largest segment of the global derivatives market.

definition: An interest-only loan is a loan where the borrower pays only the interest for a set period or for the whole term, without reducing the amount originally borrowed.
explanation: Because none of the payments go towards the principal, monthly payments on an interest-only loan are lower than on a repayment loan of the same size. However, the full amount borrowed is still owed at the end.

For example, on a 200,000 mortgage at 5%, interest-only payments would be about 833 a month. A repayment mortgage over 25 years at the same rate would cost about 1,169 a month, but the balance would be paid off by the end. With the interest-only loan, 200,000 would still be owed after 25 years.

Interest-only mortgages are often used by property investors who rent out properties, since they keep monthly costs low and plan to repay the loan by selling the property. Some homeowners use them with a separate plan, such as investments or a pension lump sum, to repay the loan at the end.

The main risk is that the borrower's repayment plan falls short, for example if investments perform poorly or property prices fall. Many lenders now require evidence of a credible repayment strategy before offering interest-only mortgages.

definition: An internal audit is an independent review carried out within an organisation to evaluate and improve its risk management, internal controls and governance processes.
explanation: Internal auditors work for the organisation, either as employees or as outsourced advisers, but they report independently, usually to the audit committee of the board, so they can give objective assessments.

Their work goes beyond the financial statements. Internal auditors may review whether purchasing procedures prevent fraud, whether IT systems are secure, whether the company complies with laws and regulations, and whether operations are efficient.

For example, an internal audit of a company's payments process might find that one employee can both set up new suppliers and approve payments to them, creating a fraud risk. The auditor would recommend separating these duties.

Internal audit differs from external audit. External auditors are independent firms that give a public opinion on the financial statements for shareholders. Internal auditors serve the organisation itself, helping management and the board strengthen controls and manage risks.

Many listed companies are required or expected to have an internal audit function. A strong internal audit can help catch problems early, before they turn into financial losses, regulatory penalties or damage to reputation.

definition: Internal control is the set of policies, procedures and checks an organisation uses to ensure its financial reporting is reliable, its operations are effective and it complies with laws, while protecting its assets from loss or fraud.
explanation: Internal controls are built into everyday processes. They include approvals, such as requiring a manager to authorise payments above a certain amount; separation of duties, so no single person controls an entire transaction; reconciliations, such as matching bank statements to the accounts; physical controls, such as locked storage; and IT controls, such as passwords and access rights.
For example, a company might require two people to approve any payment over 10,000 and reconcile its bank accounts every month. These controls make it harder for errors or fraud to go unnoticed.
Good internal control reduces the risk of mistakes, theft and misleading financial statements. It also helps managers run the business efficiently.

In some countries, listed companies must formally assess and report on the effectiveness of their internal controls over financial reporting, and auditors must test them. In the United States, this requirement comes from the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

No system of internal control is perfect. Controls can be overridden by senior management, bypassed through collusion or fail because of human error, so they provide reasonable rather than absolute assurance.

definition: The internal rate of return (IRR) is the annual rate of return a project or investment is expected to earn, calculated as the discount rate at which its net present value equals zero.
explanation: IRR expresses a project's profitability as a single percentage, which makes it easy to compare with a company's cost of capital or with other investments.

Take the same machine that costs 50,000 and produces 15,000, 18,000, 20,000 and 12,000 over four years. Its IRR is about 11.6%. That means the project earns the equivalent of 11.6% a year on the money invested. If the company's required return is 8%, the project clears the hurdle comfortably.
IRR usually cannot be calculated by hand; it is found by trial and error or with a spreadsheet or financial calculator.

IRR has limitations. It assumes cash flows received can be reinvested at the IRR itself, which may be unrealistic. For projects with unusual cash flows, such as large costs in later years, there can be more than one IRR or none at all. When comparing projects of different sizes, a smaller project may have a higher IRR but add less value overall. For these reasons, IRR is usually used alongside net present value rather than instead of it.

definition: International diversification is spreading investments across different countries and regions, rather than concentrating them in one's home market, to reduce risk and access wider opportunities.
explanation: Many investors tend to hold mostly investments from their own country, a pattern called home bias. International diversification reduces dependence on a single economy, currency, political system or stock market.

Different countries' markets do not always move together. An economic slowdown, policy change or industry decline in one country may not affect others in the same way. Holding investments across many countries can therefore smooth out returns.

For example, an investor whose home market is dominated by banks and energy companies might diversify internationally to gain exposure to technology, healthcare and consumer companies that are more common in other markets.
International diversification also provides access to growth in other economies and to companies that may not be available at home.

It brings additional considerations. Currency movements can add to or reduce returns. Some markets carry political, legal or liquidity risks. And in severe global crises, markets around the world often fall together, reducing the benefit of diversification just when it is most needed. Many investors use global or international index funds as a simple way to diversify across countries.

definition: International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) are a set of accounting rules used in many countries around the world so that companies' financial statements are prepared in a consistent and comparable way.
explanation: IFRS are issued by the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). They are required or permitted for listed companies in many jurisdictions, including the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and many countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America. The United States uses its own framework, US GAAP.
The goal of IFRS is a common financial language across borders. An investor comparing a German car maker with a Korean one can be more confident that the figures were prepared on a similar basis.

IFRS are often described as more principles-based than US GAAP. They set out broad principles and expect companies to apply judgment, while US GAAP has historically included more detailed rules for specific situations. In practice, the two frameworks have moved closer together over the years.

IFRS also use some different names. For example, the balance sheet is formally called the statement of financial position, and the income statement is part of the statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income.

definition: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international organisation that works to promote global financial stability, international monetary cooperation and economic growth, including by lending to member countries facing balance of payments problems.
explanation: The IMF was created in 1944 at the Bretton Woods conference, alongside the World Bank, and is based in Washington, DC. It has around 190 member countries.

The IMF has three main roles. It monitors the economic policies of member countries and the global economy, publishing regular assessments and forecasts. It provides loans to countries experiencing financial crises, such as difficulty paying for imports or servicing foreign debts. And it offers technical assistance and training to help countries improve their economic management.

IMF loans often come with conditions, requiring the borrowing country to adopt policies such as reducing budget deficits, reforming its banking system or changing its exchange rate policy. For example, during the European debt crisis, the IMF participated in rescue programmes for countries such as Greece, Ireland and Portugal.

These conditions have been controversial. Critics argue that they have sometimes required harsh austerity that deepened recessions and hurt vulnerable people. Supporters argue that the IMF provides crucial support when no one else will lend, helping to prevent crises from spreading.

definition: Interpolation is a method of estimating an unknown value that lies between two or more known values.
explanation: When data are available only at certain points, interpolation fills in the gaps. The simplest form, linear interpolation, assumes the value changes in a straight line between known points.

For example, if the two-year interest rate is 4% and the five-year rate is 5%, a linear interpolation estimates the three-year rate as about 4.33%, a third of the way between them, since three years is one third of the distance from two to five.

Interpolation is widely used in finance. Analysts interpolate yield curves to find rates for maturities that are not directly quoted, estimate values between data points in tables and fill in missing data in time series.

More sophisticated methods, such as cubic splines, fit smooth curves through the known points, which can be more realistic for yield curves. Interpolation is generally more reliable than extrapolation, because it stays within the range of known data, but it still assumes the pattern between points is smooth and predictable.

definition: An option is in the money when exercising it immediately would be profitable: for a call, when the underlying price is above the strike price; for a put, when it is below.
explanation: An in-the-money option has intrinsic value. The further it is in the money, the more intrinsic value it has.
For example, if a share trades at 75, a call option with a strike price of 60 is in the money by 15. A put option with a strike price of 80 on the same share is in the money by 5.

In-the-money options are more expensive than at-the-money or out-of-the-money options, because their premium includes intrinsic value as well as time value. They also tend to move more closely with the price of the underlying asset. A deep in-the-money call might rise by nearly 1 for every 1 rise in the share price.

Being in the money does not necessarily mean the buyer has made a profit. The buyer also paid a premium. If you paid 18 for the call with a strike of 60, the share must rise above 78 for you to profit at expiry, even though the option is in the money at 75.
At expiry, options that are in the money by a small amount are often exercised automatically by the exchange.

definition: Intrinsic value is the estimated true worth of an asset based on its fundamental characteristics, such as the cash it is expected to generate, rather than its current market price.
explanation: Market prices can be swayed by emotions, trends and short-term news. Intrinsic value tries to look past these to what an asset is really worth based on its underlying economics.

For a company, intrinsic value is often estimated using a discounted cash flow analysis: forecasting the cash the business will generate in future and discounting it to today. Other methods use dividends, earnings or assets.

For example, an analyst might estimate that a company's future cash flows are worth 45 per share today. If the shares trade at 35, the analyst would see them as undervalued and potentially a good investment. If they trade at 60, they may look overvalued.
Value investors focus on buying assets below their intrinsic value, often leaving a margin of safety to allow for errors in their estimates.

Intrinsic value is an estimate, not a fact. It depends on assumptions about future growth, profits and risk, so different investors may reach different conclusions. The term also has a separate meaning for options, where it refers to the amount by which an option is in the money.

definition: The intrinsic value of an option is the amount it would be worth if it were exercised immediately. It is never less than zero.
explanation: For a call option, intrinsic value is the underlying asset's current price minus the strike price, if that is positive. For a put option, it is the strike price minus the current price, if that is positive. If exercising would not be profitable, the intrinsic value is zero.

For example, if a share trades at 62, a call with a strike price of 55 has an intrinsic value of 7. A put with a strike price of 55 on the same share has an intrinsic value of zero, because selling at 55 something worth 62 would make no sense. A put with a strike of 70 would have an intrinsic value of 8.
An option with intrinsic value is said to be in the money. An option with no intrinsic value is either at the money or out of the money.

An option's price, its premium, is usually higher than its intrinsic value, because it also includes time value. At expiry, however, time value disappears, and the option's value equals its intrinsic value. The term intrinsic value has a different meaning when applied to shares or companies, where it refers to their estimated fundamental worth.

definition: Inventory is the goods a business holds for sale, along with the materials and partly finished products used to make them.
explanation: For a shop, inventory is the stock on its shelves and in its storeroom. For a manufacturer, it includes raw materials, work in progress and finished goods ready for sale. Inventory is recorded as a current asset on the balance sheet, because it is expected to be sold within a year.
When inventory is sold, its cost moves from the balance sheet to the income statement as cost of goods sold. The difference between the selling price and that cost gives gross profit.

Valuing inventory involves choices. When identical items were bought at different prices, the business must decide which cost to assign to the items sold. Common methods include first-in, first-out (FIFO), which assumes the oldest items are sold first, and weighted average cost. Accounting rules also require inventory to be reduced in value if it can only be sold for less than it cost.

Managing inventory is a balancing act. Too little means lost sales; too much ties up cash, needs storage and risks becoming damaged or out of date. Businesses track how quickly inventory sells to strike the right balance.

definition: Inventory turnover is the number of times a business sells and replaces its inventory during a period, usually calculated as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory.
explanation: Inventory turnover shows how efficiently a business manages its stock. Higher turnover means goods are sold quickly, so less cash is tied up in inventory and there is less risk of goods becoming outdated or damaged.

For example, a retailer with annual cost of goods sold of 1,200,000 and average inventory of 200,000 has an inventory turnover of 6. On average, it sells through its stock about every 61 days, which is 365 divided by 6.
What counts as good turnover depends on the industry. Supermarkets selling perishable food turn their inventory many times a year, while furniture or jewellery retailers turn it much less often.

A falling turnover may signal weak sales or overstocking. A very high turnover can be efficient, but may also mean the business risks running out of stock and losing sales. Turnover is closely linked to days inventory outstanding, which expresses the same idea in days.

definition: Investing is putting money into assets, such as shares, bonds, funds or property, with the aim of growing wealth or earning income over time.
explanation: When you invest, you give up using money today in the hope of having more in the future. The return comes from income, such as interest, dividends or rent, and from increases in the value of what you own.

Investing differs from saving. Saving usually means keeping money safe and easy to reach, often in a bank account, with little risk and modest returns. Investing accepts some risk, including the possibility of losses, in exchange for the chance of higher returns over time.

The longer the time horizon, the more powerful investing becomes, because returns can compound. If 10,000 earns an average of 6% a year, it grows to about 17,900 in ten years and about 32,100 in twenty, though actual returns vary from year to year and are never guaranteed.

Sensible investing usually involves knowing your goals and time frame, spreading money across different assets to reduce risk, keeping costs low and avoiding decisions driven by short-term fear or excitement. Money that may be needed soon is usually better kept in savings than invested.

definition: An investment is something you buy or put money into with the expectation that it will produce income or grow in value over time.
explanation: The key difference between spending and investing is the purpose. When you spend money, you use it for something now. When you invest money, you give up using it today in the hope of having more later.

Common investments include shares in companies, bonds, funds, property, savings products and businesses. Each offers a different mix of potential return and risk. A savings account offers low but steady returns. Shares can grow much more over long periods but can also fall sharply in the short term. Property can provide rent and price growth but is expensive to buy and slow to sell.
The word is also used in a business sense. When a company spends money on new equipment, research or a new factory, it is making an investment, expecting the spending to produce future profits.

All investments carry some risk, and returns are never guaranteed, especially in the short term. Good investing usually involves understanding what you are buying, spreading money across different assets and matching the investment to how long you can leave the money untouched.

definition: An investment bank is a financial institution that helps companies and governments raise money in financial markets, advises on mergers and acquisitions, and trades securities.
explanation: Unlike commercial banks, investment banks do not mainly take deposits from the public and make everyday loans. Their work centres on large financial transactions.

A key role is underwriting. When a company wants to raise money by selling shares in an initial public offering or by issuing bonds, an investment bank helps price the securities, prepare documents and find investors, often guaranteeing to buy any that remain unsold.

Investment banks also advise companies on mergers and acquisitions, helping them buy, sell or combine businesses and negotiate terms. Many have trading divisions that buy and sell shares, bonds, currencies and derivatives for clients and for themselves, and research teams that analyse companies and markets.
For example, an investment bank might advise a company on buying a competitor for 2 billion and then help it raise the money by issuing bonds.
Investment banks earn fees for advice and underwriting, and profits from trading. Many large banking groups combine investment banking with commercial and retail banking.

definition: An investment horizon is the length of time an investor expects to hold an investment or a portfolio before needing to use the money.
explanation: The investment horizon is one of the most important factors in choosing investments. It determines how much risk an investor can reasonably take and which types of assets are suitable.

Money needed soon, within a year or two, generally belongs in safe, stable assets, such as savings accounts or short-term bonds, because there is little time to recover from a market fall. Money not needed for ten or twenty years can usually be invested in higher-risk, higher-return assets, such as shares, because there is more time to ride out market ups and downs.
For example, someone saving for a house deposit needed in eighteen months would usually avoid shares, while a 30-year-old saving for retirement could reasonably invest mostly in shares.

Investment horizons often differ for different goals. One person might have a short horizon for an emergency fund, a medium horizon for a child's education and a long horizon for retirement, each with a different investment approach.
As a goal approaches, the investment horizon shortens, and investors often gradually shift towards lower-risk investments. This is the principle behind target-date funds.

definition: An investment objective is the specific goal an investor wants their money to achieve, such as long-term growth, regular income or keeping capital safe.
explanation: Before choosing investments, it helps to be clear about what the money is for. The investment objective guides every other decision, including which assets to hold, how much risk to accept and how long to stay invested.

Common objectives include capital growth, aiming to increase the value of investments over the long term; income, aiming to receive regular payments such as dividends or interest; capital preservation, aiming above all to avoid losses; and a balance of growth and income.

For example, a 30-year-old saving for retirement might choose long-term growth and accept large ups and downs along the way. A retired person relying on investments for living costs might prioritise steady income and lower volatility. Someone saving for a home deposit needed in two years would likely prioritise keeping the money safe.

Investment funds state their objectives in their documents, so investors can choose funds that match their own goals. Financial advisers also start by understanding a client's objectives, time horizon and tolerance for risk.

definition: Investment value is the value of an asset to a particular investor, based on that investor's own goals, circumstances and expected benefits.
explanation: Unlike fair market value, which describes a price between typical buyers and sellers, investment value is specific to one buyer or owner. It reflects what the asset is worth to them in particular.

Different investors can place very different values on the same asset. A company might be worth 50 million to most buyers. But a competitor that expects to save 10 million a year by merging operations, or a buyer who wants access to its technology, might value it at 70 million. That 70 million is the competitor's investment value.
Investment value depends on factors such as expected synergies, tax position, financing costs, required return and strategic fit.

The concept matters in negotiations and acquisitions. A buyer should know its own investment value to decide the maximum price it can pay without destroying value. A seller who understands that a particular buyer places a high value on the business may be able to negotiate a higher price. Valuation professionals are careful to state which standard of value they are using, because the result can differ significantly.

definition: An investor is a person or organisation that puts money into assets, such as shares, bonds, property or businesses, expecting to earn a return.
explanation: Investors range from individuals saving for retirement to huge institutions. Individual investors, often called retail investors, invest their own money, usually through brokerage accounts, pension plans or funds. Institutional investors, such as pension funds, insurance companies, mutual funds and endowments, invest very large sums on behalf of many people.

Investors differ in their goals, time horizons and attitudes to risk. A 25-year-old saving for retirement can usually accept more ups and downs than a 70-year-old who needs a steady income now. Some investors want regular income, others want long-term growth, and some prioritise keeping their money safe.
Investors also differ in approach. Some try to pick individual winners or time the market. Others buy broad, low-cost index funds and hold them for many years.

Investors play an important role in the economy. By buying shares and bonds, they provide companies and governments with money to grow, build and operate. In return, they share in the profits through dividends, interest and rising asset values, while also bearing the risk of losses.

definition: An iron condor is an options strategy that combines four options to profit when an asset's price stays within a set range, by selling a put and a call close to the current price and buying a further-away put and call for protection.
explanation: An iron condor combines two credit spreads: a bull put spread below the current price and a bear call spread above it. The trader receives a net premium upfront and keeps it if the price stays between the two inner exercise prices until expiry.

For example, with a share trading at 100, a trader sells a put with an exercise price of 95 and a call with an exercise price of 105, and buys a put at 90 and a call at 110. Suppose the net premium received is 3.00. If the share stays between 95 and 105, the trader keeps the full 3.00. The maximum loss, if the share falls below 90 or rises above 110, is the 5.00 gap between exercise prices minus the 3.00 received, or 2.00.
Iron condors are popular when traders expect low volatility. Both profit and loss are limited, making the risk defined in advance.

The trade-off is that the potential profit is usually smaller than the potential loss, so the strategy needs to succeed most of the time. Sharp moves or rising volatility can quickly turn it into a loss.

definition: Issued shares are the shares a company has actually sold or given to shareholders, including any it has later bought back and holds in treasury.
explanation: Issued shares sit between authorized shares and outstanding shares. Authorized shares are the maximum the company may issue. Issued shares are those it has actually issued. Outstanding shares are issued shares minus any treasury shares the company has bought back and still holds.
For example, a company with 60,000,000 issued shares that holds 5,000,000 in treasury has 55,000,000 shares outstanding.
The difference matters for calculations. Earnings per share, market capitalization and voting rights are based on outstanding shares, since treasury shares do not receive dividends or vote.

The number of issued shares changes when the company sells new shares, issues shares to employees, converts securities such as convertible bonds into shares or cancels shares it has bought back. Many companies cancel repurchased shares rather than holding them in treasury, which reduces issued shares directly.

definition: In card payments, an issuer is the bank or financial institution that provides a payment card to a customer, approves transactions and is responsible for collecting payment from the cardholder.
explanation: The issuer, or issuing bank, sets the terms of the card, including the credit limit, interest rate, fees and rewards. When the cardholder makes a purchase, the issuer decides whether to approve it, based on available funds or credit and fraud checks.

The issuer pays the merchant's acquirer for approved transactions, through the card network, and then collects the money from the cardholder, either immediately from a debit account or through a monthly credit card bill.

For example, when a customer pays with a credit card, the issuing bank checks the account, approves the purchase within seconds and later bills the customer. It earns income from interest, annual fees and interchange fees paid by merchants' banks.

Issuers handle disputes and chargebacks and are responsible for protecting cardholders from fraud. In securities markets, the term issuer has a different meaning: a company, government or other organisation that issues shares, bonds or other securities to investors.

definition: An itemized deduction is a specific allowable expense, such as certain mortgage interest, state and local taxes, medical costs or charitable gifts, that a taxpayer lists individually to reduce taxable income. The term is used mainly in the United States.
explanation: In the US federal tax system, taxpayers can reduce their taxable income in one of two ways. They can take the standard deduction, a fixed amount based on filing status, or they can itemize, adding up their eligible expenses and deducting the total. They choose whichever is larger.
For example, if a taxpayer's standard deduction would be 14,000 but their eligible itemized expenses add up to 16,500, itemizing reduces their taxable income by an extra 2,500.

Itemizing requires records, such as receipts and statements, and many items have their own limits or conditions. Because the standard deduction is fairly large, most US taxpayers do not itemize. Itemizing is more common among people with large mortgage interest payments, high state and local taxes or significant charitable giving.
Many other countries do not use this choice. Instead, they offer a personal allowance and a separate list of reliefs that can be claimed in addition to it.

definition: Job costing is a method of tracking the costs of individual jobs, projects or orders separately, used when each piece of work is different, such as custom manufacturing, construction or professional services.
explanation: In job costing, each job has its own cost record. Direct materials and direct labour used on the job are recorded against it, and overheads are added using a predetermined rate, such as a rate per labour hour.

For example, a print shop takes a custom order. Materials cost 4,000, the job uses 30 labour hours at 40 an hour, or 1,200, and overheads are charged at 25 per labour hour, or 750. The total job cost is 5,950. The shop can compare this with the price charged to see the job's profit.
Job costing is used by businesses such as builders, furniture makers, repair shops, law firms, consultants and advertising agencies, where each customer's work is distinct.

It helps businesses price new jobs accurately, track profitability by customer or project and spot cost overruns while work is in progress. It contrasts with process costing, used where identical units are produced continuously and costs are averaged across them.

definition: A joint venture is an arrangement in which two or more parties share control of a business or project, with major decisions requiring the agreement of all the controlling parties.
explanation: Companies form joint ventures to combine resources, share risks and costs, enter new markets or access each other's technology or expertise. For example, a foreign company might form a joint venture with a local partner to operate in a country where it lacks experience or where rules require local ownership.

The key feature is joint control: no single party can make important decisions alone. This distinguishes a joint venture from a subsidiary, which one parent controls, and from an associate, over which the investor has influence but not control.

In accounting, investments in joint ventures are generally recorded using the equity method, in which the investor recognises its share of the venture's profits or losses rather than consolidating its assets and liabilities line by line. Under IFRS, arrangements in which the parties have direct rights to specific assets and obligations for specific liabilities are classed differently, as joint operations.
For example, two energy companies might each own 50% of a joint venture that builds and runs a wind farm, sharing its profits equally.
Joint ventures can succeed when partners have complementary strengths, but they can also suffer from disagreements over strategy and control.

definition: A journal entry is the record of a single business transaction, showing the date, the accounts affected, the amounts debited and credited and a short description.
explanation: A journal entry is the first step in recording a transaction in double-entry bookkeeping. It shows which accounts change and by how much, with total debits always equal to total credits.

Suppose a business pays 1,500 of rent from its bank account on 1 March. The journal entry would show a debit of 1,500 to rent expense and a credit of 1,500 to cash, with the date and a note such as "March office rent".
Journal entries are listed in the order transactions happen, in a record called the journal. They are then posted to individual accounts in the general ledger.

Besides everyday transactions, accountants make special journal entries at the end of each period. Adjusting entries record items such as accrued expenses and depreciation. Closing entries reset revenue and expense accounts for the next period. Each journal entry should be supported by evidence, such as an invoice, receipt or contract, so that it can be checked later by managers or auditors.

definition: A key performance indicator (KPI) is a measurable value that shows how well a business, team or individual is achieving an important objective.
explanation: KPIs turn goals into numbers that can be tracked. Instead of a vague aim such as "keep customers happy", a business might track a specific KPI such as the percentage of customers who renew each year.

Good KPIs are clearly linked to strategy, measurable, understood by the people responsible for them and tracked regularly. They often come with targets, so performance can be judged as on track or off track.

KPIs vary by business and role. A shop might track sales per square metre and average transaction value. A subscription business might track monthly recurring revenue and churn rate. A factory might track output per hour and defect rates. A finance team might track how quickly customers pay.
For example, if a call centre sets a KPI of answering 90% of calls within 30 seconds and actually answers 82%, managers know there is a problem to investigate.

Choosing the right KPIs matters. Measuring too many dilutes focus, and measuring the wrong things can encourage unhelpful behaviour, such as rushing calls to hit a time target at the expense of quality.

definition: Keynesian economics is a school of economic thought, based on the work of John Maynard Keynes, which holds that total demand is the main driver of output and employment in the short run, and that governments should act to stabilise the economy during downturns.
explanation: Keynes developed his ideas during the Great Depression of the 1930s, most famously in his 1936 book The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. He challenged the view that markets always correct themselves quickly.

Keynes argued that economies can remain stuck with high unemployment for long periods if demand is too weak. Because wages and prices adjust slowly, falling demand leads to lower output and job losses rather than quickly falling prices. In such situations, he argued, governments should increase spending or cut taxes to boost demand, even if this means running budget deficits.
For example, Keynesian thinking supports government stimulus programmes during recessions, such as infrastructure spending or payments to households, to replace lost private demand.

Keynesian economics dominated policy in many countries from the 1940s to the 1970s. It lost influence after the stagflation of the 1970s, but Keynesian ideas, combined with other approaches, still shape how governments and central banks respond to recessions.
