Preferred stockholders must receive their dividends before any dividends can be paid to common stockholders. Many preferred shares are cumulative, which means that if the company skips a dividend, the missed amount must be paid later before common stockholders get anything.

For example, a preferred share with a face value of 100 and a 6% dividend rate pays 6 a year. If the company cannot pay one year, a cumulative preferred share would be owed 12 the next year before common shareholders receive any dividend.

In a bankruptcy, preferred stockholders are paid after lenders and bondholders but before common stockholders. In return for this greater safety, they usually give up voting rights and the potential for large gains, because their dividends do not usually rise when the company does well.

definition: Pre-money valuation is the value of a company immediately before it receives new investment in a funding round.
explanation: Pre-money valuation is used mainly in start-up and venture capital financing. It determines how much of the company new investors will own in exchange for their investment.

For example, if a start-up has a pre-money valuation of 16 million and investors put in 4 million, the post-money valuation becomes 20 million. The investors own 4 million divided by 20 million, or 20% of the company, and the existing shareholders keep 80%.

Pre-money valuation is usually the result of negotiation between founders and investors. For young companies with little revenue or profit, it depends on factors such as the strength of the team, the size of the market, early customer traction, the technology, comparable deals and the amount of competition among investors.

Founders generally prefer a higher pre-money valuation, since it means giving up less ownership for the same amount of money. But a valuation that is too high can make future funding rounds difficult if the company cannot grow into it, possibly leading to a down round, where new shares are sold at a lower price.

definition: A prepaid expense is a payment made in advance for goods or services that will be received or used in future periods. It is recorded as an asset until it is used up.
explanation: When a business pays for something before it benefits from it, the payment is not yet an expense. It is an asset, because the business has a right to receive the goods or services later.

Common examples are insurance premiums, rent paid in advance, software subscriptions and service contracts. As each period passes and the benefit is used, part of the prepaid amount is moved from the balance sheet to the income statement as an expense.

Suppose a company pays 6,000 on 1 July for six months of rent. On that day, it records a prepaid rent asset of 6,000. At the end of each month, 1,000 is moved to rent expense. By 31 December, the prepaid rent has been used up and the asset is zero.
Prepaid expenses usually appear among current assets, because they are typically used within a year. They are the opposite of accrued expenses, which are costs used before they are paid.

definition: Prepayment risk is the risk that borrowers repay their loans earlier than expected, especially when interest rates fall, returning money to lenders or investors sooner and forcing them to reinvest at lower rates.
explanation: Many loans, especially mortgages, allow borrowers to repay early. When interest rates fall, borrowers often refinance at lower rates, repaying their existing loans.

For investors in mortgage-backed securities and other loan-based investments, this can be a disadvantage. They receive their money back sooner than expected, just when interest rates are low, so they can only reinvest at lower yields. They also lose the higher interest payments they expected.

For example, an investor holding mortgage-backed securities paying 6% might find that, after rates fall to 4%, many homeowners refinance, and the investor receives principal back that can only be reinvested at around 4%.

The opposite risk, extension risk, occurs when rates rise and prepayments slow, so investors are stuck with lower-yielding assets for longer. Because of these risks, mortgage-backed securities behave differently from ordinary bonds, and their prices rise less when rates fall. Prepayment models attempt to forecast borrower behaviour.

definition: Present value is what a future amount of money is worth today, after allowing for the return that money could earn in the meantime.
explanation: Money in the future is worth less than money today, because money today can be invested. Present value answers the question: how much would I need to invest today to end up with a particular amount later?

Suppose you will receive 10,000 in five years and you could earn 5% a year elsewhere. The present value of that 10,000 is about 7,835. If you invested 7,835 today at 5% a year, it would grow to 10,000 in five years. So, to you, the promise of 10,000 later is worth about 7,835 now.

This process of shrinking a future amount back to today is called discounting, and the rate used is called the discount rate. A higher discount rate or a longer wait makes the present value smaller. At 8% instead of 5%, the same 10,000 in five years would be worth only about 6,806 today.

Present value lets you compare money received at different times on an equal footing. It is used to price bonds, value businesses, compare loan offers and decide whether an investment is worth its cost.

definition: Pretax income is a company's profit before income tax expense is deducted. It is also called profit before tax or earnings before tax.
explanation: Pretax income sits near the bottom of the income statement. It is calculated by starting with revenue, subtracting cost of sales and operating expenses to reach operating income, then adding or subtracting non-operating items such as interest income, interest expense and investment gains or losses.
For example, a company with operating income of 2 million, interest expense of 300,000 and interest income of 50,000 has pretax income of 1.75 million.
Income tax expense is then deducted from pretax income to arrive at net income.

Pretax income is useful for comparing companies that face different tax rates, because it removes the effect of tax differences. It is also the starting point for calculating a company's effective tax rate: income tax expense divided by pretax income.
Pretax income differs from EBIT because it is calculated after interest. A company with a lot of debt will have a larger gap between EBIT and pretax income than a similar company with little debt.

definition: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price set by a government that sellers are not allowed to exceed.
explanation: Governments set price ceilings to make essential goods more affordable, especially during crises or for products seen as necessities, such as rent, basic food, fuel or medicines.

A price ceiling only has an effect if it is set below the equilibrium price. In that case, it lowers the price for buyers, but it also creates a shortage. At the lower price, more people want to buy, while producers are willing to supply less.

For example, if the market price of bread is 3 and the government sets a ceiling of 2, more people want bread at 2, but bakers make less because it is less profitable. The result can be empty shelves, long queues and informal or illegal markets where bread is sold above the legal price.

Price ceilings can also reduce quality, as sellers cut costs, and discourage investment in new supply. Supporters argue they protect people from unaffordable prices, while critics argue that targeted support, such as payments to people on low incomes, can help without creating shortages.

definition: Price discovery is the process by which buyers and sellers interacting in a market determine an asset's price, as new information and changing views are reflected in trades.
explanation: Markets bring together many participants with different information, opinions and needs. As they place buy and sell orders, prices move to the level at which supply and demand balance. This price reflects the market's combined assessment of the asset's value at that moment.
For example, when a company releases unexpectedly strong results, buyers rush in and sellers raise their asking prices. Within minutes, the share price adjusts upwards to reflect the new information.

Efficient price discovery requires transparent markets, active trading, many participants and access to information. Futures markets often play a key role in price discovery for commodities, since many traders express their views there.

Price discovery can be weaker in illiquid markets, private markets and markets with limited transparency, where prices may be set less often and may not reflect all available information. Good price discovery benefits the wider economy by helping capital flow to its most valued uses.

definition: Price discrimination is the practice of charging different customers different prices for the same or a very similar product, based on their willingness to pay rather than differences in cost.
explanation: Businesses use price discrimination to earn more from customers who value a product highly, while still selling to those who would only buy at a lower price.

Common examples include discounts for students and older people, airline tickets that cost more when booked close to departure, cinema tickets that are cheaper in the afternoon, software sold at different prices in different countries, and bulk discounts for large orders.
For example, an airline knows business travellers booking at short notice will pay much more than holidaymakers booking months ahead, so it charges different prices for seats on the same flight.

For price discrimination to work, a business needs some market power, a way to separate customers into groups and a way to prevent customers who buy cheaply from reselling to others. It can increase total output and allow some customers to buy who otherwise could not, but it can also transfer value from consumers to businesses. Some forms may be illegal, for example if based on protected characteristics or if they harm competition.

definition: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity of a good that people buy responds to a change in its price.
explanation: Elasticity compares the percentage change in quantity demanded with the percentage change in price. If a small price rise causes a large fall in purchases, demand is elastic. If purchases barely change, demand is inelastic.

Suppose a café raises the price of coffee from 4.00 to 4.40, about a 10% increase, and weekly sales fall from 1,000 to 920 cups, about an 8% decrease. The elasticity is roughly −0.8. Because the figure is less than 1 in absolute size, demand is inelastic: sales fell, but proportionally less than the price rose. The café's revenue actually rises, from 4,000 to 4,048 a week.

Demand tends to be more elastic when close substitutes exist, when the product takes up a large share of a budget, when it is a luxury and over longer periods, as people have time to adjust. Essential medicines and fuel in the short term tend to have inelastic demand. A particular brand of soft drink tends to have elastic demand.
Elasticity helps businesses set prices and helps governments predict how taxes will affect consumption and revenue.

definition: Price elasticity of supply measures how strongly the quantity producers supply responds to a change in the price of a good.
explanation: It compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in price. If producers can quickly increase output when prices rise, supply is elastic. If output is hard to change, supply is inelastic.

For example, if the price of a product rises by 10% and producers increase the quantity supplied by 15%, the price elasticity of supply is 1.5, so supply is elastic. If quantity supplied rises by only 3%, the elasticity is 0.3, so supply is inelastic.

Several factors affect it. Supply is more elastic when production can be increased easily, when spare capacity or stocks are available, when inputs are easy to obtain and over longer periods. Supply is less elastic for goods that take a long time to produce or that depend on fixed resources.

For instance, the supply of new housing in a city is usually inelastic in the short term, because building takes years and land is limited. That is why rising demand for homes often leads mainly to higher prices rather than many more homes in the short run.

definition: A price floor is a legal minimum price set by a government, below which a good or service cannot be sold.
explanation: Governments set price floors to protect producers or workers from prices they consider too low. Common examples include minimum wages, which set a floor on the price of labour, and minimum prices for certain agricultural products.
A price floor only has an effect if it is set above the equilibrium price. At the higher price, producers want to sell more but buyers want to buy less, creating a surplus.

For example, if the market price of milk is 0.80 per litre and the government sets a minimum price of 1.00, farmers will want to produce more milk, but consumers will buy less. The extra milk may go unsold unless the government buys it, which has led to stockpiles of products in some countries in the past.

Price floors can raise incomes for some producers, but they can also cause waste, higher prices for consumers and deadweight loss. With minimum wages, the debate centres on how much they raise workers' pay compared with any effect on employment, which depends on the level of the minimum wage and the labour market.

definition: The price-to-book ratio (P/B) compares a company's share price with its book value per share, which is the value of its net assets as shown in its accounts.
explanation: Book value is a company's total assets minus its total liabilities, the shareholders' equity on the balance sheet. Dividing it by the number of shares gives book value per share. The P/B ratio then shows how much investors are paying for each unit of those accounting net assets.
For example, if a company's share price is 30 and its book value per share is 20, its P/B ratio is 1.5. Investors are paying 1.5 times the accounting value of the company's net assets.

A P/B ratio below 1 can suggest that shares are trading for less than the value of the company's net assets, which may indicate undervaluation or that investors expect the assets to lose value or the company to make losses. A high P/B ratio often reflects expectations of strong future profits or valuable assets not shown on the balance sheet, such as brands.

P/B is especially useful for valuing banks and insurers, whose assets are mainly financial and recorded close to market value. It is less useful for companies whose main value lies in intangible assets that do not appear on the balance sheet, such as many technology firms.

definition: The price-to-cash-flow ratio compares a company's share price with its operating cash flow per share, showing how much investors are paying for each unit of cash the business generates.
explanation: The ratio is calculated by dividing the share price by operating cash flow per share, or equivalently, market capitalization by total operating cash flow.
For example, a company with a market capitalization of 1.2 billion and operating cash flow of 150 million has a price-to-cash-flow ratio of 8.

Some investors prefer cash flow to earnings because it is harder to influence through accounting choices and is not reduced by non-cash charges such as depreciation and amortization. A company with steady profits but weak cash flow may be facing problems, such as customers paying slowly, that the price-to-earnings ratio would not reveal.

A low price-to-cash-flow ratio can suggest a share is good value, while a high one suggests investors expect strong growth. As with other multiples, comparisons are most useful within the same industry.

The ratio does not account for capital expenditure, the money a business must spend to maintain and grow its assets. For that reason, analysts often also look at the price-to-free-cash-flow ratio, which subtracts capital spending.

definition: The price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) is a company's share price divided by its earnings per share. It shows how much investors are paying for each unit of the company's profit.
explanation: The P/E ratio is one of the most widely used measures of how expensive a share is. If a share trades at 60 and the company earned 4 per share over the past year, the P/E ratio is 15. Investors are paying 15 for every 1 of annual earnings.

A high P/E often means investors expect strong future growth, so they are willing to pay more today for current earnings. A low P/E may mean the company is expected to grow slowly, faces risks or is undervalued by the market.

P/E ratios vary a great deal between industries. Fast-growing technology companies often have high P/E ratios, while banks and utilities often have lower ones. Comparing a company's P/E with its peers and its own history is usually more meaningful than looking at the number alone.

The ratio has limitations. It cannot be used meaningfully when earnings are negative, it can be distorted by one-off gains or losses and it ignores debt. Analysts often look at both trailing P/E, based on past earnings, and forward P/E, based on expected earnings.

definition: The price-to-free-cash-flow ratio compares a company's market capitalization with its free cash flow, showing how much investors are paying for each unit of cash available after the business has funded its operations and capital investment.
explanation: Free cash flow is operating cash flow minus capital expenditure. It represents cash that could be used to pay dividends, buy back shares, reduce debt or make acquisitions. The price-to-free-cash-flow ratio divides market capitalization by this figure.
For example, a company with a market capitalization of 2 billion and free cash flow of 125 million has a price-to-free-cash-flow ratio of 16.

Many investors regard free cash flow as the most meaningful measure of what a business produces for its owners, because it accounts for the spending needed to maintain and grow the business. A company with high earnings but heavy capital spending may produce little free cash flow, which this ratio would reveal.
A low ratio can indicate good value. The inverse of the ratio, free cash flow divided by market capitalization, is called the free cash flow yield. In this example, it is 6.25%.
Free cash flow can vary a lot from year to year, especially when companies make large one-off investments, so analysts often look at averages over several years.

definition: The price-to-sales ratio (P/S) compares a company's market capitalization with its total revenue, showing how much investors are paying for each unit of sales.
explanation: The P/S ratio is calculated by dividing market capitalization by annual revenue, or equivalently, share price by revenue per share.
For example, a company with a market capitalization of 3 billion and annual revenue of 1.5 billion has a P/S ratio of 2.

P/S is useful for valuing companies that are not yet profitable, such as young, fast-growing businesses, because price-to-earnings ratios cannot be used when earnings are negative. Revenue is also harder to manipulate through accounting choices than earnings.

Its major limitation is that it ignores profitability. A company with high sales but very thin or negative profit margins may not deserve a high P/S ratio. Two companies with the same revenue can have very different values if one earns a 25% margin and the other loses money. P/S also ignores debt, which is why some analysts prefer EV/Revenue. P/S ratios are most meaningful when comparing companies in the same industry with similar margins.

definition: Price-volume-mix analysis is a method of explaining changes in revenue or profit between two periods by separating the effects of changes in selling prices, sales volumes and the mix of products sold.
explanation: When revenue changes, managers want to know why. Did prices rise, did the company sell more, or did customers shift towards more or less expensive products? Price-volume-mix analysis answers these questions.

For a simple example with one product, revenue rises from 50,000, from 1,000 units at 50, to 57,200, from 1,100 units at 52. The volume effect is 100 extra units at the old price of 50, or 5,000. The price effect is the 2 price increase on 1,100 units, or 2,200. Together, they explain the 7,200 increase.
With several products, a mix effect is added, capturing how a shift between higher-priced and lower-priced products changes revenue even if total volume and individual prices stay the same.

The analysis is widely used in management reporting, budgeting and investor presentations. Results can vary depending on the calculation method and order chosen, so the approach should be applied consistently.

definition: The primary market is where new securities are created and sold for the first time, with the money going to the issuing company or government.
explanation: When a company sells new shares or a government issues new bonds, the sale happens in the primary market. The issuer receives the money raised, which it can use for investment, expansion or to repay other debts.

The best-known example is an initial public offering (IPO), when a company sells shares to the public for the first time. Other examples include later sales of new shares by listed companies, new bond issues by companies and governments, and auctions of new government bonds.
Investment banks often help issuers in the primary market. They advise on pricing, find investors and may guarantee to buy any securities that are not sold, a service called underwriting.
For example, if a company issues 10 million new shares at 20 each, it raises 200 million, minus fees, in the primary market.
Once securities have been issued, they trade between investors in the secondary market, where the issuer does not receive any money from the trades.

definition: The prime rate is the interest rate that commercial banks in the United States and some other countries charge their most creditworthy customers, used as a benchmark for many other loans.
explanation: In the United States, the prime rate moves closely with the Federal Reserve's policy rate. Most major US banks set their prime rate at about 3 percentage points above the upper limit of the federal funds target range, and change it whenever the Federal Reserve changes rates.

Many variable-rate loans are priced as the prime rate plus a margin. Examples include credit cards, home equity lines of credit, some business loans and some student loans. For example, if the prime rate is 7.5%, a credit card might charge prime plus 14%, or 21.5%.
Because of this link, when the Federal Reserve raises or lowers interest rates, the cost of many consumer and business loans in the United States changes almost immediately.

Canada also uses a prime rate, set by its major banks and linked to the Bank of Canada's policy rate. Many other countries do not use a prime rate in the same way. In the United Kingdom, for example, many variable-rate loans and mortgages are linked to the Bank of England's Bank Rate or to a lender's own standard variable rate.

definition: Principal is the original amount of money borrowed or invested, before any interest is added.
explanation: In a loan, the principal is the amount you actually receive and must pay back. If you borrow 15,000 for a car, the principal is 15,000. Interest is charged on top of it, so you repay more than 15,000 in total.

As you make loan payments, each payment is usually split between interest and principal. Early in a long loan, much of each payment goes to interest. Later, more of it reduces the principal. The amount of principal still owed at any time is called the outstanding balance.
In savings and investments, the principal is the amount you originally put in. If you deposit 5,000 in an account and it earns interest of 200, the principal is still 5,000 and the balance is 5,200.

Making extra payments that go directly towards the principal reduces the balance faster, which lowers the interest charged in later periods and can shorten the life of a loan. For investments, "protecting the principal" means avoiding losses on the amount originally invested.

definition: Principal repayment is the part of a loan payment that reduces the original amount borrowed, as opposed to the part that pays interest.
explanation: Most loan payments are made up of two parts: interest, which is the cost of borrowing, and principal, which pays down the debt itself. Only the principal portion reduces the amount you owe.

With a typical repayment loan, payments stay the same each month, but the split changes over time. Early on, when the balance is high, most of each payment goes towards interest. As the balance falls, less interest is due, so more of each payment goes towards principal.

For example, on a loan of 10,000 at 6% a year, repaid monthly over three years, each payment is about 304. In the first month, about 50 goes to interest and about 254 reduces the balance. By the final months, almost all of each payment goes towards principal.

Making extra principal repayments, where the loan allows it, reduces the balance faster and cuts the total interest paid. Some loans charge fees for early repayment, so it is worth checking the terms. With interest-only loans, regular payments cover only the interest, and the principal must be repaid separately.

definition: The principal-agent problem is a conflict of interest that arises when one party, the agent, is expected to act on behalf of another, the principal, but has different interests and more information than the principal.
explanation: Principals hire agents to act for them because they lack the time, expertise or ability to do things themselves. But agents may be tempted to serve their own interests rather than those of the principal, and it can be difficult for the principal to monitor what the agent is doing.

A classic example is the relationship between shareholders and company managers. Shareholders, the principals, want managers to maximise the long-term value of the company. Managers, the agents, might instead pursue higher salaries, empire-building acquisitions, short-term results that boost bonuses, or a quieter life.
Other examples include clients and financial advisers, homeowners and estate agents, and voters and politicians.

Solutions include aligning incentives, for example by paying managers partly in shares; monitoring through boards of directors, audits and disclosure requirements; legal duties such as fiduciary obligations; and contracts that link pay to performance. The costs that arise from managing this problem are called agency costs.

definition: A prior-period error is a mistake in a company's financial statements for one or more earlier periods, caused by misusing or failing to use reliable information that was available at the time.
explanation: Errors can arise from mathematical mistakes, misapplying accounting policies, overlooking or misinterpreting facts, or fraud. If they are material, they must be corrected by restating the earlier figures, not simply adjusted in the current year's results.

Under IFRS, material prior-period errors are corrected retrospectively: comparative figures are restated as if the error had never happened, and the opening balances for the earliest period shown are adjusted. US GAAP has a similar approach, with restatements for material errors.

For example, if a company discovers that it double-counted 2,000,000 of revenue last year, it must restate last year's figures in this year's financial statements and disclose the nature and effect of the error.

A prior-period error differs from a change in accounting estimate. A new estimate based on new information is not an error. An error is a mistake that could have been avoided with information available at the time. Restatements due to errors can damage investor confidence and may indicate weaknesses in internal controls.

definition: The prisoner's dilemma is a classic example in game theory showing why two individuals acting in their own interest may both end up worse off than if they had cooperated.
explanation: In the standard story, two suspects are arrested and questioned separately. If both stay silent, each gets a short sentence. If one confesses and the other stays silent, the one who confesses goes free and the other gets a long sentence. If both confess, both get medium sentences.

Whatever the other suspect does, each is better off confessing. So both confess and receive medium sentences, even though both staying silent would have given each a shorter sentence. Rational individual choices lead to a worse outcome for both.
For example, two competing companies might both be better off keeping prices high, but each has an incentive to cut prices to win customers. If both cut, both earn lower profits.

The prisoner's dilemma helps explain price wars, arms races, overfishing and difficulties in tackling climate change. Cooperation is more likely when the game is repeated many times, allowing players to build trust and punish betrayal, or when agreements can be enforced.

definition: Private banking is a set of personalised banking, investment and financial planning services offered to wealthy individuals and families.
explanation: Private banking clients usually need to hold a substantial amount of money with the bank, with minimum thresholds that vary widely between institutions. In return, they receive a dedicated relationship manager and tailored services.

Services typically include investment management, tax and estate planning, specialised lending such as loans secured against investment portfolios or high-value property, foreign exchange, trust services and help with planning how wealth will pass to the next generation. Some private banks also arrange services such as art financing or philanthropy advice.
For example, a business owner who has just sold their company might use a private bank to manage the proceeds, plan for taxes and set up arrangements for their children's future.

Private banking is offered by specialist private banks and by private banking divisions of large universal banks. Fees may be charged as a percentage of assets managed, for specific services or through the products clients buy. As with any investment service, it is worth understanding exactly how the bank is paid.

definition: A private company is a company whose shares are not traded publicly and are usually owned by a small group, such as founders, families, employees or private investors.
explanation: Most companies in the world are private, from small family businesses to some very large international firms. Their shares cannot be bought on a stock exchange, and ownership changes only through private sales.

Private companies have fewer reporting obligations than public companies. In many countries, they still file basic accounts, but they do not have to publish detailed quarterly results or meet stock exchange rules. This allows them to keep more information confidential and to focus on long-term goals without pressure from public investors.

The main disadvantage is access to capital. Private companies cannot easily raise money from the public, so they rely on bank loans, the owners' own money, profits and private investors such as venture capital or private equity funds. It is also harder for owners to sell their shares, because there is no public market.
Many companies start private and later go public through an initial public offering. Public companies can also become private again, for example when bought by a private equity firm.

definition: Private equity is investment in companies that are not listed on a public stock exchange, typically by specialist firms that buy significant stakes and work to improve the companies before selling them for a profit.
explanation: Private equity firms raise money from institutional investors, such as pension funds, insurers and endowments, and wealthy individuals. These investors commit capital to funds that typically last around ten years, managed by the private equity firm.

The term private equity is often used broadly to include venture capital and growth equity, but it most commonly refers to buyouts, in which firms acquire controlling stakes in established companies, often using significant borrowing, in deals known as leveraged buyouts.

After buying a company, private equity firms aim to increase its value, for example by improving management, cutting costs, expanding into new markets, making acquisitions or reorganising operations. They then sell the company, usually within three to seven years, to another company, another private equity firm or public investors through a stock market listing.
For example, a private equity firm might buy a regional chain of veterinary clinics, expand it through acquisitions across the country and sell it several years later for a much higher price.
Supporters argue that private equity improves company performance. Critics point to high fees, heavy use of debt, job cuts and cases where companies were weakened by the debt placed on them.

definition: A private good is a product or service that is excludable, meaning people who do not pay can be prevented from using it, and rivalrous, meaning one person's use reduces its availability to others.
explanation: Most things people buy every day are private goods: food, clothing, phones, cars, haircuts and cinema tickets. If you eat a sandwich, no one else can eat it. And a shop can refuse to give you a sandwich unless you pay.

Because sellers can charge for private goods and each unit can only be used by one person, markets generally provide them efficiently. Producers have a clear incentive to make them, and buyers pay according to how much they value them.

Private goods contrast with public goods, which are non-excludable and non-rivalrous, such as national defence. Between the two are other categories. Common resources, such as fish in the ocean, are rivalrous but hard to exclude people from. Club goods, such as a private gym or streaming service, are excludable but not very rivalrous until they become crowded.
Understanding these categories helps explain why some things are sold in markets, while others are provided or regulated by governments.

definition: A private key is a secret code, usually a long string of numbers and letters, that proves ownership of cryptocurrency or other blockchain assets and allows the owner to authorise transactions.
explanation: Blockchain systems use public-key cryptography. Each user has a pair of keys. The public key, or an address derived from it, can be shared openly, like an account number, so others can send assets to it. The private key must be kept secret, because anyone who has it can spend the assets.
When a user sends cryptocurrency, their wallet uses the private key to create a digital signature, proving the transaction is authorised without revealing the key itself.

For example, if someone stores their private key on a piece of paper and loses it, they may permanently lose access to their cryptocurrency. If a hacker steals it, they can transfer the assets away, and the transaction usually cannot be reversed.

Wallets often generate a recovery phrase, a list of words that can restore the private key. Users can keep keys themselves, which gives full control but full responsibility, or rely on a custodian such as an exchange, which is convenient but depends on the custodian's security and solvency.

definition: Pro forma financial statements are financial statements prepared to show how a company's results or position would have looked if a particular event, such as an acquisition or financing, had happened at an earlier date.
explanation: "Pro forma" means "as a matter of form". These statements adjust actual or forecast figures to illustrate the effect of a specific transaction or change.

For example, if a company completes a large acquisition halfway through the year, its reported results include the acquired business only for the second half. Pro forma statements might show the combined results as if the acquisition had happened at the start of the year, helping investors understand the size of the enlarged group.
Pro forma statements are also used when a company plans to raise money, restructure, go public or spin off a division, and in business plans to show expected results under certain assumptions.
They can be useful, but they are hypothetical. They depend on the assumptions and adjustments chosen by the company, which may not be audited in the same way as historical statements.

The term is also sometimes used for adjusted profit figures that exclude certain costs. These should be read carefully, because companies may remove expenses that are, in reality, ongoing. Regulators often require pro forma figures to be reconciled to standard accounting measures.

definition: Probability is a measure of how likely an event is to happen, expressed as a number between 0, meaning it will certainly not happen, and 1, meaning it will certainly happen.
explanation: Probabilities can also be written as percentages, from 0% to 100%, or as fractions. A fair coin has a probability of 0.5, or 50%, of landing heads. A standard six-sided die has a probability of 1 in 6, or about 17%, of landing on any particular number.

Probabilities can be based on logic, as with coins and dice; on historical data, such as the share of loans of a certain type that have defaulted in the past; or on judgment, such as an analyst's estimate of the chance a merger will be approved.

Probability is fundamental to finance. Insurers use it to estimate the likelihood of claims and set premiums. Lenders use it to estimate the chance that borrowers will default. Investors use it to think about the range of possible returns and risks. Options prices depend on the probability of different price movements.

People often misjudge probabilities. They tend to overestimate the likelihood of dramatic, memorable events and underestimate common risks. Thinking carefully about probabilities, rather than relying on intuition, can lead to better financial decisions.

definition: A probability distribution is a description of all the possible values a random variable can take and how likely each value is.
explanation: A probability distribution shows the full picture of uncertainty. For a simple example, the distribution for rolling a fair die gives each number from 1 to 6 a probability of one-sixth.

Some distributions are especially common. The normal distribution, shaped like a bell, describes many natural phenomena and is often used as an approximation for investment returns. Most outcomes cluster around the average, with fewer outcomes further away. The binomial distribution describes the number of successes in a fixed number of trials, such as how many of 100 loans default. The lognormal distribution is often used for asset prices, which cannot fall below zero.

Distributions are summarised by measures such as the mean, which shows the centre; the standard deviation, which shows the spread; skewness, which shows whether the distribution leans to one side; and kurtosis, which shows how heavy its tails are.

In finance, understanding the distribution of returns is crucial for managing risk. A common problem is assuming returns follow a normal distribution when, in reality, extreme outcomes occur more often. Models built on this assumption may underestimate the chance of large losses.

definition: Process costing is a method of calculating product costs used when identical units are produced in a continuous process, by adding up the costs of each production stage and dividing them by the number of units produced.
explanation: In industries such as chemicals, oil refining, food and drink, paper and cement, products move through a series of stages and individual units are indistinguishable. Tracking each unit separately would be impossible, so costs are averaged.

Costs are collected for each process or department over a period. They are then spread across the units produced. For example, if a bottling process incurs costs of 100,000 in a month and fills 20,000 bottles, the cost per bottle for that process is 5.

A complication is partly finished goods. Process costing uses equivalent units, which convert partly completed units into a number of fully completed ones. For example, 1,000 units that are 40% complete count as 400 equivalent units for conversion costs.
Process costing is simpler than tracking individual jobs but provides less detail. It contrasts with job costing, used when each order is distinct. Some businesses use a hybrid of the two.

definition: Procurement is the process by which an organisation finds, selects and buys the goods and services it needs from outside suppliers.
explanation: Procurement covers the full purchasing process, including identifying needs, finding and evaluating suppliers, negotiating prices and terms, placing orders, receiving goods, paying invoices and managing supplier relationships.

Effective procurement can significantly affect a company's profitability. Purchased goods and services often make up a large share of total costs, so even small improvements in prices or terms can increase profits considerably. Procurement also affects quality, reliability and risk, since dependence on poor suppliers can disrupt operations.

For example, a manufacturer might run a competitive tender for its packaging materials, inviting several suppliers to bid, and choose the one offering the best combination of price, quality and delivery reliability.

Public sector procurement, by governments and public bodies, is usually subject to strict rules to ensure fairness, transparency and value for taxpayers' money, often requiring open competitive tenders for larger contracts.

Modern procurement increasingly considers wider factors beyond price, such as suppliers' environmental impact, labour practices, financial stability and resilience to disruption. Many organisations use specialised software to manage procurement and analyse spending.

definition: The Producer Price Index (PPI) measures the average change over time in the prices that domestic producers receive for their goods and services, reflecting price changes at the wholesale or factory level.
explanation: While the Consumer Price Index tracks prices paid by households, the PPI tracks prices at earlier stages of production, such as raw materials, intermediate goods used in manufacturing and finished goods sold by producers.
For example, if the prices of steel, chemicals and manufactured goods sold by factories rise, the PPI will increase, even before consumers see higher prices in shops.

The PPI is watched closely as a possible early signal of consumer inflation. When producers face higher costs, they often pass at least some of those increases on to consumers, so a rising PPI can suggest that consumer prices may rise later. However, the link is not exact, since businesses may absorb some cost increases by accepting lower profit margins.
Different countries publish their own producer price measures, sometimes called output and input price indices. Businesses also use the PPI to adjust long-term contracts for changes in costs.

definition: Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives for a good and the minimum price at which they would have been willing to sell it. It measures the extra benefit producers gain from selling.
explanation: Each producer has a minimum price at which they are willing to sell, usually related to their cost of production. If a farmer would sell tomatoes for as little as 1 per kilogram but the market price is 1.60, they gain 0.60 of producer surplus on each kilogram sold.
Across a whole market, producer surplus adds up these gains for all sellers. On a supply and demand graph, it is the area above the supply curve and below the market price, up to the quantity sold.

Producer surplus is closely linked to profit but is not identical, because it focuses on the gains from each extra sale above the minimum acceptable price rather than total profit after all fixed costs.

When prices rise, producer surplus grows, both for existing sellers and for new ones who enter the market. When prices fall, it shrinks. Consumer surplus and producer surplus together make up total surplus, a measure economists use to judge how much overall benefit a market creates for society.

definition: Productivity is a measure of how efficiently inputs, such as labour and capital, are turned into output, commonly measured as output per worker or output per hour worked.
explanation: Productivity shows how much an economy, industry or business produces with the resources it uses. Higher productivity means more output from the same effort, or the same output with less.

For example, if a factory with 50 workers produces 1,000 units a day, its output per worker is 20 units. If new equipment raises output to 1,100 units with the same staff, output per worker rises to 22 units, a 10% increase in labour productivity.

Productivity growth is the main long-term driver of rising living standards. When workers produce more per hour, businesses can afford to pay higher wages without raising prices, and the economy can grow without simply requiring more hours of work.

Productivity is improved by better technology and equipment, better education and skills, improved management and organisation, and more efficient markets. Slow productivity growth, which many developed economies have experienced in recent decades, is a major concern for economists because it limits how quickly incomes can rise.

definition: Product-market fit is the point at which a product clearly satisfies a strong market need, so that customers actively want it, keep using it and recommend it to others.
explanation: The term is widely used in the start-up world, where finding product-market fit is often seen as the most important milestone for a new company. Before reaching it, a start-up is still searching for the right product, customers or business model. After reaching it, the focus shifts towards growth and scaling.

Signs of product-market fit include rapid growth driven by word of mouth, high customer retention, customers who would be very disappointed if the product disappeared, strong demand that outpaces the company's ability to supply it, and sales cycles becoming shorter.

For example, a start-up offering a scheduling tool might find that after several redesigns, customers suddenly begin signing up in large numbers through recommendations, use the product daily and rarely cancel. These are strong signals of product-market fit.

There is no single metric that proves product-market fit, and some companies believe they have it when they do not. Scaling a business before achieving it, by spending heavily on marketing and hiring, is a common reason start-ups fail, because they spend money acquiring customers who do not stay.

definition: Professional indemnity insurance is insurance that protects professionals and businesses providing advice or services against claims from clients who suffer financial loss because of errors, negligence or failure to perform their work properly.
explanation: Professionals such as accountants, lawyers, architects, engineers, consultants, financial advisers and IT providers can be sued if their advice or work causes a client to lose money. Professional indemnity insurance covers the cost of defending such claims and any compensation awarded, up to the policy limit.

For example, if an architect's design error leads to costly structural repairs, the client might claim against the architect. The architect's professional indemnity insurance would cover legal costs and compensation.

In many professions, professional indemnity insurance is required by regulators or professional bodies. In the United States, similar cover is commonly called errors and omissions insurance, or malpractice insurance in fields such as medicine and law.

Many professional indemnity policies are written on a claims-made basis, meaning they cover claims made during the policy period, regardless of when the work was done, so professionals often need to keep cover in place, or buy run-off cover, after retiring or closing a business.

definition: A profit center is a department, division or unit of a business whose manager is responsible for both its revenues and its costs, and is therefore accountable for its profit.
explanation: Profit centers are typically units that sell to customers, such as product divisions, regional businesses, individual stores or branches. Their managers can influence prices, sales volume, product mix and costs.
For example, a retail chain treats each store as a profit center. Store managers are evaluated on their store's profit, taking account of sales, staff costs, stock losses and local expenses.
Profit centers encourage managers to think like business owners, balancing growth and cost control. They make it easier to see which parts of a business are performing well.

Measuring profit fairly can be difficult, especially when units share costs or trade with each other. Allocations of head office costs and internal transfer prices can affect reported profits in ways managers cannot control. Profit centers are one part of responsibility accounting, alongside cost centers, which control costs only, revenue centers, which are judged on sales, and investment centers, which are judged on returns on the capital they use.

definition: The profitability index compares the present value of a project's future cash flows with its initial cost. A value above 1 means the project is expected to create value.
explanation: The profitability index divides the present value of future cash flows by the initial investment. It shows how much value is created for each unit invested.

For example, a project costing 50,000 whose future cash flows are worth 54,018 in today's money has a profitability index of about 1.08. Each unit invested is expected to return 1.08 in present-value terms. A project with an index of exactly 1 just covers its cost; one below 1 would destroy value.
The profitability index always agrees with net present value on whether a single project is acceptable, because an index above 1 means NPV is positive.

Its main use is ranking projects when money is limited. Suppose a company has 1 million to invest and several projects to choose from. Picking projects with the highest profitability index helps get the most total value from the limited budget. However, for comparing mutually exclusive projects of very different sizes, net present value is usually the better guide, because it measures the total amount of value created.

definition: A progressive tax is a tax system in which the tax rate increases as income or the amount being taxed increases, so higher earners pay a larger share of their income in tax.
explanation: Most income tax systems are progressive. They divide income into bands, each taxed at a different rate. Importantly, a higher rate applies only to the income within that band, not to the person's entire income.

For example, suppose income up to 20,000 is taxed at 10% and income above that is taxed at 30%. Someone earning 50,000 pays 2,000 on the first 20,000 and 9,000 on the remaining 30,000, a total of 11,000. Their average tax rate is 22%, even though their top rate is 30%.

A common misunderstanding is that moving into a higher tax band reduces take-home pay. Because only the extra income is taxed at the higher rate, earning more always leaves you with more after tax under a standard progressive income tax.

Progressive taxes are based on the idea that people with higher incomes can afford to contribute a larger share. Critics argue that very high top rates may discourage work, investment or entrepreneurship. The degree of progressivity varies widely between countries.

definition: Proof of stake is a method used by some blockchains to agree on which transactions are valid, in which participants called validators lock up, or stake, their own cryptocurrency for the right to propose and confirm new blocks.
explanation: Instead of competing with computing power, as in proof of work, validators are chosen to create and confirm blocks based partly on how much cryptocurrency they have staked. They earn rewards for honest work, and they can lose part of their stake, a penalty called slashing, if they act dishonestly or fail to perform their duties.
Ethereum switched from proof of work to proof of stake in September 2022, in an upgrade known as the Merge, cutting its energy use dramatically.
For example, a validator on a proof-of-stake network might lock up a set amount of cryptocurrency, run software to check and confirm transactions, and earn a share of new tokens and fees as a reward.

Proof of stake uses far less energy than proof of work. Critics argue it can favour those who already hold large amounts of cryptocurrency, potentially concentrating control. Many holders stake through exchanges or staking services, which raises questions about custody and regulation.

definition: Proof of work is a method used by some blockchains to agree on which transactions are valid, in which participants called miners compete to solve difficult computational puzzles, and the winner adds the next block and earns a reward.
explanation: Public blockchains need a way for many independent computers to agree on a single history of transactions without trusting a central authority. Proof of work achieves this by making it costly to add blocks.

Miners use powerful computers to repeatedly guess a number that, combined with the block's data, produces a result meeting a difficulty target. The first to find a valid answer broadcasts the block, and others verify it easily. The miner receives newly created coins and transaction fees.
Bitcoin uses proof of work. To rewrite past transactions, an attacker would need to control more computing power than the rest of the network combined, which is extremely expensive.

The main criticism of proof of work is its very high energy use, since miners consume large amounts of electricity. It can also concentrate mining in places with cheap power and among large operators. These concerns led some blockchains, including Ethereum in 2022, to switch to proof of stake.

definition: Property insurance is insurance that protects against financial loss from damage to or loss of physical property, such as buildings, contents, vehicles and equipment.
explanation: Property insurance covers losses caused by events such as fire, theft, storms, water damage and vandalism, depending on the policy. It is used by homeowners, renters, landlords and businesses.

Home insurance typically has two parts: buildings insurance, covering the structure of the property, and contents insurance, covering possessions inside. Renters usually need only contents insurance, since the landlord insures the building. Businesses insure premises, stock, equipment and sometimes the income lost while damaged property is repaired, called business interruption insurance.

Policies pay out in different ways. Replacement cost cover pays the cost of replacing items with new equivalents. Actual cash value cover pays the item's value after depreciation, which is usually less.

For example, if a fire damages a kitchen, a homeowner's buildings insurance would cover repairs to the structure and fittings, while contents insurance would cover damaged appliances and belongings, both minus any excess.

Property insurance policies list covered perils and exclusions. Flood and earthquake damage are often excluded from standard policies in some countries and must be insured separately. Underinsuring property can lead to reduced payouts.

definition: Property, plant and equipment (PP&E) are the physical, long-term assets a business uses to produce goods or services, such as land, buildings, machinery, vehicles and computers.
explanation: PP&E are also called fixed assets. They are expected to be used for more than one year and are not intended for sale in the normal course of business.

On the balance sheet, PP&E are usually shown at their original cost minus accumulated depreciation and any impairment, giving net PP&E. Land is not depreciated, but buildings, machinery and equipment are, because they wear out or become outdated. Under IFRS, companies may choose instead to show some PP&E at revalued amounts.
For example, a factory might report PP&E with a cost of 12 million and accumulated depreciation of 5 million, giving a net book value of 7 million.

PP&E are especially large for capital-intensive businesses, such as manufacturers, airlines, utilities and telecommunications companies. Investors watch how much a company spends on new PP&E, known as capital expenditure, compared with depreciation. Spending far less than depreciation for long periods can mean assets are ageing and may soon need costly replacement.

definition: Property tax is a tax charged on the ownership of land and buildings, usually based on the assessed value of the property and collected by local governments.
explanation: Property taxes are a major source of funding for local services, such as schools, roads, police, fire services and waste collection. Owners usually pay them annually or in instalments.

The tax is typically calculated by multiplying the property's assessed value by a local tax rate. For example, under a hypothetical rate of 1%, a home assessed at 300,000 would owe 3,000 a year. Assessed values may be updated periodically to reflect market prices, and owners can often appeal if they think the assessment is too high.

Systems vary widely. Some countries tax the value of the land and buildings; others use bands based on property value, or charge occupiers rather than owners. Many offer reductions for primary residences, older people or low-income households.

Property taxes affect the true cost of owning a home or commercial property. Homebuyers often include them in their monthly budget, and many mortgage lenders collect property tax payments along with the mortgage through an escrow account, paying the tax on the owner's behalf when it is due.

definition: Prospect theory is a theory of how people make decisions involving risk, showing that they judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point and feel losses more strongly than equivalent gains.
explanation: Prospect theory was developed by psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979, and Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002 partly for this work. It challenged the traditional view that people make rational choices to maximise their total wealth.

The theory has several key ideas. People evaluate outcomes as changes from a reference point, such as the price paid for a share, rather than as final wealth. Losses hurt more than gains of the same size feel good, often roughly twice as much. People tend to be cautious when facing gains but willing to take risks to avoid losses. And they overweight small probabilities, which helps explain the appeal of lottery tickets and insurance.
For example, many people prefer a certain gain of 500 over a 50% chance of 1,000, but prefer a 50% chance of losing 1,000 over a certain loss of 500.
Prospect theory is a cornerstone of behavioral finance. It helps explain the disposition effect, demand for insurance and many patterns in markets.

definition: A prospectus is a formal legal document that a company or fund must publish when offering securities to the public, describing the investment, its risks and key information investors need to make a decision.
explanation: Securities laws in most countries require a prospectus when shares, bonds or fund units are offered to the public, to ensure investors receive full and accurate information.

A company prospectus typically describes the business, its history, management, financial statements, how the money raised will be used, the risks involved, the terms of the securities and details of major shareholders. A fund prospectus explains the fund's objective, investment strategy, fees, risks and past performance.
For example, before a company's initial public offering, it publishes a prospectus that potential investors can read before deciding whether to buy shares.
Prospectuses are usually reviewed or approved by securities regulators, and companies can be held legally responsible for misleading statements in them.

They can be long and detailed, sometimes hundreds of pages. Many jurisdictions also require shorter summary documents, such as key information documents for funds, to help ordinary investors understand the most important points, especially costs and risks. Reading the risk factors and fees sections is often particularly valuable.

definition: A protective put is an options strategy in which an investor who owns shares buys a put option on those shares to limit potential losses if the price falls.
explanation: A protective put works like insurance. The investor keeps all the upside if the share price rises, minus the cost of the put, but is protected from losses below the put's strike price.

For example, an investor owns shares trading at 50 and buys a put with a strike price of 45 for a premium of 2. If the share falls to 30, the investor can sell at 45. Their maximum loss is limited to 5 from the fall to the strike price plus the 2 premium, a total of 7 per share, however far the share falls. If the share rises to 70, they gain 20 on the shares, less the 2 premium, for a net gain of 18.
The cost of protection depends on the strike price chosen and the time until expiry. A strike price closer to the current price gives more protection but costs more.

Protective puts are useful when an investor wants to keep a position but is worried about a short-term fall, such as before an earnings announcement. The premium is a real cost, so buying protection continuously can significantly reduce long-term returns.
note: A married put is a protective put bought at the same time as the shares. "Protective put" usually refers to a put added to shares already owned. The economic effect is the same.

definition: Provisions are liabilities of uncertain timing or amount that a company records when it has a present obligation from a past event, is likely to have to pay and can estimate the amount reliably.
explanation: Provisions recognise obligations that are real but not yet fixed in amount or date. Common examples include expected costs of warranty repairs, legal claims the company is likely to lose, restructuring costs once a plan has been announced, and obligations to restore a site or dismantle equipment at the end of its use.

For example, a manufacturer that sells products with a one-year warranty may expect 2% of products to need repair at an average cost of 100. If it sold 50,000 products, it would record a warranty provision of about 100,000.

Under IFRS, a provision is recognised when there is a present obligation, an outflow of resources is probable and a reliable estimate can be made. US GAAP uses a similar idea but different terms. If the obligation is only possible rather than probable, or cannot be estimated reliably, it is disclosed as a contingent liability instead.

Provisions involve judgment, so they are reviewed at each reporting date. Releasing an unused provision increases profit, which is why auditors check them closely. A loan loss provision in banking is one specific example of the general idea.

definition: Proxy voting is voting on company matters by a shareholder who does not attend the meeting in person, by authorising someone else, or submitting instructions, to vote on their behalf.
explanation: Companies hold shareholder meetings to vote on matters such as electing directors, approving executive pay, appointing auditors and approving major transactions. Most shareholders do not attend, so they vote by proxy, usually online, by post or through their broker.
Before the meeting, companies send shareholders a proxy statement explaining the items to be voted on and the board's recommendations.
For example, an investor holding shares through a broker might receive an online notice and vote for or against each director and proposal on the company's agenda.

Institutional investors, such as pension funds and asset managers, cast a large share of votes and often have voting policies. Many rely on proxy advisory firms for research and recommendations. Proxy voting is an important part of corporate governance, allowing shareholders to hold boards to account. A proxy fight occurs when a shareholder group campaigns to persuade other shareholders to vote against management, often to replace directors.

definition: A public company is a company whose shares can be bought and sold by members of the public, usually on a stock exchange.
explanation: A company becomes public, usually through an initial public offering, when it sells shares to outside investors and lists them on an exchange. After that, anyone with a brokerage account can buy its shares.

Being public has advantages. The company can raise large amounts of money by issuing shares or bonds, its shares can be used to pay for acquisitions or reward employees, and shareholders can easily sell their stakes. It also often raises the company's profile.

There are significant responsibilities. Public companies must publish audited financial statements and other important information regularly, follow strict rules on disclosure and governance and respond to shareholders, who can vote on major issues. They face pressure from investors and analysts to deliver results every quarter.
For example, a public company must announce material news, such as a large contract loss, promptly so that all investors have access to the same information.
In some countries, "public company" can also mean a company eligible to offer shares to the public even if they are not listed. The term should not be confused with a government-owned company.

definition: A public good is a product or service that is non-excludable, meaning people cannot easily be prevented from using it, and non-rivalrous, meaning one person's use does not reduce its availability to others.
explanation: Classic examples of public goods include national defence, street lighting, flood defences and public fireworks displays. Once street lights are installed, everyone walking down the street benefits, and one person's use does not leave less light for anyone else.

Public goods create a problem for private markets, called the free-rider problem. Because people can benefit without paying, many will choose not to pay. A private company would struggle to sell street lighting to individual residents, because each might wait for others to pay and then enjoy the light for free.
As a result, public goods tend to be underprovided if left to the market. This is why governments usually provide them and fund them through taxation.

Few goods are perfectly public. Some, like a free public park, can become crowded, which makes them partly rivalrous. Others, like a toll road, can exclude non-payers. Economists therefore treat public goods as one end of a range, with private goods at the other end.

definition: A pump and dump is a fraudulent scheme in which promoters artificially inflate the price of an asset, usually a little-known share or cryptocurrency, through false or misleading hype, then sell their holdings at the inflated price.
explanation: Pump and dump schemes typically target assets with low prices and low trading volumes, which are easier to move. The promoters buy cheaply, then promote the asset aggressively through emails, social media, online forums or paid influencers, often with exaggerated claims about upcoming news, new products or guaranteed gains.

As new buyers rush in, the price rises. The promoters then sell, or dump, their holdings at the high price. Once the selling begins and the hype stops, the price usually collapses, leaving later buyers with heavy losses.
For example, promoters might buy shares in a tiny company at 0.10, spread rumours of a major partnership, push the price to 0.80 and then sell, after which the shares fall back below 0.10.

Pump and dump schemes are illegal market manipulation in most countries. Warning signs include unsolicited tips, pressure to buy quickly, promises of huge returns and promotions of obscure assets with little public information.

definition: A purchase price adjustment is a change to the price paid in an acquisition after completion, based on the actual financial position of the business at completion, usually its cash, debt and working capital.
explanation: Between signing a deal and completing it, a business continues to operate, and its cash, debt and working capital change. Purchase price adjustments ensure the buyer pays for the business as it actually is at completion.

Typically, the parties agree an estimated price at completion based on the seller's estimates. After completion, completion accounts are prepared, showing the actual figures. The price is then adjusted up or down, and any difference is paid.
For example, if the estimated price assumed working capital of 10,000,000 and the completion accounts show 9,500,000, the seller refunds 500,000 to the buyer.

Purchase price adjustments are common in many markets, particularly the United States. Disputes over adjustments often arise from different accounting interpretations, so agreements usually set out detailed accounting principles and a process for resolving disagreements, often involving an independent accountant. The alternative approach, a locked-box mechanism, fixes the price in advance with no adjustments.

definition: Purchase price allocation (PPA) is the process of assigning the price paid in an acquisition to the identifiable assets acquired and liabilities assumed, measured at fair value, with any remaining amount recorded as goodwill.
explanation: When one company acquires another, accounting standards under IFRS and US GAAP require the buyer to record the target's assets and liabilities at their fair values on the acquisition date, not at their old book values.

This includes intangible assets that may not have appeared on the target's balance sheet, such as customer relationships, brands, technology and patents. Any excess of the purchase price over the net fair value of identifiable assets and liabilities is recorded as goodwill.

For example, a company pays 500,000,000 for a business whose identifiable assets and liabilities have a net fair value of 350,000,000, including newly recognised intangible assets. The remaining 150,000,000 is recorded as goodwill.

Purchase price allocation affects future profits. Intangible assets with limited lives are amortized, reducing reported earnings, while goodwill is not amortized but tested for impairment. Higher values for inventory and fixed assets also increase future costs. Specialist valuation firms are often hired to estimate fair values.

definition: The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a monthly economic indicator based on surveys of purchasing managers at companies, showing whether business conditions in manufacturing or services are improving or worsening.
explanation: PMI surveys ask purchasing managers whether key measures, such as new orders, output, employment, supplier delivery times and inventories, have increased, decreased or stayed the same compared with the previous month. The answers are combined into an index.

A reading above 50 indicates that activity is expanding compared with the previous month, while a reading below 50 indicates it is contracting. For example, a manufacturing PMI of 53 suggests factory activity is growing, while a reading of 47 suggests it is shrinking.

PMIs are widely followed because they are released early each month, before most official data, and are seen as leading indicators of economic trends. They are published for many countries and regions, often separately for manufacturing and services.

Because PMIs measure the breadth of change rather than its size, they show the direction of activity more reliably than its exact pace. They are based on surveys, so they can also be affected by sentiment.

definition: Purchasing power is the amount of goods and services that a sum of money can buy. When prices rise, the same amount of money buys less, so its purchasing power falls.
explanation: The number on a banknote does not change, but what it can buy does. Purchasing power describes that real buying ability.

Suppose a basket of groceries costs 50 this year. If you have 500, you can buy 10 baskets. If prices rise by 10% and the basket now costs 55, your 500 buys only about 9 baskets. Your money is the same, but its purchasing power has fallen by about 9%.

The main force that reduces purchasing power is inflation, the general rise in prices over time. Even low inflation adds up: at 3% a year, prices roughly double in about 23 years, so money kept in cash for that long would buy only about half as much.

This is why savers look for returns that at least match inflation. If your savings earn 2% a year while prices rise by 3%, your balance grows, but your purchasing power shrinks. Wages work the same way: a pay rise smaller than inflation is, in real terms, a pay cut.

definition: Purchasing power parity (PPP) is an economic theory and measurement method that compares currencies by the amount of goods and services they can buy, so that the same basket of goods should cost the same in different countries once prices are converted into a common currency.
explanation: PPP has two main uses. First, it is used as a theory of exchange rates: over the long term, exchange rates should move towards the level at which identical goods cost the same everywhere. Second, it is used to compare living standards and economic output across countries more fairly.

A well-known informal illustration is comparing the price of a hamburger in different countries. Suppose a burger costs 5 dollars in the United States and 600 yen in Japan. The implied PPP exchange rate is 120 yen per dollar. If the actual exchange rate is 150 yen per dollar, the yen buys more in Japan than its market rate suggests, implying it is undervalued by about 20%.

PPP-adjusted figures are widely used for international comparisons of GDP and incomes. Market exchange rates can understate living standards in countries where many local goods and services are cheap.
In practice, exchange rates can differ from PPP for long periods, because of trade barriers, transport costs, taxes and goods and services that cannot easily be traded.

definition: A put option is a contract that gives its buyer the right, but not the obligation, to sell an asset at a set price, the strike price, on or before a specific date.
explanation: The buyer of a put pays a premium for the right to sell. They benefit if the price of the underlying asset falls below the strike price.

Suppose you buy a put option on a share with a strike price of 50, paying a premium of 2 per share. If the share falls to 42 by expiry, you can sell at 50, so the option is worth 8 per share. After subtracting the premium, your profit is 6 per share. Your break-even price is 48, the strike minus the premium.
If the share stays at or above 50, the put expires worthless and you lose the premium. The maximum loss for the buyer is the premium, while the maximum gain occurs if the share falls to zero.

Puts are often used for protection. An investor who owns shares can buy puts to limit potential losses, much like buying insurance. Puts can also be used to speculate on falling prices without short selling.
The seller of a put receives the premium but must buy the shares at the strike price if the buyer exercises, even if the market price is much lower.

definition: A p-value is the probability of seeing results at least as extreme as those observed, assuming that there is actually no real effect or difference, the null hypothesis.
explanation: P-values are used in hypothesis testing to judge whether results are likely to reflect a real effect or could easily have happened by chance.

For example, suppose a fund manager claims their strategy beats the market. Their returns over several years are higher than the market's, and a statistical test gives a p-value of 0.03. This means that if the strategy actually had no advantage, there would be only about a 3% chance of seeing outperformance this large or larger purely by luck.

A small p-value suggests the observed result would be unusual if there were no real effect, so it provides evidence against the null hypothesis. Researchers often use a threshold of 0.05: results with a p-value below this are called statistically significant.

P-values are widely misunderstood. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that the result happened by chance. It also says nothing about how large or important an effect is. A tiny, unimportant effect can have a very small p-value in a large data set. Testing many ideas and reporting only those with low p-values can also produce misleading conclusions.

definition: A qualified dividend is a dividend that meets United States tax requirements to be taxed at the lower rates that apply to long-term capital gains, rather than at ordinary income tax rates.
explanation: In the US federal tax system, dividends are divided into two types. Ordinary dividends are taxed at the same rates as wages and other ordinary income. Qualified dividends receive lower rates, which can make a large difference for investors in higher tax brackets.

To qualify, a dividend must generally be paid by a US company or a qualifying foreign company, and the investor must have held the shares for more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date.

For example, an investor who buys shares just before the ex-dividend date and sells them a few days later would usually receive an ordinary dividend, taxed at the higher rate, because the holding period was not met.

Some payments do not qualify regardless of holding period, including most distributions from real estate investment trusts and interest-like payments from money market funds. Brokers report how much of an investor's dividends were qualified. Other countries have their own methods of taxing dividends, such as dividend allowances or credits for corporate tax already paid.

definition: A qualified opinion is an audit opinion stating that a company's financial statements are fairly presented except for a specific matter, where the auditor has found a material problem or could not obtain enough evidence, but the issue is not widespread.
explanation: Auditors express one of several types of opinion. An unmodified, or clean, opinion means the statements are fairly presented. A qualified opinion means they are fairly presented except for a particular issue, which the auditor explains.
