A qualified opinion may arise because a company has applied an accounting rule incorrectly in one area, such as valuing inventory, or because the auditor could not obtain enough evidence on a specific item, for example because records for an overseas subsidiary were destroyed.

For example, an auditor might state that the financial statements are fairly presented, except that the company has not recorded an impairment of a particular investment, which would have reduced profit by a stated amount.

A qualified opinion is a warning sign, but it is less serious than an adverse opinion or a disclaimer of opinion, which apply when problems are pervasive. Investors and lenders take qualified opinions seriously, and some loan agreements treat them as a breach of conditions.

definition: Quality of earnings is the extent to which a company's reported profits reflect its true, sustainable, cash-generating performance, rather than one-off items, aggressive accounting or estimates.
explanation: Two companies can report the same profit with very different quality. High-quality earnings are recurring, backed by cash flow and based on conservative, consistent accounting. Low-quality earnings rely on one-time gains, optimistic estimates or accounting choices that boost profits without matching cash.

Analysts assess quality by comparing net income with operating cash flow, looking for large or growing accruals, identifying one-off gains and losses, checking changes in accounting policies and estimates and examining trends in receivables and inventory relative to sales.

For example, if a company's profits rise because it sold a building, or because it extended the estimated lives of its assets to cut depreciation, its earnings quality is lower than if profits rose because of higher sales and margins.
In acquisitions, buyers often commission a quality of earnings report from accountants, which adjusts reported profits to show the sustainable earnings the business really generates.

definition: Quantitative easing (QE) is a monetary policy in which a central bank creates new money to buy large amounts of financial assets, usually government bonds, to lower long-term interest rates and support the economy.
explanation: Central banks usually influence the economy by changing short-term interest rates. But when those rates are already close to zero and the economy still needs support, they may turn to quantitative easing.

By buying large quantities of bonds, the central bank pushes up their prices and lowers their yields. This reduces long-term borrowing costs for governments, businesses and households, including mortgage rates. It also puts money into the hands of the sellers, who may use it to buy other assets, such as corporate bonds or shares, which can support asset prices and make it easier for companies to raise money.
Quantitative easing was used extensively by major central banks after the 2008 financial crisis and again during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Supporters credit QE with helping to prevent deeper recessions. Critics argue that it inflated asset prices, benefiting wealthier people who own more assets, and made it harder to control inflation later. Reversing QE, by shrinking the central bank's holdings, is called quantitative tightening.

definition: Quantitative tightening (QT) is a monetary policy in which a central bank reduces the amount of financial assets it holds, shrinking its balance sheet and withdrawing money from the financial system.
explanation: Quantitative tightening is the reverse of quantitative easing. After years of buying bonds to support the economy, central banks may decide to reduce their holdings once the economy has recovered or inflation has risen.

QT can be carried out in two ways. The central bank can let bonds mature without reinvesting the money it receives, which gradually shrinks its holdings. Or it can actively sell bonds in the market, which reduces holdings more quickly.
For example, a central bank holding large amounts of government bonds might stop reinvesting the proceeds from maturing bonds, allowing its holdings to fall by a set amount each month.

QT tends to push long-term interest rates higher, because the central bank is no longer a major buyer of bonds. It works alongside interest rate increases to tighten financial conditions and reduce inflation. Central banks usually carry out QT gradually and with advance notice, because the effects on markets are uncertain and sudden moves could cause financial instability.

definition: A quarterly report is a financial report a company publishes every three months, showing its results and financial position for that quarter, usually in less detail than the annual report.
explanation: Quarterly reports give investors more frequent updates on how a company is performing. They typically include a condensed income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement, along with management commentary on the period's results and outlook.
Quarterly financial statements are usually reviewed by the auditor rather than fully audited, so they carry less assurance than annual accounts.
For example, a company might report that third-quarter revenue rose 8% compared with the same quarter last year, explain the main drivers and update its forecast for the full year.

Requirements vary by country. In the United States, listed companies must file quarterly reports with the securities regulator. In some other markets, companies report half-yearly instead, with quarterly updates being optional or limited to key figures.

Quarterly reporting helps markets stay informed and react quickly to changes. Critics argue that it can encourage short-term thinking, with managers focusing on hitting quarterly targets rather than long-term value. Many companies also hold conference calls with analysts when releasing their quarterly results.

definition: Quarter-over-quarter growth compares a figure for one three-month period with the immediately preceding three-month period, expressed as a percentage change.
explanation: Quarter-over-quarter growth, often written as QoQ, shows the most recent change in performance. It is calculated as this quarter's figure minus last quarter's, divided by last quarter's.
For example, if a company's revenue is 5.25 million in the second quarter and 5 million in the first quarter, quarter-over-quarter growth is 5%.

QoQ growth reacts quickly to changes, making it useful for spotting turning points early. A business that sees growth slowing from 6% to 2% to 0% across three quarters may be heading into trouble well before the annual figures show it.

Its weakness is that it is affected by seasonal patterns. A retailer's fourth quarter, including the holiday season, will almost always show strong QoQ growth, and its first quarter will often show a decline. For this reason, QoQ figures are often adjusted for seasonality or read alongside year-over-year growth. Economic statistics, such as GDP, are commonly reported on a seasonally adjusted quarter-over-quarter basis.

definition: The quick ratio is a company's most liquid current assets, typically cash, short-term investments and receivables, divided by its current liabilities. It tests whether short-term obligations could be met without selling inventory.
explanation: The quick ratio, also called the acid-test ratio, is a stricter version of the current ratio. It excludes inventory and usually prepaid expenses, because these may not be turned into cash quickly or at full value.

For example, a company has current assets of 500,000, including inventory of 150,000, and current liabilities of 250,000. Its quick assets are 350,000, giving a quick ratio of 1.4. Its current ratio, by comparison, is 2.0.

A quick ratio of 1 or more suggests the company can meet its short-term obligations from its most liquid assets alone. A ratio well below 1 may mean it depends on selling inventory to pay its bills, which can be risky if sales slow.

The quick ratio is particularly useful for businesses that hold large or slow-moving inventories, such as manufacturers or retailers of seasonal goods, where the current ratio might give an overly comfortable picture.

As with other liquidity ratios, what counts as healthy depends on the industry and the business model. Comparing the ratio with competitors and with the company's own history gives the most useful insight.

definition: A quota, in trade, is a government limit on the quantity or value of a particular good that can be imported or exported during a set period.
explanation: While a tariff makes imports more expensive, a quota directly limits how much can come in. For example, a country might allow only 100,000 tonnes of sugar to be imported each year.

By restricting supply, an import quota usually raises the domestic price of the product. This benefits domestic producers, who face less foreign competition and can sell at higher prices. It costs consumers, who pay more and have less choice.

Unlike a tariff, a quota does not automatically raise revenue for the government. The extra profit created by higher prices often goes to the businesses that hold the right to import the limited quantity. Governments sometimes sell import licences to capture some of this value.

Quotas can be used to protect strategic industries, to manage trade relationships or to prevent sudden surges of imports. They are generally considered less transparent than tariffs and are restricted under many international trade agreements. The word "quota" is also used in other contexts, such as fishing quotas that limit catches to protect fish stocks.

definition: A random variable is a quantity whose value depends on the outcome of an uncertain event, with each possible value having a certain probability.
explanation: Random variables are used to describe uncertain outcomes in numbers. For example, the number that comes up when a die is rolled is a random variable, with possible values from 1 to 6. Tomorrow's return on a share is also a random variable, since it could take many possible values.

There are two main types. A discrete random variable can take only specific, separate values, such as the number of defaults in a group of loans or the number of customers who visit a shop in a day. A continuous random variable can take any value within a range, such as an interest rate, a share price or the time until a machine breaks down.

The pattern of possible values and their probabilities is called the random variable's probability distribution. From the distribution, analysts can calculate summary measures, such as the expected value, which shows the average outcome, and the variance or standard deviation, which shows how spread out the outcomes are.

In finance, treating returns, losses, interest rates and other uncertain quantities as random variables allows analysts to model risk, price options and insurance, and estimate the chances of different outcomes.

definition: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values in a set of data. It is the simplest measure of how spread out the data are.
explanation: To calculate the range, subtract the smallest value from the largest. For the values 3, 5, 5, 7 and 10, the range is 10 minus 3, which is 7.

The range gives a quick sense of spread. For example, if a share's price moved between 42 and 58 over a year, its trading range was 16. If a company's monthly sales varied between 80,000 and 150,000, the range of 70,000 shows how much they fluctuated.

The range is easy to understand, but it has significant limitations. It depends only on the two most extreme values and ignores everything in between. A single unusual value, or outlier, can make the range very large even if all other values are close together. It also tends to increase as more data are collected, simply because more extreme values are likely to appear.

For these reasons, statisticians often use other measures of spread alongside or instead of the range, such as the interquartile range, which covers the middle 50% of the data, the variance and the standard deviation.

definition: The rate of return is the gain or loss on an investment expressed as a percentage of the amount originally invested, usually over a year.
explanation: Expressing returns as a percentage makes investments of different sizes comparable. A profit of 500 sounds better than a profit of 300, but not if the first required an investment of 10,000 and the second only 2,000. The first is a 5% return; the second is 15%.

To calculate a simple rate of return, take the ending value, add any income received, subtract the starting value, and divide by the starting value. If you invest 4,000, receive 100 in income and the investment ends at 4,300, your rate of return is 400 divided by 4,000, or 10%.

When an investment is held for several years, returns are usually converted into an annual rate so they can be compared. If 10,000 grows to 12,100 over two years, the total return is 21%, but the annual rate of return is 10%, because 10% growth in the first year and another 10% in the second produces 21% in total.
Rates of return can be quoted before or after fees, taxes and inflation. The real rate of return, after inflation, shows how much purchasing power has actually grown.

definition: Ratio analysis is the use of relationships between figures in a company's financial statements, expressed as ratios, to assess its profitability, liquidity, efficiency, debt and value.
explanation: Raw numbers can be hard to interpret. A profit of 5 million might be excellent for a small company and poor for a large one. Ratios put figures into context by comparing them with each other, such as profit with revenue, or debt with equity.

Ratios are usually grouped into families. Profitability ratios, such as operating margin and return on equity, show how well a company turns sales and capital into profit. Liquidity ratios, such as the current ratio, show whether it can meet short-term bills. Efficiency ratios, such as asset turnover and days sales outstanding, show how well it uses its resources. Leverage ratios, such as debt-to-equity, show how much it relies on borrowing. Valuation ratios, such as price-to-earnings, relate market value to financial results.
For example, a company with revenue of 2 million and operating income of 300,000 has an operating margin of 15%, which can be compared with competitors or with its own past results.

Ratios are most useful when compared over time or against similar companies. A single ratio on its own rarely tells the full story, and differences in accounting policies or business models can make comparisons misleading if not considered.

definition: Rational expectations is an economic theory that people form their expectations about the future, such as future inflation, using all available information and an understanding of how the economy works, so that their predictions are not systematically wrong.
explanation: The idea was introduced by economist John Muth in 1961 and developed by Robert Lucas and others in the 1970s. It contrasts with adaptive expectations, where people simply base their forecasts on past experience.

Under rational expectations, people may make mistakes, but those mistakes are random rather than consistently in one direction. If a government repeatedly tried to boost the economy with surprise inflation, people would learn to anticipate it, and the policy would lose its effect.

For example, if a central bank credibly announces it will keep inflation at 2%, workers and businesses with rational expectations will set wages and prices accordingly, making it easier to achieve the target.

The theory had a major influence on economics and policy, emphasising the importance of central bank credibility and predictable rules. Critics argue that real people have limited information and often behave less rationally than the theory assumes, as research in behavioral economics shows.

definition: Raw materials are the basic inputs a manufacturer buys to turn into finished products, such as wood for furniture, steel for cars or flour for bread.
explanation: Raw materials are the first stage of a manufacturer's inventory. They have been purchased but not yet used in production. Once they enter the production process, they become work in progress, and when the product is complete, they become part of finished goods.
On the balance sheet, raw materials are included in inventory as a current asset. Their cost includes the purchase price plus costs of getting them ready for use, such as shipping and import duties.
For example, a furniture maker might hold 20,000 of timber, 3,000 of screws and fittings and 2,000 of varnish at the end of the month. Together, these are its raw materials inventory of 25,000.

Managing raw materials is important for both cost and production. Running out can stop a factory, while holding too much ties up cash and risks waste. Prices of many raw materials, such as metals, energy and agricultural products, can change significantly, which directly affects a manufacturer's costs and profit margins.

definition: The real exchange rate is the exchange rate between two currencies adjusted for differences in price levels between the two countries, showing the relative cost of goods and services in each.
explanation: The nominal exchange rate tells you how many units of one currency you can get for another. The real exchange rate also accounts for inflation, showing whether goods in one country have become more or less expensive compared with another.

For example, suppose one euro buys 1.10 US dollars and stays at that nominal rate for a year, while prices in the euro area rise by 5% and US prices rise by 2%. Euro area goods have become about 3% more expensive relative to US goods. In real terms, the euro has appreciated, even though the nominal rate is unchanged.

The real exchange rate is a better measure of competitiveness than the nominal rate. A rise in the real exchange rate makes a country's exports more expensive and imports cheaper, which can reduce net exports.

Economists often use a real effective exchange rate, which compares a currency against a weighted basket of trading partners' currencies, adjusted for inflation. The real exchange rate is linked to purchasing power parity, which suggests that over long periods real exchange rates tend to return to an equilibrium level.

definition: Real GDP is the value of all goods and services produced in an economy, adjusted for changes in prices, so that it measures changes in the actual quantity of output rather than changes caused by inflation.
explanation: Gross domestic product measured at current prices can rise simply because prices have gone up, even if the economy produces no more than before. Real GDP removes this effect by valuing output at the prices of a chosen base year, or by using a price index to strip out inflation.

For example, if an economy's nominal GDP rises from 1,000 billion to 1,060 billion in a year while prices rise by 4%, its real GDP has grown by only about 1.9%. Most of the increase came from higher prices, not from producing more.

Real GDP is the main measure used to judge whether an economy is growing or shrinking. When economists, central banks and news reports talk about the economic growth rate, they almost always mean the growth rate of real GDP. Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP are a common, though informal, sign of recession.
Real GDP is also used to compare economic performance over long periods, since comparing nominal figures from decades apart would be heavily distorted by inflation.

definition: The real interest rate is the interest rate after adjusting for inflation. It shows how much your purchasing power actually grows when you save, or how much borrowing really costs.
explanation: Interest rates are usually quoted in nominal terms, but inflation reduces what money can buy. The real interest rate removes the effect of rising prices so you can see the true gain or cost.

A simple approximation is to subtract inflation from the nominal rate. If a savings account pays 5% and inflation is 3%, the real interest rate is about 2%. Your balance grows by 5%, but because prices have risen by 3%, you can buy only about 2% more than before. The precise figure is slightly lower, about 1.94%, but the simple subtraction is close enough for most purposes.
Real interest rates can be negative. If savings pay 2% while inflation is 5%, the real rate is about −3%, meaning savers lose purchasing power even as their balances grow.

For borrowers, the effect is reversed. High inflation reduces the real burden of fixed-rate debt, because repayments are made with money that is worth less. Central banks watch real interest rates closely, because they shape decisions to save, borrow and invest.

definition: A real option is a right, but not an obligation, that a company has to make a future business decision, such as expanding, delaying, changing or abandoning an investment, as circumstances change.
explanation: Traditional investment analysis, such as net present value, often assumes a company commits to a project and follows a fixed plan. In reality, managers can react to new information. Real options capture the value of this flexibility.

Common types include the option to expand if demand is strong, the option to abandon if results are poor, the option to delay investment until uncertainty clears, and the option to switch inputs or outputs, such as a power plant that can run on more than one fuel.
For example, a company building a factory may buy extra land, giving it the option to expand later if sales grow. The land has value beyond its immediate use because it keeps that choice open.

Real options can make a project worth more than its basic net present value suggests, especially when uncertainty is high. They can be valued with methods borrowed from financial option pricing, although estimating inputs such as volatility for real projects is difficult, so the analysis is often used to guide judgment rather than give precise values.

definition: Real return is the return on an investment after adjusting for inflation. It shows how much an investor's purchasing power has actually increased.
explanation: An investment can grow in money terms while losing value in terms of what the money can buy. Real return removes the effect of rising prices.

A simple approximation is to subtract the inflation rate from the nominal return. If an investment earns 7% in a year when inflation is 3%, its real return is about 4%. The more precise calculation gives about 3.9%, because the investment's gain is also measured in money that has lost some value.

Real returns can be negative even when nominal returns are positive. A savings account paying 2% during a year of 5% inflation has a real return of about −3%, so the saver can buy less at the end of the year than at the start.
Real return is the most meaningful measure for long-term goals such as retirement, because what matters is the lifestyle savings can support, not the number in the account.

Historically, different asset classes have produced very different real returns over long periods. Shares have tended to outpace inflation by more than bonds or cash, but with much greater short-term volatility.

definition: Real value is the value of money or an amount after adjusting for inflation. It shows what the money can actually buy, so amounts from different years can be compared fairly.
explanation: Prices rise over time, so the same amount of money buys less in the future than it does today. Real value removes the effect of rising prices and expresses amounts in terms of purchasing power.

For example, suppose prices rise by an average of 3% a year. In ten years, 1,000 will buy only about as much as 744 buys today. The nominal amount is still 1,000, but its real value in today's money is about 744.

Real values are essential when comparing figures across time. A country's economy that grew from 100 billion to 110 billion in nominal terms may not have grown at all in real terms if prices rose by 10% over the same period.

The same logic applies to returns. If your savings earn 5% while inflation is 3%, your nominal return is 5% but your real return is only about 2%. Thinking in real terms is the best way to judge whether savings, wages or investments are truly growing.
note: Inflation-adjusted value means the same thing as real value. Both describe an amount expressed in constant purchasing power.

definition: A realized gain is the profit an investor locks in by actually selling an asset for more than they paid for it.
explanation: An investment can increase in value on paper, but the profit becomes real only when the investment is sold. At that point, the gain is realized.

For example, an investor buys shares for 3,000. A year later, they are worth 4,000. That 1,000 increase is unrealized while the investor still holds the shares. If the investor sells them for 4,000, the 1,000 becomes a realized gain.

Realized gains matter mainly for tax. In most countries, capital gains tax is charged only on realized gains, not on increases in value that have not yet been sold. This means investors can often influence when they pay tax by choosing when to sell.

Realized gains can be offset by realized losses. If an investor realizes a gain of 1,000 on one investment and a loss of 400 on another in the same tax year, the net taxable gain may be 600, depending on local rules.
For funds, realized gains on investments sold during the year are often distributed to investors, who may then owe tax on them even if they did not sell their fund units.

definition: A real-time payment is an electronic payment between bank accounts that is processed and settled almost instantly, usually within seconds, and is available at any time of day, every day of the year.
explanation: Traditional bank transfers often took hours or days to arrive, especially outside working hours. Real-time payment systems allow money to move between accounts almost immediately, with the recipient able to use the funds straight away.

Many countries have introduced real-time payment systems. Examples include the Faster Payments Service in the United Kingdom, the Unified Payments Interface in India, Pix in Brazil, FedNow and the RTP network in the United States, and the instant payment scheme of the Single Euro Payments Area in Europe.
For example, someone selling a used bike can receive payment instantly from the buyer's banking app, confirming the money has arrived before handing over the bike.

Real-time payments improve convenience for consumers and cash flow for businesses, which can receive money immediately instead of waiting days. They also support new services, such as instant payment requests and QR-code payments in shops.

Because they are instant and generally irreversible, real-time payments are attractive to fraudsters. Banks use fraud detection systems, confirmation of the payee's name and, in some countries, reimbursement rules to protect customers.

definition: Rebalancing is the process of buying and selling investments to bring a portfolio back to its target asset allocation after market movements have changed it.
explanation: Over time, different investments grow at different rates, so a portfolio drifts away from its intended mix. Rebalancing restores the original balance of risk.

Suppose you start with 100,000 split 60% shares and 40% bonds. After a strong year for shares, your shares are worth 72,000 and your bonds 40,000, a total of 112,000. Shares now make up about 64% of the portfolio. To return to 60%, you would sell about 4,800 of shares and buy bonds with the proceeds.
Rebalancing has a useful side effect: it naturally sells assets that have risen and buys those that have fallen, which is the opposite of what emotions often push investors to do.

There are two common approaches. Calendar rebalancing happens at fixed intervals, such as once a year. Threshold rebalancing happens whenever an asset moves more than a set amount, such as five percentage points, away from its target. Transaction costs and taxes should be considered, which is why many investors rebalance only occasionally or use new contributions to restore balance.

definition: A recapitalization is a significant change in a company's capital structure, its mix of debt and equity, such as borrowing to pay a large dividend or buy back shares, or issuing equity to repay debt.
explanation: Companies recapitalize for different reasons. A leveraged recapitalization involves taking on new debt and using the proceeds to pay a special dividend or buy back shares. This returns cash to shareholders and increases leverage. Private equity owners sometimes use a similar move, called a dividend recapitalization, to take money out of a company before selling it.
For example, a private equity-owned company with debt of 100,000,000 might borrow an additional 150,000,000 and pay it to its owners as a dividend.

Conversely, a company with too much debt might recapitalize by issuing new shares or converting debt into equity, reducing leverage and the risk of financial distress. This is common in restructurings.

Recapitalizations can also be used defensively, for example to make a company less attractive to a hostile bidder. The effects depend on the direction: adding debt increases financial risk and potential returns to shareholders, while reducing debt lowers risk.

definition: A recession is a significant, widespread and lasting decline in economic activity, typically seen in falling output, income, employment and spending.
explanation: Economies tend to move in cycles of expansion and contraction. A recession is a period of contraction, when businesses produce less, people spend less, unemployment rises and incomes fall.

A common rule of thumb is that a recession occurs when real GDP falls for two consecutive quarters. Many official bodies, however, use broader judgments, looking at employment, income, sales and industrial production, and consider how deep, widespread and long-lasting the decline is.

Recessions can be triggered by many things: high interest rates used to fight inflation, financial crises, sudden rises in energy prices, falling confidence or large shocks such as pandemics. During a recession, a fall in spending can feed on itself: lower spending leads businesses to cut jobs, which reduces incomes and leads to even lower spending.

Governments and central banks usually respond by cutting interest rates, increasing public spending or lowering taxes to support demand. For households, recessions highlight the value of emergency savings and manageable debt. For investors, share prices often fall before and during recessions, although markets frequently begin to recover before the economy does.

definition: Reconciliation is the process of comparing two sets of records to check that they agree, and investigating and correcting any differences.
explanation: Businesses keep many related records that should match. Reconciliation checks that they do. Common examples include matching the cash balance in the accounts to the bank statement, matching amounts owed to a supplier with the supplier's statement, and matching subsidiary ledgers, such as a list of customer balances, with totals in the general ledger.

For example, a company's records show 45,000 owed to a supplier, but the supplier's statement shows 47,000. Investigating the 2,000 difference might reveal an invoice that has not yet been recorded, or a payment the supplier has not yet received.
Differences usually arise from timing, such as items recorded by one side but not yet by the other, or from errors, such as amounts entered incorrectly or transactions missing or duplicated.

Regular reconciliation is a key internal control. It catches errors early, helps detect fraud and ensures financial statements are accurate. Most businesses reconcile important accounts monthly as part of their financial close process.
A reconciliation is complete when every difference has been explained and any necessary corrections have been recorded.

definition: The record date is the date on which a company checks its register to identify which shareholders are entitled to receive a dividend or other distribution.
explanation: When a company declares a dividend, it announces several dates. The declaration date is when the dividend is approved. The record date is when the company determines who its shareholders are. The payment date is when the money is actually paid.

Only investors listed as shareholders on the record date receive the dividend. Because share purchases take time to settle, buyers must purchase the shares before the ex-dividend date, which is set by the exchange in relation to the record date, to appear on the register in time.

For example, a company might declare a dividend on 1 June, with a record date of 15 June and a payment date of 1 July. An investor who owns the shares at the close of the record date, having bought them before the ex-dividend date, will receive the payment on 1 July.
Record dates are also used for other corporate actions, such as rights issues, voting at shareholder meetings and share splits, to determine which shareholders are entitled to participate.
For most investors, the ex-dividend date is the more practical date to watch, since it determines whether a purchase or sale includes the right to the upcoming dividend.

definition: Recoverable amount is the higher of an asset's fair value less costs to sell and its value in use, and it is the figure an asset's carrying amount is compared with in an impairment test under IFRS.
explanation: Under IFRS, an asset should not be carried in the accounts at more than the company can recover from it, either by selling it or by continuing to use it. The recoverable amount captures the better of these two options.

Fair value less costs to sell is what the asset could be sold for in an orderly sale, minus selling costs. Value in use is the present value of the future cash flows the company expects from using the asset.

For example, a factory has a carrying amount of 1,000. It could be sold for 700 after costs, and its value in use is estimated at 820. The recoverable amount is the higher figure, 820. Because this is below the carrying amount, the company records an impairment loss of 180.

Impairment tests are often done for groups of assets that produce cash together, called cash-generating units, especially for goodwill. US GAAP uses a different approach for most long-lived assets, first testing whether undiscounted cash flows cover the carrying amount, and then measuring any impairment against fair value.

definition: The recovery rate is the percentage of a debt's value that creditors recover after a borrower defaults, through bankruptcy, restructuring or sale of assets.
explanation: When a borrower defaults, lenders rarely lose everything. They may recover part of what they are owed from the sale of collateral, a restructuring or bankruptcy proceedings. The recovery rate measures this.
For example, if a bond with a face value of 1,000 recovers 400 after the issuer defaults, the recovery rate is 40%. The loss given default is the opposite: 60%.

Recovery rates depend on factors such as the seniority of the debt, whether it is secured, the value of the borrower's assets, the industry, the legal system and economic conditions at the time of default. Senior secured loans have historically had much higher average recovery rates than unsecured or subordinated bonds.

Recovery rates are key inputs for credit risk models, bond pricing, credit default swaps and bank capital requirements. Expected loss on a loan is often estimated as the probability of default multiplied by the loss given default and the amount exposed. Recovery rates tend to be lower during recessions, when many companies default at the same time and asset values fall.

definition: Recurring revenue is income that a business expects to receive regularly and predictably, usually through subscriptions, contracts or repeated purchases.
explanation: Recurring revenue comes from customers who pay on an ongoing basis, such as monthly or annual subscriptions for software, streaming services, gym memberships, maintenance contracts or utilities.

Businesses with a high proportion of recurring revenue are often valued more highly than those relying on one-off sales, because their future income is more predictable. This makes planning easier, reduces risk and gives investors more confidence in forecasts.

Companies often track recurring revenue using measures such as monthly recurring revenue or annual recurring revenue. For example, a software company with 2,000 customers each paying 100 a month has monthly recurring revenue of 200,000, or annual recurring revenue of 2.4 million.

Other measures related to recurring revenue include churn, the rate at which customers cancel; customer lifetime value; and net revenue retention, which shows whether existing customers are spending more or less over time.

Recurring revenue is not guaranteed. Customers can cancel subscriptions, and contracts can end. A business with recurring revenue but high churn may struggle to grow, since it must constantly replace lost customers.

definition: Refinancing is replacing an existing loan with a new one, usually to get a lower interest rate, change the repayment period or release cash.
explanation: When you refinance, you take out a new loan and use it to pay off the old one. The main reasons are to reduce the interest rate, to lower monthly payments by spreading the debt over a longer period, to switch between fixed and variable rates or to borrow extra money against an asset such as a home.

The savings can be significant. On a 200,000 mortgage over 25 years, cutting the interest rate from 7% to 5.5% lowers the monthly payment from about 1,414 to about 1,228, a saving of roughly 185 a month.

Refinancing has costs, though. There may be arrangement fees, legal or valuation costs and penalties for repaying the original loan early. These need to be compared with the savings to see whether refinancing is worthwhile and how long it takes to break even.
Extending the loan term can also be a trap. Lower monthly payments may feel better, but stretching the debt over more years can increase the total interest paid, even at a lower rate.

definition: A refundable tax credit is a tax credit that can reduce a person's tax bill below zero, so any amount left over after the tax is cleared is paid to them as a refund.
explanation: A tax credit reduces the tax owed directly, unit for unit, unlike a deduction, which reduces the income that is taxed. With a refundable credit, the taxpayer receives the full value of the credit even if it is larger than the tax they owe.
For example, if someone owes 800 in tax and qualifies for a refundable credit of 1,000, the credit wipes out the 800 and the remaining 200 is paid to them.

Governments often use refundable credits to support lower-income households, because people with little or no tax liability can still benefit. Examples include credits for working families and for children in several countries.

Because they involve payments to taxpayers, refundable credits can be targets for fraud and errors, and tax authorities may check claims carefully. Some credits are partly refundable, meaning only a portion of any excess is paid out. The opposite is a nonrefundable credit, which can only reduce tax to zero.

definition: A registered investment adviser is a firm or individual in the United States that provides investment advice for a fee and is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission or a state securities regulator.
explanation: Registered investment advisers, often called RIAs, are regulated mainly under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940. Larger advisers register with the Securities and Exchange Commission, while smaller ones usually register with the state where they operate.

RIAs owe their clients a fiduciary duty, which means they must act in the client's best interest, disclose conflicts of interest and seek the best execution for trades. They must provide clients with a disclosure document describing their services, fees, conflicts and disciplinary history.
For example, a financial planner who charges clients a percentage of the assets they manage, or a flat fee for a financial plan, would typically be registered as an investment adviser.

RIAs differ from broker-dealers, who are generally paid through commissions and held to a best-interest standard when making recommendations to retail customers. Many professionals are dually registered. Other countries regulate investment advisers differently; in the United Kingdom, for example, advisers must be authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.

definition: Regression analysis is a set of statistical methods for estimating how one variable, the dependent variable, is related to one or more other variables, the independent variables.
explanation: Regression analysis helps answer questions such as: how much do sales rise when advertising spending increases? How much does a share price tend to move when the overall market moves? How does house price relate to size, location and age?

The analysis fits a mathematical relationship to data. The simplest version, linear regression, finds the straight line that best fits the data points. The result shows the estimated effect of each independent variable on the dependent variable, along with measures of how well the model fits and how reliable the estimates are.
For example, a retailer might find that each additional 1,000 spent on advertising is associated with about 4,000 of extra sales, after accounting for seasonal effects.
Regression is widely used in finance for forecasting, estimating risk measures such as beta, valuing assets and testing economic theories.

Like correlation, regression shows association, not necessarily cause and effect. Results can be misleading if important variables are left out, if the relationship is not really linear or if the data contain unusual values. Careful interpretation is essential.

definition: A regressive tax is a tax that takes a larger share of income from people with lower incomes than from people with higher incomes.
explanation: A tax can be regressive even if everyone pays the same rate. This happens because lower-income households typically spend a larger proportion of their income on the goods and services being taxed.

For example, a tax of 1 on every litre of fuel costs a household earning 20,000 and a household earning 100,000 roughly the same amount if they buy similar quantities. But that tax represents a much larger share of the lower-income household's earnings.

Sales taxes, value-added taxes and excise duties on goods such as tobacco, alcohol and fuel are often considered regressive, because poorer households spend more of their income on consumption, while wealthier households save more. Fixed charges that are the same for everyone, such as some licence fees, are also regressive.

Governments sometimes reduce the regressive effects of such taxes by exempting or applying lower rates to essentials such as food and children's clothing, or by providing benefits or tax credits to lower-income households. Regressive taxes are the opposite of progressive taxes.

definition: RegTech, short for regulatory technology, is the use of technology, such as data analytics, automation and artificial intelligence, to help businesses comply with regulations more efficiently and effectively.
explanation: Financial institutions face complex and constantly changing rules, covering areas such as anti-money laundering, sanctions, risk management, reporting and consumer protection. Meeting these requirements manually is expensive and error-prone. RegTech aims to automate and improve compliance.

Common RegTech applications include digital identity verification for customer onboarding, automated screening against sanctions lists, transaction monitoring to detect suspicious activity, regulatory reporting, tracking changes in regulations and monitoring employee communications for misconduct.

For example, a bank might use software that analyses millions of transactions to spot patterns associated with money laundering, flagging suspicious cases for human review rather than relying on simple rules that generate many false alarms.

RegTech can reduce compliance costs, improve accuracy and speed up processes. Challenges include integrating new tools with older systems, ensuring that automated decisions are explainable and keeping up with changing rules. Regulators themselves use similar technology, sometimes called SupTech, for supervision.

definition: Regulatory capital is the minimum amount and quality of capital that banks, insurers and other financial institutions are required by regulators to hold, to absorb losses and protect depositors, policyholders and the financial system.
explanation: Financial institutions are highly leveraged, so relatively small losses could wipe out their capital. Regulators require them to maintain capital buffers based on the risks they take.

For banks, regulatory capital requirements are set out in the Basel framework and national rules. They define what counts as capital, such as Common Equity Tier 1, Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2, and set minimum ratios relative to risk-weighted assets, plus buffers and a leverage ratio. For insurers, frameworks such as Solvency II in Europe set capital requirements based on the risks in their insurance and investment activities.
For example, a bank with risk-weighted assets of 100,000,000,000 must hold at least a minimum percentage of that amount in Common Equity Tier 1 capital, plus additional buffers.

Regulatory capital differs from economic capital, which is a firm's own estimate of the capital it needs. Institutions must meet regulatory requirements regardless of their internal estimates, and falling below minimums can trigger restrictions on dividends and bonuses or regulatory intervention.

definition: Reinsurance is insurance bought by insurance companies to protect themselves against large losses, transferring part of the risks they have taken on to another insurer, called a reinsurer.
explanation: Insurers face the risk that a single catastrophic event, such as a major hurricane or earthquake, or an unusually high number of claims, could produce losses large enough to threaten their financial stability. Reinsurance spreads these risks more widely.

There are two broad forms. In proportional reinsurance, the reinsurer takes a fixed share of the premiums and pays the same share of the claims. In non-proportional reinsurance, the reinsurer pays only when losses exceed a certain level. For example, an insurer might keep the first 10 million of losses from any single event, with a reinsurer covering losses between 10 million and 100 million.
Reinsurance allows insurers to write more policies than their capital alone would support, to reduce the volatility of their results and to protect against catastrophic events.

The largest reinsurers operate globally and spread their risks across many countries and types of insurance. Reinsurers sometimes buy reinsurance themselves, called retrocession. Some catastrophe risks are also transferred to investors through catastrophe bonds, which pay high interest but can lose their principal if a specified disaster occurs.

definition: Reinvestment risk is the risk that future cash flows from an investment, such as interest payments or maturing principal, will have to be reinvested at lower rates of return than the original investment.
explanation: Reinvestment risk is especially important for bond investors and savers. When interest rates fall, the coupons they receive and the principal returned at maturity must be reinvested at the new, lower rates.

For example, an investor holds a five-year bond paying 5% a year. When it matures, interest rates have fallen to 2%. The investor can now only reinvest the money at 2%, reducing their future income significantly.

Reinvestment risk also affects callable bonds. Issuers tend to repay callable bonds early when interest rates fall, forcing investors to reinvest at lower rates just when they would prefer to keep their higher-yielding bonds.

Reinvestment risk works in the opposite direction from interest rate risk. When rates rise, bond prices fall, but reinvested cash earns more. When rates fall, bond prices rise, but reinvested cash earns less.

Investors can reduce reinvestment risk by buying longer-term bonds, zero-coupon bonds that pay no interest until maturity, or by spreading investments across bonds with different maturities, a strategy known as laddering.

definition: A related-party disclosure is information in a company's financial statements about its relationships and transactions with related parties, such as directors, major shareholders, their families and companies they control.
explanation: Transactions with related parties may not be carried out on the same terms as transactions with independent parties. A company might, for example, rent offices from its chief executive's family company or sell goods to a business owned by a major shareholder. Disclosure lets readers judge whether such dealings may have affected the accounts.

Accounting standards require companies to disclose the nature of related-party relationships, the amounts of transactions, outstanding balances and any guarantees. Pay for key management, such as directors, is usually disclosed too. IFRS sets out these rules in IAS 24, and US GAAP has similar requirements.
For example, a company's notes might state that it paid 150,000 in rent during the year to a property company owned by one of its directors, with no balance outstanding at year-end.

Investors and auditors pay close attention to related-party disclosures, because undisclosed related-party dealings have been a feature of several accounting scandals. Stock exchange rules may also require independent approval of large related-party transactions.

definition: A related-party transaction is a deal or arrangement between a company and parties that have a close relationship with it, such as its directors, major shareholders, their family members or other companies they control.
explanation: Transactions between related parties may not be made on the same terms as deals between independent parties. A company might buy goods from a business owned by its chief executive at a higher price than the market rate, or lend money to a major shareholder on unusually favourable terms.

Such transactions are not necessarily wrong. Many are perfectly normal, such as group companies trading with each other. But they create a risk that one party benefits at the expense of others, especially minority shareholders.

For example, a company might rent its head office from a property firm owned by its chairman. If the rent is above market rates, value is effectively being transferred from the company's shareholders to the chairman.

Accounting standards require companies to disclose related-party relationships and significant transactions in their financial statements, including the nature of the relationship and the amounts involved. Many stock exchanges and company laws also require independent directors or shareholders to approve significant related-party transactions.
Investors and auditors look closely at these disclosures, because hidden or unfair related-party transactions have played a role in a number of corporate scandals.

definition: A relevant cost is a cost that will differ between the options being considered in a decision. Only relevant costs, and relevant revenues, should affect the choice.
explanation: When making a decision, it is tempting to include every cost involved. But costs that will be the same whatever option is chosen, or that have already been spent, do not help choose between alternatives.

For a cost to be relevant, it must be a future cost and it must differ between the options. Sunk costs are never relevant, because they have already been incurred. Fixed costs that will continue regardless of the decision are usually not relevant either.

For example, a company is deciding whether to accept a special order for 1,000 units at 40 each. The variable cost of making each unit is 30, and the factory has spare capacity, so rent and other fixed costs will not change. The relevant costs are the 30,000 of variable costs. Against 40,000 of revenue, the order adds 10,000 of profit, so it is worth accepting, even though the full cost per unit including overheads might be higher than 40.
Opportunity costs, the benefits given up by choosing one option over another, are relevant and should be included. Thinking in terms of relevant costs leads to clearer, better business decisions.

definition: A remittance is money sent by a person working in one country to family or others in another country, usually their home country.
explanation: Remittances are an important source of income for many households and countries. Migrant workers often send part of their earnings home to support relatives, pay for education, healthcare and housing or invest in small businesses.

For some countries, remittances represent a large share of the economy, sometimes more than a fifth of GDP, and can exceed foreign aid or foreign investment. Countries such as India, Mexico, the Philippines and Egypt receive very large amounts of remittances each year.
For example, a worker employed in the Gulf might send money each month to family in South Asia through a money transfer service or a mobile app.

Remittances can be sent through banks, specialist money transfer companies, mobile money services and online platforms. Costs can be significant, including transfer fees and exchange rate markups, and they have historically been higher for smaller amounts and for some routes. Reducing remittance costs is a goal of international development agencies, since lower fees mean more money reaches families. Digital services have increased competition and reduced costs on many routes.

definition: Rent is the regular payment a tenant makes to a landlord for the right to use a property, such as a home, office or piece of land, for an agreed period.
explanation: Renting lets people and businesses use property without buying it. The tenant pays rent, usually monthly, and the landlord remains the owner and is typically responsible for major repairs and the building's structure.

The terms are set out in a rental agreement or lease, which states the amount of rent, how often it is paid, how long the agreement lasts, whether and how the rent can rise, and the responsibilities of each side. Tenants usually pay a security deposit at the start, which is returned at the end if the property is left in good condition.
For example, a tenant might pay 1,200 a month for a flat on a one-year agreement, with a deposit of 2,400.

Renting and buying each have advantages. Renting offers flexibility, lower upfront costs and less responsibility for maintenance. Buying builds equity over time and protects against future rent increases, but requires a large deposit and ties up money. For many households, rent is their largest monthly expense, so it plays a central role in budgeting.

definition: Rent control is a government rule that limits how much landlords can charge for renting a home, or how much they can increase rent each year.
explanation: Rent control aims to keep housing affordable, protect tenants from sudden rent rises and allow people to remain in their communities. It can take the form of a fixed maximum rent, a cap on annual increases, such as no more than 3% a year, or rules linking increases to inflation.
In the short term, rent control can provide stability and lower costs for existing tenants. Someone in a rent-controlled flat may pay much less than the market rate in a fast-growing city.

Many economists, however, warn of longer-term side effects. Because rents are held below market levels, demand exceeds supply, which can create shortages. Landlords may have less incentive to maintain properties or build new rental housing, some may convert flats to other uses and tenants may stay in homes that no longer suit them because moving would mean paying market rents.
The effects depend on how the rules are designed. Many modern schemes allow moderate increases and exempt new buildings, to protect tenants while reducing the impact on new housing supply.

definition: Rent-seeking is the pursuit of income or wealth by manipulating the political, legal or economic environment, such as by lobbying for favourable regulations, subsidies or protection, rather than by creating new value.
explanation: Businesses and individuals normally earn income by producing goods and services people want. Rent-seeking instead tries to capture a larger share of existing wealth, often at others' expense.

Examples include lobbying for tariffs that protect an industry from foreign competition, seeking exclusive licences or monopoly rights, pushing for regulations that create barriers for new competitors, and obtaining subsidies or tax breaks that benefit a narrow group.
For example, an industry might lobby for strict licensing rules that make it costly for new firms to enter, allowing existing firms to charge higher prices.

Economists consider rent-seeking wasteful, because resources are spent on securing advantages rather than on productive activity, and because the resulting policies often reduce competition and efficiency. The concept was developed by economists including Gordon Tullock and Anne Krueger. Distinguishing legitimate advocacy from rent-seeking can be difficult in practice.

definition: Replacement cost is the amount it would cost today to replace an asset with a new one of similar quality and usefulness.
explanation: Replacement cost focuses on current prices, not on what was originally paid. Because of inflation, technological change and wear and tear, the replacement cost of an asset can differ significantly from its original cost or its value on the balance sheet.

Replacement cost is used in several areas. In insurance, many property policies pay out the cost of replacing damaged items or rebuilding a property, rather than their depreciated value. For example, a house insurance policy may cover the cost of rebuilding the home at current construction prices, which may be very different from its market value.

In valuation, replacement cost helps set a reference point for what a business or asset is worth. If a company's market value is far below the cost of building its assets from scratch, it might be undervalued, or it might reflect poor returns on those assets. The ratio of market value to replacement cost of assets, known as Tobin's q, is sometimes used to study this.
In accounting, replacement cost is one possible basis for measuring assets and calculating the true cost of goods sold during periods of inflation.

definition: The repo rate is the interest rate charged on a repurchase agreement, the short-term borrowing in which one party sells securities and agrees to buy them back at a slightly higher price. In some countries, it is also the name of the central bank's main policy rate.
explanation: In a repurchase agreement, the difference between the sale price and the repurchase price represents the interest paid by the borrower. Expressed as an annual percentage, this is the repo rate.

For example, a bank that sells bonds for 10,000,000 and agrees to buy them back the next day for 10,001,000 is effectively paying 1,000 in interest for one night, equal to an annual repo rate of about 3.6% on a 365-day basis.

Market repo rates reflect the supply and demand for short-term secured funding and the quality of the collateral. They are watched closely as a sign of conditions in funding markets. In the United States, SOFR is based on repo transactions.

In several countries, including India and South Africa, the repo rate is the central bank's key policy rate, the rate at which it lends to commercial banks against collateral. Changes in this rate influence borrowing costs across the economy, much like the federal funds rate in the United States.

definition: A reporting period is the span of time covered by a set of financial statements, such as a month, a quarter or a year.
explanation: Businesses measure their performance over set periods so that results can be compared over time. The income statement and cash flow statement cover a reporting period, while the balance sheet shows the position at the end of it.
Public companies typically report annually and, in many countries, also quarterly or half-yearly. Internally, most businesses prepare monthly reports so managers can spot problems early.

Choosing consistent reporting periods matters. Comparing a three-month period with a twelve-month one would be meaningless, and comparing a busy holiday quarter with a quiet one can be misleading. Analysts therefore often compare a quarter with the same quarter in the previous year.

Under accrual accounting, much of the work at the end of each reporting period involves making sure income and expenses are recorded in the right period. A sale delivered on the last day of the period belongs in that period, even if the invoice is paid later.

definition: Repossession is the process by which a lender takes back an asset that was used as security for a loan, such as a car or home, when the borrower fails to keep up with payments.
explanation: When a loan is secured against an asset, the lender has the right to take that asset if the borrower defaults. The lender can then sell it to recover some or all of the money owed.

Repossession is common with car loans, other vehicle finance and mortgages. In the United Kingdom and several other countries, home repossession is the term used for what is called foreclosure in the United States.

For example, if someone stops making payments on their car loan, the lender may repossess the car and sell it at auction. If the sale raises less than the outstanding loan and costs, the borrower may still owe the difference, sometimes called a shortfall or deficiency.

The rules vary widely between countries and types of loan. Many places require lenders to give warnings and try to agree a repayment plan before repossessing, and some require court orders, especially for homes. In the United Kingdom, for example, a lender cannot repossess a home without a court order, and if a borrower has repaid at least a third of a hire purchase agreement, the lender usually needs a court order to take back the goods. Borrowers facing difficulties should contact their lender early and seek free debt advice.

definition: Representations and warranties are statements of fact made by the seller, and sometimes the buyer, in an acquisition agreement about matters such as the business's financial statements, legal compliance, contracts, assets and liabilities.
explanation: Buyers cannot know everything about a business, even after due diligence. Representations and warranties allocate risk. The seller confirms certain facts, and if they turn out to be untrue, the buyer may be able to claim compensation.

Typical statements cover the accuracy of financial statements, ownership of assets and intellectual property, absence of undisclosed liabilities or lawsuits, compliance with laws, the validity of key contracts, tax matters and employee issues.
For example, the seller might warrant that the company is not involved in any litigation. If a major lawsuit filed before completion later comes to light, the buyer may claim damages.

Agreements usually limit claims, for example by setting a minimum claim size, a maximum total liability and a time limit. Sellers disclose known exceptions against the warranties in a disclosure letter or schedule. Representations and warranties insurance, which covers buyers for losses from breaches, has become common, allowing sellers to limit their liability. The legal distinction between representations and warranties varies between jurisdictions.

definition: A repurchase agreement is a short-term borrowing arrangement in which one party sells securities, usually government bonds, to another and agrees to buy them back at a slightly higher price on a set future date.
explanation: A repurchase agreement, commonly called a repo, is effectively a secured loan. The seller receives cash and the buyer receives securities as collateral. When the agreement ends, the seller repays the cash plus interest by buying back the securities at a higher price. The difference between the two prices represents the interest, known as the repo rate.

For example, a bank sells government bonds worth 10 million to an investor and agrees to buy them back the next day for 10,001,000. The bank has effectively borrowed 10 million overnight, paying 1,000 in interest.
From the other side, the transaction is called a reverse repo: the investor lends cash and receives securities as collateral.

Repos are widely used by banks, investment funds, money market funds and central banks. They are a key source of short-term funding and a major tool for central banks implementing monetary policy. Because the loan is backed by collateral, repo rates are usually lower than unsecured borrowing rates. Lenders often apply a haircut, lending slightly less than the collateral's value, to protect against falls in its price.

definition: Reputational risk is the risk that damage to an organisation's reputation will lead to loss of customers, revenue, investors, partners or employees, or to higher costs and regulatory scrutiny.
explanation: A strong reputation is valuable. It attracts customers, talented staff and investors, and it can allow a company to charge higher prices. When that reputation is damaged, the financial consequences can be severe.

Reputational damage can arise from many sources, including product failures or safety problems, scandals involving executives or employees, data breaches, poor treatment of customers or workers, environmental damage, unethical business practices and association with controversial people or activities. Social media can spread negative news very quickly.

For example, a bank found to have opened accounts for customers without their permission might suffer lasting damage to its reputation, leading customers to leave, regulators to impose fines and restrictions, and its share price to fall.

Reputational risk is often a consequence of other risks, such as operational, legal or compliance failures. It is difficult to measure but can be managed through strong governance, ethical culture, careful selection of business partners, transparent communication and a prepared plan for responding to crises.

definition: A required minimum distribution (RMD) is the minimum amount the owner of certain United States retirement accounts must withdraw each year once they reach a set age.
explanation: Tax-deferred retirement accounts, such as traditional IRAs and 401(k) plans, let money grow without tax for many years. RMDs ensure that tax is eventually collected, by requiring withdrawals to begin at a certain age. Under current law, that age is 73, rising to 75 for people born in 1960 or later.

The amount is usually calculated by dividing the account balance at the end of the previous year by a life expectancy figure from tables published by the tax authority. For example, an account worth 500,000 divided by a factor of 26.5 gives an RMD of about 18,900.
Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income. Missing an RMD triggers a penalty on the amount that should have been withdrawn, although the penalty is reduced if the shortfall is corrected quickly.

Roth IRAs do not require withdrawals during the original owner's lifetime, and since 2024 the same applies to Roth accounts in employer plans. Inherited accounts follow separate rules, which often require the account to be emptied within ten years.

definition: The required rate of return is the minimum annual return an investor expects to earn from an investment, given its level of risk, before they are willing to invest.
explanation: Investors have choices. They can put money in a safe government bond or in riskier assets such as shares. The required rate of return reflects the return needed to compensate for the time value of money and for the risk of the specific investment.

It is often built from a risk-free rate plus a risk premium. For example, if government bonds yield 4% and an investor believes a particular share needs an extra 5% to justify its risk, their required rate of return is 9%.

For companies, the required rate of return of shareholders is the cost of equity, often estimated using the Capital Asset Pricing Model. For whole businesses or projects, it is often the weighted average cost of capital.

The required rate of return is used as the discount rate in valuation models, such as the dividend discount model and discounted cash flow analysis. A higher required return leads to a lower present value. If an investment's expected return is below the investor's required return, the investor should not invest, because better risk-adjusted options are available elsewhere.

definition: Research and development expense is the cost of creating new products, improving existing ones or developing new processes and technologies.
explanation: Research and development, usually called R&D, covers the salaries of scientists, engineers and designers, laboratory costs, materials used in experiments and other spending aimed at innovation. It is especially important for technology, pharmaceutical and engineering companies.

On the income statement, R&D is usually shown as a separate operating expense. Under most accounting rules, research costs are expensed as they are incurred, because their future benefits are uncertain. Under IFRS, certain development costs can be recorded as an intangible asset once a project meets strict conditions showing it is likely to produce future benefits. US GAAP generally requires R&D to be expensed, with some exceptions such as certain software costs.
For example, a drug company might spend 2 billion a year on R&D, most of which will never lead to a successful product.

Investors often look at R&D as a percentage of revenue. High R&D spending reduces current profit but may build future growth. Cutting R&D can boost short-term profits while weakening a company's long-term competitiveness.

definition: A reserve currency is a foreign currency held in significant amounts by central banks and governments as part of their foreign exchange reserves, and widely used in international trade and finance.
explanation: Central banks hold reserves of foreign currencies to support their own currency, pay for imports, service foreign debt and provide stability in a crisis. They prefer currencies that are stable, widely accepted and backed by deep, liquid financial markets.

The US dollar is the dominant reserve currency, accounting for more than half of global foreign exchange reserves. The euro is the second most important. Others include the Japanese yen, the British pound, the Chinese renminbi, and the Canadian and Australian dollars.
For example, many commodities, including oil, are priced in US dollars, and much international trade and borrowing takes place in dollars, which increases global demand for dollar reserves.

Issuing a major reserve currency brings advantages, such as lower borrowing costs and the ability to borrow in one's own currency. Economists sometimes describe this as an exorbitant privilege. It also brings responsibilities and risks, since domestic policy decisions affect the global economy. The dominance of the dollar is a recurring topic of debate.

definition: The reserve ratio is the proportion of a bank's deposits that it holds as reserves, either as cash in its vaults or as deposits at the central bank, rather than lending out.
explanation: Banks do not keep all deposits as cash. They lend most of the money and hold only a fraction as reserves to meet day-to-day withdrawals. The reserve ratio measures that fraction.
For example, if a bank has 100 million of deposits and holds 10 million in reserves, its reserve ratio is 10%.

Some central banks set a minimum required reserve ratio as a policy tool. Raising it forces banks to hold more reserves and lend less, which can slow the economy. Lowering it frees up money for lending. In recent years, several major central banks have reduced or removed reserve requirements, relying instead on interest rates and liquidity rules to guide banking activity. Others still use reserve requirements actively.

The reserve ratio is linked to the idea of money creation in a fractional reserve banking system. When banks lend out deposits, the loans are spent and deposited elsewhere, allowing further lending. In practice, the amount of lending is also limited by capital requirements, demand for loans and central bank policy.

definition: A reserve requirement is a rule set by a central bank requiring banks to hold a minimum percentage of their customers' deposits as reserves, either as cash in their vaults or on deposit with the central bank.
explanation: Reserve requirements were traditionally used to ensure banks kept enough liquid funds to meet withdrawals and as a tool of monetary policy. Raising the requirement reduces the amount banks can lend, while lowering it allows more lending.
For example, with a 10% reserve requirement, a bank receiving 1,000 in deposits must hold at least 100 in reserves and can lend or invest the rest.

Many central banks now rely more on interest rates, and on capital and liquidity regulations, than on reserve requirements. The US Federal Reserve reduced its reserve requirement to zero in March 2020. Some countries, such as the United Kingdom and Canada, have no reserve requirements at all.

Others, including China and India, still use reserve requirements actively as a policy tool. For example, the People's Bank of China adjusts its reserve requirement ratio to influence lending. The role of reserve requirements has also changed as banks' liquidity is now governed by international standards such as the liquidity coverage ratio.

definition: Residual income is the profit a company or division earns above the minimum return required on the capital invested in it.
explanation: Accounting profit ignores the cost of shareholders' money. Residual income charges for it, so that a business only shows residual income if it earns more than its investors require.

At the company level, residual income is often calculated as net income minus a charge for equity, equal to equity multiplied by the cost of equity. For example, a company with net income of 12,000,000, equity of 80,000,000 and a cost of equity of 10% has residual income of 12,000,000 minus 8,000,000, or 4,000,000.

In management accounting, residual income is used to evaluate divisions, by subtracting a capital charge from their operating profit. Unlike return on investment, it encourages managers to accept any project earning more than the required rate, even if it lowers the division's average return.

Residual income is also the basis of a valuation method, the residual income model, which values a company as its book value plus the present value of expected future residual income. It is closely related to economic profit.

definition: Residual value is the estimated amount an asset will be worth, or could be sold for, at the end of its useful life, after deducting the expected costs of disposal.
explanation: Residual value, also called salvage value, reduces the total amount that is depreciated over an asset's life. Only the difference between cost and residual value is spread across the years of use.

For example, a machine costs 50,000, is expected to be used for five years and to be sold for 5,000 at the end. The depreciable amount is 45,000, so straight-line depreciation is 9,000 a year rather than 10,000.
Residual values are estimates and are reviewed regularly. If a company expects to sell its vehicles for more than originally thought, it raises the residual value and reduces future depreciation.

The term is also important in leasing. In a car lease, the residual value is the expected value of the car at the end of the lease. Lease payments largely cover the difference between the car's price and its residual value, so a higher residual value usually means lower monthly payments. If the car is worth less than expected at the end, whoever bears that risk, the leasing company or the customer, takes the loss.

definition: Responsibility accounting is a management accounting system that assigns costs, revenues and assets to the managers who control them, and measures each manager's performance on the items they can influence.
explanation: The core principle is that managers should be held responsible only for what they can control. Reports are organised by area of responsibility, so each manager sees the results they are accountable for.

Units are usually classified as cost centers, where managers control costs; revenue centers, where they control sales; profit centers, where they control both; and investment centers, where they also control the capital invested and are judged on return.

For example, a factory manager may be responsible for production costs and efficiency, but not for selling prices set by the sales team. A responsibility report for the factory would focus on costs and output compared with budget.

Responsibility accounting improves accountability and motivation and makes performance reviews fairer. Its challenges include separating controllable from uncontrollable items, which is not always clear, and avoiding behaviour where managers improve their own unit's numbers at the expense of the whole business.

definition: A restatement is the revision of previously published financial statements to correct a material error or to reflect a change in accounting policy.
explanation: Sometimes a company discovers that its earlier financial statements were wrong. The cause might be a calculation error, a misapplication of accounting rules, an oversight or fraud. If the error is material, the company must correct the past figures. That correction is a restatement.

For example, a company might find that revenue from several large contracts was recognised a year too early. It would restate the previous year's accounts to move that revenue into the correct period, reducing the profit originally reported.

Restatements also happen for less troubling reasons. When a company changes an accounting policy or a new accounting standard takes effect, it usually restates comparative figures from earlier years so readers can compare periods on the same basis.

Restatements caused by errors are a serious matter for investors. They can reduce confidence in management and the reliability of financial reporting, and often lead to falls in the share price, regulatory investigations or lawsuits.
When restating, companies explain the nature of the error or change and show its effect on each affected line item in the notes to their financial statements.

definition: Restricted cash is cash that a company holds but cannot freely use, because it is set aside for a specific purpose by a contract, law or regulation.
