explanation: Savings accounts offer a safe place to build up money while earning some interest. They are commonly used for emergency funds and short-term goals, such as a holiday or a deposit on a home.

Interest rates vary between banks and account types. Instant-access accounts let you withdraw at any time but may pay lower rates. Notice accounts require you to give advance warning before withdrawing, and often pay more. Some accounts offer bonus rates if you make no withdrawals in a month.
For example, if you keep 5,000 in a savings account paying 3.5% a year, you would earn about 175 in interest over a year, slightly more if interest compounds monthly.

Savings accounts are low-risk, and in many countries deposits are protected up to a limit by deposit insurance. However, interest rates are often variable and may not keep pace with inflation, so money kept there for many years can lose purchasing power. It is worth comparing rates regularly, because banks often reduce rates on older accounts while offering better deals to new customers.

definition: A savings bank is a financial institution whose main purpose is to accept savings deposits and pay interest on them, often lending mainly for home purchases.
explanation: Savings banks were historically set up to encourage ordinary people to save, at a time when commercial banks mostly served businesses and wealthy customers. Many began as community-based or mutual institutions, owned by their depositors rather than by shareholders.
Their business model traditionally centred on taking savings deposits and lending that money as mortgages to local homebuyers. In some countries, they remain important regional lenders.

Over time, the differences between savings banks and commercial banks have narrowed in many places. Many savings banks now offer current accounts, cards, personal loans and business banking, and some have converted into shareholder-owned banks.

The exact meaning varies by country. Examples include savings and loan associations and savings institutions in the United States, building societies in the United Kingdom and savings banks in Germany and Spain, many of which are closely tied to their local regions. Deposits at regulated savings banks are generally covered by the same deposit insurance as other banks.

definition: Scalability is the ability of a business to grow its revenue significantly without a proportional increase in costs.
explanation: A scalable business can serve many more customers without needing equivalent increases in staff, equipment or other resources. As a result, profit margins tend to rise as the business grows.

Software companies are classic examples. Once a software product has been developed, selling it to one more customer costs very little. Revenue can increase rapidly while costs grow slowly, especially when products are delivered online. Platforms and marketplaces can also be highly scalable.

By contrast, many service businesses, such as consulting, law or hairdressing, are less scalable, because serving more customers usually requires hiring more skilled people. A restaurant can only serve as many diners as its kitchen and tables allow, unless it opens new locations.

For example, a company selling online design software might grow from 10,000 to 100,000 customers with only a modest increase in staff, while a design agency serving ten times more clients would need many more designers.

Investors, especially venture capitalists, look for scalable business models because they offer the potential for rapid growth and high returns. Scalability also depends on processes, technology and management being able to handle growth smoothly.

definition: Scarcity is the basic economic problem that resources are limited while human wants are virtually unlimited, so people and societies must make choices.
explanation: There is never enough time, money, land, labour or materials to produce everything everyone wants. This is true for individuals, businesses and whole countries. Scarcity means every choice involves giving something up.

For an individual, scarcity might mean choosing between spending money on a holiday or saving it for a house. For a business, it might mean choosing between hiring more staff or buying new equipment. For a government, it might mean choosing between spending more on healthcare or on education.
Because of scarcity, every choice has an opportunity cost: the value of the next best alternative that is given up.

Scarcity is also why prices exist. When something is scarce relative to demand, its price tends to rise, which encourages people to use less of it and producers to supply more. Scarcity is not the same as poverty. Even very wealthy people and countries face scarcity, because their resources are still finite and they still have to choose.

definition: Scenario analysis is a planning method that estimates how financial results would change under several different possible futures, such as a base case, an optimistic case and a pessimistic case.
explanation: The future is uncertain, and a single forecast can give a false sense of certainty. Scenario analysis builds a few coherent stories about how the future might unfold and works out the financial results for each.

Each scenario changes several assumptions together in a way that makes sense. A pessimistic scenario might combine lower sales, falling prices and higher costs, reflecting a recession. An optimistic scenario might combine strong demand, higher prices and a successful product launch.

For example, a company might forecast profit of 5 million in its base case, 8 million in its best case and a loss of 1 million in its worst case. Seeing this range helps managers decide whether a plan is acceptable even if things go badly, and what actions to prepare in case they do.
Scenario analysis differs from sensitivity analysis, which changes one assumption at a time to see its individual effect. The two are often used together to understand risk.

definition: Seasonality is a regular, predictable pattern in data that repeats over a fixed period, such as each year, quarter, month or week.
explanation: Many economic and business activities follow seasonal patterns. Retail sales rise sharply before major holidays. Ice cream sales peak in summer. Heating fuel demand rises in winter. Tourism, agriculture and construction all have strong seasonal patterns. Unemployment may rise at certain times of year, for example after temporary holiday jobs end.
For example, a toy retailer might earn a large share of its annual revenue in the weeks before a major gift-giving holiday, with much lower sales in the other months.

Seasonality matters for businesses because it affects staffing, stock levels, cash flow and financing needs. A seasonal business may need to borrow to build stock before its busy period and repay the loan afterwards.

It also matters for interpreting data. Comparing December sales with November sales might suggest booming growth, when the rise simply reflects normal seasonal patterns. To avoid such misinterpretation, statistical agencies often publish seasonally adjusted figures, and analysts compare results with the same period in the previous year.
In financial markets, some investors study seasonal patterns in returns, although such patterns are often unreliable once trading costs are considered.

definition: Seasonally adjusted data is data that has been statistically modified to remove the effects of regular seasonal patterns, making it easier to see underlying trends and compare one period with another.
explanation: Many economic statistics, such as employment, retail sales and production, rise and fall at predictable times of year. Without adjustment, these seasonal swings can hide what is really happening in the economy.

For example, unemployment often rises in January after temporary holiday jobs end. If unemployment rises in January by about the usual seasonal amount, the seasonally adjusted figure would show little change, correctly indicating that the labour market has not really weakened. If unemployment rises much more than usual, the adjusted figure would show an increase.

Statistical agencies use specialised methods, based on patterns observed in past years, to estimate and remove seasonal effects. Adjustments can also account for differences such as the number of working days in a month or the timing of holidays that move from year to year.

Most headline economic figures are reported on a seasonally adjusted basis, so that changes from month to month or quarter to quarter can be compared meaningfully. Seasonal adjustment involves estimates, and figures may be revised as more data becomes available. Unusual events, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, can make seasonal patterns harder to estimate.

definition: A seasoned equity offering is the sale of new shares by a company whose shares are already publicly traded, to raise additional capital.
explanation: After its initial public offering, a company may need more money for growth, acquisitions, paying down debt or strengthening its balance sheet. Issuing new shares through a seasoned equity offering, also called a follow-on offering, is one way to raise it.
For example, a listed company might issue 10,000,000 new shares at 20 each, raising 200,000,000 before fees.

Seasoned offerings can be marketed to investors over several days, sold quickly to institutional investors in an accelerated offering, or offered first to existing shareholders through a rights issue.

Issuing new shares dilutes existing shareholders, and the share price often falls when an offering is announced. Research suggests this partly reflects a signal: managers may prefer to issue shares when they believe the shares are fully priced, so investors may interpret an offering as a sign that the shares are overvalued. New shares are usually priced at a small discount to the current market price to attract buyers.

definition: A secondary buyout is the sale of a company from one private equity firm to another private equity firm.
explanation: Private equity firms typically buy companies, improve them and sell them within several years. Instead of selling to a strategic buyer or listing the company on a stock market, they may sell it to another private equity firm.

For example, a private equity firm that bought a business services company five years ago and doubled its profits might sell it to a larger private equity firm, which sees opportunities for further growth through acquisitions or international expansion.

Secondary buyouts have become a major exit route, especially when stock markets are weak or strategic buyers are scarce. They allow the first firm to return money to its investors on schedule, while the buyer acquires a business that is already used to private equity ownership.

Critics question whether secondary buyouts create value or simply pass businesses between firms, adding fees each time, especially when the easiest improvements have already been made. Investors in both funds may sometimes effectively own the same company before and after the deal. Subsequent sales to further private equity owners are sometimes called tertiary buyouts.

definition: The secondary market is where investors buy and sell securities that have already been issued, trading with each other rather than with the original issuer.
explanation: Most trading on stock exchanges is secondary market trading. When you buy shares of a listed company through a broker, you are almost always buying them from another investor, not from the company. The company receives no money from that trade.

The secondary market is essential even though issuers do not receive money from it. It provides liquidity: investors know they can sell their securities later if they need cash, which makes them more willing to buy in the first place. It also provides price discovery, as constant trading shows what investors think securities are worth.

For example, a company might sell shares at 20 in its IPO. Over the following years, those shares might trade between investors on the stock exchange at prices from 15 to 60, depending on how the company performs and how investors view its prospects.
The prices set in the secondary market also matter to companies. A higher share price makes it easier and cheaper to raise new money in the primary market and can be used to pay for acquisitions.

definition: A secondary offering is a sale of shares by a company that is already publicly listed, or by its existing major shareholders, after its initial public offering.
explanation: The term covers two different situations. In a primary secondary offering, sometimes called a follow-on offering, the company issues new shares to raise more money. In a non-dilutive secondary offering, existing shareholders, such as founders, early investors or private equity owners, sell some of their shares to the public, and the money goes to them rather than to the company.

When a company issues new shares, existing shareholders' ownership is diluted. For example, if a company with 100 million shares issues another 10 million, an investor who owned 1% now owns about 0.91%. Share prices often fall when a dilutive offering is announced.

When existing shareholders sell, the number of shares does not change, so there is no dilution. However, the market may interpret large sales by insiders as a sign they think the shares are fully valued.
Companies use secondary offerings to fund expansion, acquisitions or debt repayment. Investors watch them because they can affect the share price and reveal how insiders see the company's prospects.

definition: A secured credit card is a credit card that requires the cardholder to pay a cash deposit, which usually sets the credit limit and serves as security for the card issuer.
explanation: Secured credit cards are designed for people with no credit history or poor credit, who may not qualify for ordinary credit cards. The deposit reduces the issuer's risk.

For example, a person deposits 500 and receives a secured card with a credit limit of 500. They use the card like a normal credit card and receive a monthly bill. If they fail to pay, the issuer can use the deposit to cover the debt.

The main benefit is building or rebuilding credit. Many issuers report payment history to credit bureaus, so using the card responsibly and paying on time can improve the cardholder's credit score. After a period of good use, some issuers return the deposit and convert the account to an ordinary card.

Secured cards can carry high interest rates and fees, so it is worth comparing options and paying the balance in full each month. They are especially common in the United States; in some other countries, similar products for credit building include credit builder cards and loans.

definition: Secured debt is borrowing backed by an asset, called collateral, that the lender can take and sell if the borrower fails to repay.
explanation: Common examples of secured debt are mortgages, which are secured by the property, and car loans, which are secured by the vehicle. If the borrower stops paying, the lender has the legal right to repossess the asset and sell it to recover what is owed.

Because the lender has this backup, secured debt is less risky for the lender. As a result, it usually comes with lower interest rates and can allow larger amounts to be borrowed than unsecured debt. A mortgage might charge 5% while an unsecured personal loan charges 10% or more.

The risk shifts towards the borrower. If you fall behind on a secured loan, you could lose the asset, such as your home or car. If the asset is sold for less than the amount owed, you may still owe the difference.

Before taking on secured debt, it is important to be confident that repayments are affordable, even if circumstances change, because the consequences of default are more serious than for most unsecured debts.

definition: Securities lending is the temporary transfer of shares or bonds from one party to another, in return for a fee and collateral, with an agreement to return equivalent securities later.
explanation: Large investors, such as pension funds, insurers and index funds, hold securities for long periods. They can earn extra income by lending them out. Borrowers are usually banks, brokers and hedge funds.

Borrowers use securities for several purposes, most commonly short selling, where they sell borrowed shares hoping to buy them back later at a lower price. Securities are also borrowed to settle trades, support market-making and for certain hedging strategies.

For example, a pension fund lends shares worth 10,000,000 to a broker. The broker provides collateral worth slightly more, often cash or government bonds, and pays a lending fee. The pension fund receives any dividends paid during the loan in the form of equivalent payments.

Securities lending improves market liquidity and supports price discovery, but it carries risks, including the borrower failing to return the securities and losses on reinvested cash collateral. Lenders also give up the right to vote the shares while they are on loan, unless they recall them.

definition: Securitization is the process of pooling financial assets that produce regular cash flows, such as mortgages or car loans, and transforming them into securities that can be sold to investors.
explanation: A bank or other lender that has made many loans can sell them to a special company set up for the purpose. That company finances the purchase by issuing securities to investors, who receive payments from the interest and principal paid by the original borrowers.

Securities backed by mortgages are called mortgage-backed securities. Those backed by other assets, such as car loans, credit card balances, student loans or equipment leases, are called asset-backed securities. The securities are often divided into tranches with different levels of risk and return.

For example, a bank might bundle thousands of car loans into a pool and sell securities backed by that pool to pension funds and insurers. The bank receives cash it can use to make new loans, while investors earn returns from the borrowers' payments.

Securitization can make credit more widely available, spread risk across many investors and give investors access to new types of assets. However, it can also weaken lending standards if lenders sell loans on rather than keeping the risk themselves. Securitizations of poor-quality US mortgages were central to the 2008 financial crisis, leading to reforms such as requirements for issuers to retain part of the risk.

definition: A security interest is a legal right granted by a borrower to a lender over specific assets, allowing the lender to take and sell those assets if the borrower fails to repay.
explanation: A security interest turns an unsecured loan into a secured one. If the borrower defaults, the lender with the security interest can enforce it, typically by taking possession of the assets and selling them to recover the debt, ahead of unsecured creditors.

Security interests can cover many types of assets, including property, equipment, inventory, receivables, bank accounts, shares and intellectual property. A mortgage is a security interest over property.
For example, a company borrows 5,000,000 from a bank and grants a security interest over its machinery and inventory. If it defaults, the bank can sell those assets to recover the loan.

To be effective against other creditors, security interests usually must be registered or perfected under local law. In the United States, this is often done by filing a financing statement under the Uniform Commercial Code; in the United Kingdom, company charges are registered at Companies House. Priority among creditors often depends on the order in which security interests were registered.

definition: A security token is a digital token recorded on a blockchain that represents ownership of, or a claim on, a financial asset such as a share, bond or fund unit, and is therefore subject to securities laws.
explanation: Security tokens aim to combine the features of traditional financial securities with the advantages of blockchain technology, such as faster settlement, easier transfer and the ability to divide assets into smaller units.

Because they represent investments, security tokens must generally comply with securities regulations, including registration or exemption requirements, disclosure rules and restrictions on who can buy them. This distinguishes them from utility tokens, which give access to a product or service, although the line between the two is often debated.
For example, a company might issue bonds as security tokens on a blockchain, with interest payments made automatically to token holders and ownership recorded on the ledger.

In the United States, whether a token is a security is generally assessed using the Howey test, which asks whether people invest money in a common enterprise expecting profits from others' efforts. Several banks and governments have issued tokenized bonds, but trading markets for security tokens remain small compared with traditional markets.

definition: Seed capital is the initial money used to start a business, typically to develop a product, conduct market research and build a team before the company can attract larger investment.
explanation: Seed capital is the earliest stage of formal start-up funding. It often comes from founders themselves, friends and family, angel investors, accelerators, crowdfunding or specialist seed-stage venture capital funds.

At the seed stage, companies usually have an idea, a small team and perhaps an early version of their product, but limited revenue. Seed funding helps them prove their concept and demonstrate enough progress to raise a larger round, typically a Series A.
For example, a start-up developing an app might raise seed funding of 1 million to hire engineers, build the product and gain its first users.

Seed investments are often structured as convertible notes or simple agreements for future equity, which convert into shares at a later funding round, avoiding the need to agree a precise valuation at such an early stage. Equity investments with an agreed valuation are also common.
Seed investing carries very high risk, since most early-stage companies fail. Investors accept this in the hope that a small number of successful investments will produce very large returns.

definition: Segment margin is the profit a business segment, such as a product line, region or division, contributes after deducting its variable costs and the fixed costs directly traceable to it, but before shared company-wide costs.
explanation: Segment margin shows how much each part of a business contributes towards covering the company's common costs, such as head office and group IT, and towards overall profit.

It is calculated by taking the segment's revenue, subtracting its variable costs to get the contribution margin, and then subtracting fixed costs that exist only because of that segment, such as its dedicated staff, equipment and marketing.
For example, a product line has revenue of 500,000, variable costs of 300,000 and traceable fixed costs of 120,000. Its segment margin is 80,000.

Segment margin is useful for decisions about whether to keep or drop a segment. If a segment has a positive segment margin, closing it would usually reduce total profit, even if it looks unprofitable after shared costs are allocated to it, because those shared costs would remain. It is a management accounting measure and differs from the segment results reported in published financial statements.

definition: Segment reporting is the disclosure of financial information about the different parts of a company's business, such as product lines or geographic regions, as they are reviewed by its management.
explanation: A large company may run very different businesses that perform differently. Consolidated totals can hide important details, such as one division growing fast while another loses money. Segment reporting breaks results down to show these differences.

Under IFRS and US GAAP, companies report segments based on how management organises and reviews the business internally. For each reportable segment, they typically disclose revenue, a measure of profit, and often assets and other key figures.

For example, a technology company might report three segments: hardware, software and services. Its disclosures might show that hardware brings in most of the revenue but services earn the highest profit margin.
Companies also usually disclose revenue by geographic area and identify major customers when a single customer accounts for a large share of revenue.

Segment reporting helps investors understand where a company earns its money, which parts are growing or struggling and how exposed it is to particular markets or regions. It is especially useful when valuing businesses using a sum-of-the-parts approach.

definition: Segregation of duties is an internal control principle that divides key tasks in a process among different people, so that no single person can both commit and conceal an error or fraud.
explanation: The basic idea is that the person who authorises a transaction should not also be the one who records it, holds the related asset or checks it. Splitting these roles creates natural checks.

For example, in a purchasing process, one person might approve new suppliers, another place orders, a third record invoices and a fourth make payments. If one person could do all four, they could create a fake supplier, approve fake invoices and pay themselves without anyone noticing.
Similarly, the employee who handles cash receipts should not be the one who reconciles the bank account, because they could hide missing money in the records.

In small organisations with few staff, full segregation may not be practical. In those cases, other controls can compensate, such as owner review of transactions, regular independent checks or mandatory holidays that require someone else to cover a role.
Segregation of duties is one of the most important internal controls. Auditors routinely test whether it is in place, because its absence significantly increases the risk of fraud.

definition: Selection bias occurs when the individuals, groups or data included in an analysis are chosen in a way that is not random, so the results do not fairly represent the population or the effect being studied.
explanation: Selection bias is a broad category of errors that arise from how data are selected. Sampling bias and survivorship bias are specific types of selection bias.

For example, suppose a bank wants to know whether a new savings product leads customers to save more. It compares customers who chose the product with those who did not and finds the first group saves more. But customers who chose the product may already have been keener savers. The difference may reflect who chose the product, not the effect of the product itself.

In finance, selection bias can appear in many ways. Credit scoring models built only on borrowers who were approved for loans may not work well for applicants who would previously have been rejected. Studies of companies that voluntarily disclose certain information may not represent companies that choose not to.

Researchers reduce selection bias through random selection, randomised experiments where possible and statistical methods that account for how the data were selected. Recognising potential selection bias is essential before drawing conclusions from any data.

definition: Self-insurance is a risk management approach in which a person or organisation sets aside its own funds to pay for potential losses, instead of buying insurance to cover them.
explanation: Self-insurance is a form of planned risk retention. It makes sense when losses are predictable, the organisation is large enough to absorb them and the cost of insurance would exceed expected losses.

Large employers in the United States often self-insure their employees' health benefits, paying claims directly rather than buying a group policy, while hiring an insurer or administrator to process claims. Many large companies also self-insure parts of their property, motor or workers' compensation risks.

For example, a company with thousands of employees might expect its annual health claims to be fairly stable and choose to pay them directly, buying stop-loss insurance to cover unusually large claims above a set level.

Self-insurance can save money, improve cash flow and give more control, but it exposes the organisation to unexpected large losses, which is why it is often combined with insurance for catastrophic events. For individuals, building an emergency fund instead of insuring small risks, such as minor electronic devices, is a simple form of self-insurance.

definition: Seller financing is an arrangement in which the seller of a business or property lends part of the purchase price to the buyer, who repays it over time, instead of the buyer paying the full price upfront.
explanation: Seller financing, also called vendor financing or a vendor loan, is common in sales of small and medium-sized businesses, where buyers may struggle to obtain enough bank finance.

For example, a buyer agrees to purchase a business for 2,000,000. They pay 1,400,000 at completion, funded by their own money and a bank loan, and the seller agrees to receive the remaining 600,000 over five years, with interest, as a vendor note.

Seller financing can help deals happen and may allow a higher price. It also signals the seller's confidence in the business, since they will be repaid only if it continues to perform. Sellers may earn interest on the loan.

The main risk for the seller is that the buyer fails to pay, for example if the business struggles under new ownership. Seller loans are often subordinated to bank loans, meaning the bank is repaid first. Sellers may require security, personal guarantees or covenants. In property, seller financing is sometimes used where buyers cannot obtain mortgages.

definition: A selling expense is a cost incurred to market and sell a business's products or services, such as advertising, sales staff pay, commissions and delivery to customers.
explanation: Selling expenses are one group of operating expenses. They cover everything involved in finding customers, persuading them to buy and getting products to them.

Common selling expenses include advertising and promotions, salaries and commissions of sales staff, sales travel, the cost of showrooms or retail stores used for selling, packaging for shipment and delivery costs to customers.
On the income statement, selling expenses are often combined with general and administrative expenses into a single line called selling, general and administrative expenses, or SG&A.
For example, a company might spend 90,000 on advertising, 150,000 on sales staff salaries and commissions and 30,000 on deliveries in a year, giving selling expenses of 270,000.

Businesses watch selling expenses relative to revenue. If sales rise faster than selling expenses, marketing is becoming more efficient. If selling expenses rise without a matching increase in sales, the business may be spending too much to win customers.

definition: A semi-variable cost is a cost that has both a fixed part, paid regardless of activity, and a variable part that changes with the level of activity.
explanation: Many real-world costs combine fixed and variable elements. They are also called mixed costs.

A common example is a phone plan with a fixed monthly charge of 50 plus 0.10 for each minute of calls. A business that makes 2,000 minutes of calls pays 50 plus 200, a total of 250. If it makes 4,000 minutes, it pays 450. The cost rises with use, but not in direct proportion, because of the fixed element.

Other examples include utility bills with a standing charge plus usage charges, maintenance costs that include routine servicing plus extra repairs when machines are used more heavily, and sales staff paid a base salary plus commission.

For budgeting and analysis, businesses often split semi-variable costs into their fixed and variable parts. This makes it easier to forecast costs at different levels of activity and to calculate break-even points accurately.
Understanding which costs are fixed, variable or semi-variable helps managers predict how profits will respond to changes in sales and plan how to adjust costs when conditions change.

definition: Senior debt is borrowing that has the highest priority for repayment if a company goes bankrupt or is liquidated, ranking ahead of other types of debt and equity.
explanation: When a company fails, its assets are used to repay its creditors in a set order. Senior debt sits at the top of this order. It is often secured, meaning it is backed by specific assets, such as property, equipment or receivables, which the lenders can claim if the company defaults.
Because senior debt is more likely to be repaid, it carries lower risk for lenders and usually pays lower interest rates than subordinated or mezzanine debt.

Common forms of senior debt include bank loans, revolving credit facilities and senior secured bonds. For example, in a leveraged buyout, the senior debt might be a term loan from banks secured on all of the company's assets, sitting ahead of subordinated bonds and equity in the order of repayment.

Senior debt agreements often include covenants that restrict the borrower's actions and give lenders early warning of problems. Senior lenders often have significant influence in restructurings, since they are first in line to recover their money. Recovery rates for senior secured debt in defaults have historically been higher than for subordinated debt.

definition: Sensitivity analysis tests how much a financial result, such as profit or project value, changes when one assumption is changed while all others are held constant.
explanation: Forecasts depend on many assumptions, but some matter much more than others. Sensitivity analysis identifies which assumptions have the biggest effect on the result.

For example, an analyst valuing a project might test what happens to its net present value if sales volume is 10% lower than expected, then if the selling price is 10% lower, then if costs are 10% higher. If a 10% fall in price wipes out all the project's value while a 10% rise in costs only reduces it slightly, the analyst knows that price is the key risk.
Results are often shown in a table, with different values of one or two assumptions along each side and the resulting outcome in each cell.

Sensitivity analysis helps decision-makers focus their attention. It shows which assumptions need the most careful research and monitoring. Its limitation is that, in reality, assumptions often change together, which is why it is commonly combined with scenario analysis.

definition: A sensitivity table is a grid in a financial model that shows how an output, such as a company's valuation, changes when two key assumptions are varied at the same time.
explanation: Financial models depend on assumptions that are uncertain. A sensitivity table makes this uncertainty visible by recalculating the result for a range of input combinations and displaying the answers in rows and columns.

For example, a valuation might place different discount rates, such as 8%, 9% and 10%, across the top of the table, and different long-term growth rates, such as 2%, 2.5% and 3%, down the side. Each cell shows the resulting value per share for that combination. A reader can quickly see that the value ranges from, say, 32 in the most cautious case to 55 in the most optimistic.

Sensitivity tables help analysts and decision-makers understand which assumptions matter most and how much confidence to place in a single estimate. They are widely used in investment banking, equity research, corporate finance and project appraisal.

In spreadsheets, sensitivity tables are often built with a data table function that recalculates the model automatically. They test one or two variables at a time. For broader questions, such as how a recession would affect several inputs at once, analysts use scenario analysis instead.

definition: Sequence-of-returns risk is the risk that poor investment returns early in retirement, while withdrawals are being made, permanently reduce how long savings will last, even if average returns over the whole period are acceptable.
explanation: When someone is saving and not withdrawing, the order of good and bad years does not affect the final result. Once regular withdrawals begin, it does. Selling investments after a fall to pay living costs locks in losses, leaving less money to benefit from any recovery.

For example, two retirees each start with 1,000,000 and withdraw 50,000 at the start of each year. One gets returns of −20%, then +10% and +10%. The other gets the same returns in reverse order. After three years, the first has about 804,100 and the second about 835,600, even though their returns were identical, just in a different order.
The risk is greatest in the years just before and after retirement, when the portfolio is largest and withdrawals are starting.

Ways to manage it include keeping a cash or bond buffer to avoid selling shares after a fall, reducing withdrawals in bad years, reducing risk gradually as retirement approaches and using guaranteed income such as annuities for part of spending.

definition: Series A is typically the first major round of venture capital financing for a start-up, following seed funding, used to grow a business that has shown early promise.
explanation: By the time a start-up raises a Series A round, it usually has a working product, some customers and evidence that its business model can work. Series A funding is used to expand the team, improve the product, enter new markets and build a repeatable way to acquire customers.

Series A rounds are usually led by venture capital firms, which receive preferred shares in exchange for their investment. Preferred shares often come with special rights, such as liquidation preferences, board seats and protections against future dilution.
For example, a software start-up with growing monthly revenue might raise a Series A round of several million from a venture capital firm, giving up perhaps 20% to 30% of the company.

The amount raised and valuations at Series A vary significantly depending on the industry, location and market conditions. Raising a Series A is often harder than raising seed funding, because investors expect clearer evidence of product-market fit. Many start-ups that raise seed funding never reach Series A. Later rounds, such as Series B and Series C, follow as the company continues to grow.

definition: Series B is a later round of venture capital financing, following Series A, used to help a start-up that has proven its business model scale up and expand.
explanation: By the Series B stage, a company typically has a solid customer base, significant revenue and a business model that has shown it can work. The focus shifts from proving the concept to growing rapidly.
Series B funding is commonly used to expand into new markets, hire more staff in sales, marketing and engineering, develop additional products, and sometimes acquire smaller companies.

Series B rounds are usually larger than Series A rounds and are often led by venture capital firms that specialise in later-stage companies, with earlier investors often investing again to maintain their ownership.
For example, a delivery start-up that has succeeded in several cities might raise a Series B round to expand across the country, hire hundreds of staff and improve its technology.

Each new round dilutes existing shareholders, but if the company's valuation rises between rounds, their stakes become more valuable even as their percentage ownership falls. Later rounds, such as Series C and beyond, may follow, often with larger amounts and investors such as growth equity firms, hedge funds and corporate investors, as the company prepares for a sale or a stock market listing.

definition: Serviceable available market (SAM) is the portion of the total addressable market that a company can realistically target with its current products, business model and geographic reach.
explanation: Total addressable market estimates the entire revenue opportunity for a type of product. SAM narrows this down to the customers the company's specific offering can actually serve.

For example, the global market for accounting software might be worth 1,000,000,000 a year. A company whose software is designed for small businesses and sold only in English-speaking countries might have a SAM of 200,000,000, because larger companies and other regions are outside its reach.
SAM is shaped by factors such as the product's features, price point, distribution channels, language, regulations and the customer segments the company targets.

SAM helps companies and investors judge a realistic growth opportunity. A huge total market means little if the company can only serve a small part of it. Expanding into new regions or customer segments, or adding product features, can increase SAM over time.

definition: Serviceable obtainable market (SOM) is the portion of the serviceable available market that a company can realistically capture in the near term, given its competition, resources and sales capacity.
explanation: SOM is the most realistic of the three market-size estimates. Total addressable market shows the full opportunity, serviceable available market shows what the company's offering could serve, and SOM estimates what the company can actually win.

For example, if a company's serviceable available market is 200,000,000 a year, it might estimate that it can capture about 10% within five years, given strong competitors and its sales capacity, giving a SOM of 20,000,000.
SOM is often estimated by considering the company's current market share, sales team size, marketing budget, growth rates of similar companies and the strength of competitors.

Start-ups commonly present TAM, SAM and SOM in investor pitches. Investors tend to be sceptical of very large TAM figures and pay closer attention to whether SOM estimates are credible and supported by evidence such as early sales, customer interest and realistic growth plans.

definition: The settlement date is the date on which a trade is completed, when the buyer pays for the securities and the seller delivers them, transferring ownership.
explanation: When you buy shares, the trade is agreed instantly, but the actual exchange of money and securities happens a short time later. That later date is the settlement date.

Settlement cycles are often described as "T plus" a number of days, where T is the trade date. Many major markets, including the United States, Canada and India, moved to T+1, meaning settlement one business day after the trade, and others have announced plans to follow. Some markets still use T+2, and some instruments, such as certain government bonds and foreign exchange trades, settle on different timetables.
For example, under T+1, shares bought on a Monday would settle on Tuesday. The buyer becomes the legal owner, and the seller receives the money, on Tuesday.

The settlement date matters for several reasons. It determines who is entitled to dividends, since ownership on the record date depends on settled trades. It affects when money from a sale becomes available to withdraw.
Shorter settlement cycles reduce the risk that one party fails to complete the trade, which is why regulators have pushed to shorten them.

definition: Settlement risk is the risk that one party in a transaction delivers payment or assets as agreed, but the other party fails to deliver its side, leading to a loss.
explanation: When two parties exchange money or securities, the exchange may not happen at exactly the same moment. If one side pays and the other defaults before delivering, the first party can lose the full value of the transaction.

Settlement risk is particularly important in foreign exchange, where two currencies are exchanged, sometimes in different time zones. It is often called Herstatt risk, after a German bank, Bankhaus Herstatt, that was closed in 1974 after receiving payments in German marks but before paying out US dollars to its counterparties.
For example, a bank pays 10,000,000 euros to another bank in exchange for US dollars. If the second bank fails before paying the dollars, the first bank may lose the euros it sent.

Settlement risk is reduced through systems that link both sides of a transaction, such as payment versus payment in foreign exchange, through CLS Bank, and delivery versus payment in securities. Shorter settlement cycles and central counterparties also reduce the risk.

definition: A share is a single unit of ownership in a company. Owning shares makes you a part-owner, entitled to a portion of the company's profits and, usually, a vote on certain decisions.
explanation: A company's ownership is divided into many equal units called shares. If a company has 10 million shares and you own 100,000, you own 1% of the company.

Shareholders can earn money through dividends, which are payments from the company's profits, and through capital gains if the share price rises. Most ordinary shares also come with voting rights, allowing shareholders to vote on matters such as electing directors.

Shares of public companies are traded on stock exchanges, where their prices change constantly as buyers and sellers react to news, company results and broader market conditions. Shares in private companies are not traded publicly and are harder to buy or sell.

Owning shares carries risk. Share prices can fall, dividends can be cut, and if a company fails, shareholders are paid last, after all lenders and creditors. In return for this risk, shares have historically offered higher long-term returns than safer investments such as bonds or cash.

definition: Share capital is the money a company has raised by issuing shares to its owners. It forms part of shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.
explanation: When a company is formed or later raises money, investors buy shares and pay cash to the company. That cash becomes share capital, which represents the owners' direct investment in the business.

In many countries, share capital is split into two parts. Each share has a nominal or par value, which is often very small, such as 0.01 or 1. Any amount paid above that value is recorded separately as share premium or additional paid-in capital. For example, if a company issues 1 million shares with a nominal value of 1 at a price of 5 each, it records 1 million of share capital and 4 million of share premium.
Share capital is different from retained earnings. Share capital comes from owners putting money in; retained earnings come from profits the business has earned and kept.

Share capital is permanent financing: the company does not have to repay it. In return, shareholders own part of the company, may receive dividends and usually have voting rights. When a company buys back its own shares, the amount of equity on its balance sheet falls.

definition: A share repurchase is when a company buys back its own shares from the market or directly from shareholders, reducing the number of shares outstanding.
explanation: Share repurchases are a way of returning cash to shareholders, alongside or instead of dividends. When a company buys back shares, each remaining share represents a larger slice of the company.

For example, a company with 100 million shares and net income of 200 million has earnings per share of 2.00. If it buys back 10 million shares and profit stays the same, earnings per share rises to about 2.22, because profit is now shared among 90 million shares.

Companies repurchase shares for several reasons: to return surplus cash, to signal that management believes the shares are undervalued, to offset dilution from employee share plans or to adjust their capital structure.

Repurchases offer flexibility. Unlike regular dividends, which shareholders expect to continue, buybacks can be increased, reduced or paused without the same negative signal. In some countries, they may also be more tax-efficient for shareholders than dividends.
Critics argue that buybacks can be used to boost earnings per share in the short term, sometimes at the expense of long-term investment, and that buying shares at high prices can destroy value.
note: Buyback means the same as share repurchase.

definition: A share sale is a transaction in which a buyer acquires the shares of a company, taking ownership of the whole company, including all its assets, liabilities and obligations.
explanation: In a share sale, also called a stock sale, the company itself does not change. Its contracts, employees, licences and history all remain in place. Only its owners change.
For example, a buyer purchases 100% of the shares in a logistics company. The company continues to own its trucks and warehouses, employ its staff and hold its contracts, but now under new ownership.

Share sales are often simpler than asset sales, because individual assets and contracts do not need to be transferred, although some contracts include change-of-control clauses requiring consent. Sellers often prefer them, as they can exit cleanly and may benefit from favourable tax treatment on the sale of shares.

The main risk for buyers is that they inherit all of the company's liabilities, including unknown ones, such as past tax issues, lawsuits or environmental problems. Buyers manage this risk through due diligence, warranties, indemnities, insurance and price adjustments.

definition: Share-based compensation is payment to employees, directors or others in the form of shares, share options or other equity instruments, recorded as an expense in the company's accounts.
explanation: Many companies, especially technology and start-up businesses, pay part of their employees' compensation in equity. This helps attract and keep talent and aligns staff interests with shareholders, because employees benefit when the share price rises.
Common forms include stock options, which give the right to buy shares at a set price; restricted stock units, which deliver shares after a vesting period; and employee share purchase plans.

Accounting rules require the fair value of these awards to be recorded as an expense, usually spread over the vesting period. For example, if a company grants options valued at 400,000 that vest over four years, it records about 100,000 of expense each year.

Share-based compensation is a non-cash expense, because no cash leaves the company when the award is granted. For that reason, some companies exclude it from adjusted profit measures. However, it has a real cost to shareholders: when the awards vest or are exercised, new shares may be issued, diluting existing owners.
Investors often look at share-based compensation as a percentage of revenue and at how much dilution it is causing over time.

definition: Shareholder activism is when shareholders use their ownership rights to push a company to make changes, such as in strategy, management, governance, capital allocation or environmental and social practices.
explanation: Activist shareholders believe a company could be run better, and they seek to influence it rather than simply selling their shares.

Activist approaches range from private discussions with management to public campaigns, submitting shareholder proposals, nominating candidates for the board and, in some cases, proxy fights to replace directors. Activist hedge funds often buy significant stakes in companies they believe are undervalued, then push for changes such as selling divisions, returning cash to shareholders, cutting costs or replacing executives.
For example, an activist investor might buy 5% of a conglomerate's shares and publicly argue that spinning off an underperforming division would unlock value.

Other activists focus on environmental, social or governance issues, such as climate policies or board diversity, and include pension funds and other long-term investors. Supporters argue activism improves accountability and performance. Critics argue some activists focus on short-term gains at the expense of long-term investment.

definition: A shareholder agreement is a contract between some or all of a company's shareholders, setting out their rights and obligations, how the company is run and what happens in situations such as the sale of shares or disputes.
explanation: A company's constitution sets out basic rules, but shareholders often agree further terms privately. A shareholder agreement is especially important in private companies, start-ups and joint ventures, where shareholders may need protection and clear processes.

Common provisions include who can appoint directors, matters that require shareholder approval, such as issuing new shares or selling the business, restrictions on transferring shares, such as rights of first refusal, drag-along and tag-along rights, dividend policies, how disputes are resolved and what happens if a shareholder leaves, dies or wants to sell.

For example, two founders and an investor might agree that the investor can appoint one director, that major decisions need the investor's consent and that a founder who leaves within two years must sell their shares back at a set price.
Shareholder agreements are usually private, unlike company constitutions, which may be publicly filed. They help prevent disputes by setting expectations clearly in advance.

definition: Shares outstanding is the total number of a company's shares currently held by all its shareholders, including insiders and institutions, but excluding shares the company has bought back and holds itself.
explanation: Shares outstanding is a basic figure used in many calculations. Market capitalization is the share price multiplied by shares outstanding. Earnings per share is net income divided by the average number of shares outstanding.

The number changes over time. It rises when a company issues new shares, for example to raise money, pay for an acquisition or reward employees with share awards. It falls when a company buys back its own shares. Shares bought back are often held as treasury shares, which do not count as outstanding, receive no dividends and carry no votes.

For example, a company with 200 million shares outstanding that buys back 10 million will have 190 million shares outstanding. If its net income stays at 380 million, earnings per share rises from 1.90 to 2.00.

Analysts also look at fully diluted shares outstanding, which includes shares that could be created from stock options, convertible bonds and similar instruments. This gives a more cautious view of how many shares might eventually share in the company's profits.

definition: The Sharpe ratio measures an investment's return above the risk-free rate for each unit of total risk, measured by the standard deviation of its returns.
explanation: The Sharpe ratio, developed by economist William Sharpe, answers the question: how much extra return am I getting for the volatility I am accepting?

It is calculated by subtracting the risk-free rate, often the yield on short-term government securities, from the investment's return, and dividing the result by the standard deviation of the investment's returns.

For example, a fund with an annual return of 10%, a risk-free rate of 3% and a standard deviation of 14% has a Sharpe ratio of 0.5. Another fund returning 8% with a standard deviation of 7% has a Sharpe ratio of about 0.71, so it delivered more return per unit of risk, even though its raw return was lower.
Higher Sharpe ratios indicate better risk-adjusted performance. The ratio is widely used to compare funds, strategies and portfolios.

It has limitations. It treats upward and downward volatility the same, although investors usually worry only about losses. It assumes returns are roughly normally distributed, which may understate the risk of rare, severe losses. And like other performance measures, it depends on the period chosen.

definition: Short interest is the total number of a company's shares that have been sold short and not yet bought back, often expressed as a percentage of the shares available for trading.
explanation: When investors sell short, they borrow shares and sell them, hoping to buy them back later at a lower price. Short interest measures how many shares are currently held in short positions.

High short interest suggests many investors expect the share price to fall. For example, if 15% of a company's freely traded shares are sold short, a significant group of investors is betting against the company.
Short interest is published regularly by exchanges or regulators in many markets. In some countries, regulators also require large individual short positions to be disclosed.

High short interest can be read in different ways. It may signal real problems, such as weak finances or suspected accounting issues. But it can also lead to a short squeeze: if the price rises, short sellers rush to buy shares to limit their losses, pushing the price up further. This happened dramatically with several heavily shorted shares in early 2021. Short interest is often considered together with days to cover.

definition: Short selling is selling a security you do not own, by borrowing it, in the hope of buying it back later at a lower price and keeping the difference as profit.
explanation: Normal investing means buying low and selling high. Short selling reverses the order: sell high first, then buy low later. The investor borrows shares, usually through their broker, sells them in the market and later buys the same number of shares to return to the lender.

For example, an investor borrows and sells 100 shares at 50, receiving 5,000. If the price falls to 40, they buy 100 shares for 4,000 and return them, making a profit of 1,000 before fees and borrowing costs.

Short selling is risky. If the price rises instead, the investor loses money. Because there is no limit to how high a price can rise, losses are potentially unlimited. If the price in the example rose to 80, buying back the shares would cost 8,000, a loss of 3,000.

Short sellers pay fees to borrow shares and must cover any dividends paid while they hold the position. They can also be forced to buy back if the lender recalls the shares. Short selling is used for speculation and for hedging, and some argue it helps markets by exposing overvalued companies.

definition: Short-term investments are financial assets that a company expects to sell or that will mature within one year, but that do not qualify as cash equivalents.
explanation: Companies often have more cash than they need for day-to-day operations. Rather than leaving it idle, they invest it in assets that earn a return but can be turned into cash fairly quickly. Those that mature or are expected to be sold within a year, but take longer than about three months or carry more risk than cash equivalents, are reported as short-term investments.
Examples include term deposits of six or twelve months, government or corporate bonds maturing within a year and shares held for trading.
For example, a company might hold 5 million in cash and cash equivalents and another 8 million in six-month deposits and short-dated bonds, reported as short-term investments within current assets.

Short-term investments add to a company's liquidity, though they may be slightly less accessible than cash. Depending on their type, they may be measured at fair value, with changes in value affecting profit or other comprehensive income, or at amortized cost.
Analysts often add cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments together when measuring how much readily available money a company has.

definition: Signaling theory is the idea that companies and their managers use actions, such as paying dividends, buying back shares or taking on debt, to convey information about the company's prospects to investors who know less than they do.
explanation: Because managers know more about their company than outside investors, they may try to signal confidence in ways that are costly or risky to fake.

For example, raising the dividend can signal that managers expect strong, stable future earnings, since cutting a dividend later is usually painful and damages credibility. Buying back shares can signal that managers believe the shares are undervalued. Taking on debt can signal confidence that future cash flows will cover interest payments.
Conversely, issuing new shares may signal that managers think the shares are overpriced, which is one reason share prices often fall when new equity is announced.

For a signal to be believable, it needs to be costly for a weak company to imitate. Signals are not always reliable, because managers may be overconfident or may try to mislead. The theory has roots in economist Michael Spence's work on signals in job markets, and it is widely used to explain dividend policy and market reactions to corporate announcements.

definition: Simple interest is interest calculated only on the original amount borrowed or saved, not on any interest already earned or charged.
explanation: With simple interest, the interest each period is always the same, because it is always based on the original principal. It does not grow over time.

Suppose you save 5,000 at a simple interest rate of 4% a year. Each year you earn 200, which is 4% of 5,000. After three years you have earned 600 in interest, and your balance is 5,600. The fourth year earns another 200, no more.
This makes simple interest easy to calculate: multiply the principal by the annual rate and by the number of years. Here, 5,000 × 0.04 × 3 = 600.

Simple interest is common for short-term loans, some car loans and certain bonds that pay a fixed amount of interest each year. Most savings accounts, credit cards and long-term investments, however, use compound interest, where interest is added to the balance and then earns interest itself. Over long periods, the difference between the two can be very large.

definition: A sinking fund is money set aside regularly for a specific future expense or debt repayment, so the full amount is available when it is needed.
explanation: Instead of facing a large bill all at once, a sinking fund spreads the cost over time. You estimate the amount needed and the date, then save a fixed amount each period.

For individuals, sinking funds are often used for predictable but irregular costs, such as annual insurance premiums, car repairs, holidays or school fees. If a car insurance bill of 6,000 is due in twelve months, saving 500 a month into a separate account means the money is ready when the bill arrives.
Sinking funds differ from emergency funds. An emergency fund is for unexpected events; a sinking fund is for expected expenses whose timing and approximate size are known.

Companies and governments use sinking funds too, especially for bonds. A bond with a sinking fund provision requires the issuer to set aside money, or to buy back part of the bonds, each year before maturity. This reduces the risk that the issuer will be unable to repay the full amount at the end, which can make the bonds safer for investors.

definition: A size premium is the extra return that some analysts add to the cost of equity for smaller companies, based on the view that small companies are riskier and have historically earned higher returns than large ones.
explanation: Research in the 1980s found that shares of smaller companies had earned higher average returns than those of larger companies over long periods, more than their betas alone would predict. This led to the idea of a size premium.

In practice, valuers, especially of private and small companies, sometimes add a size premium to the cost of equity calculated with the Capital Asset Pricing Model. For example, an analyst might add 2% to the cost of equity for a small private manufacturer, reflecting risks such as dependence on a few customers or key people, limited access to finance and less diversified operations.

The size premium is controversial. Later research found that the effect weakened after it was widely publicised, varied greatly between periods and may partly reflect other factors, such as illiquidity or poor quality among the smallest companies.
Some valuers prefer to address the specific risks of small companies directly in cash flow forecasts. Whatever approach is used, the assumptions should be explained clearly.

definition: Skewness is a measure of how asymmetrical a probability distribution is, showing whether extreme values are more likely on one side of the average than the other.
explanation: A perfectly symmetrical distribution, such as the normal distribution, has zero skewness. Its left and right sides mirror each other.

A distribution with positive skewness has a long tail on the right. Most outcomes are modest, but there is a small chance of very large positive outcomes. For example, start-up investments are positively skewed: most fail or return little, but a few return many times the money invested. Lottery tickets are also strongly positively skewed.

A distribution with negative skewness has a long tail on the left. Most outcomes are modestly positive, but there is a small chance of large losses. Strategies such as selling options can be negatively skewed, producing steady small gains for long periods but occasionally suffering large losses.

Skewness matters because averages and standard deviations alone do not capture it. Two investments with the same average return and volatility can have very different risk profiles if one is negatively skewed. Many investors are wary of negative skewness, since it means rare but painful losses. Stock market returns have often shown slight negative skewness, with sharp falls more common than equally sharp rises.

definition: A small-cap stock is a share in a company with a relatively small market capitalization compared with other listed companies.
explanation: Companies are often grouped by size, measured by market capitalization: share price multiplied by the number of shares. Small-cap companies sit at the lower end of this range. The exact boundaries vary between markets and index providers, and they change over time as markets grow.
Small-cap companies are often younger, more focused businesses with room to grow. Some become much larger over time, delivering strong returns to early investors.
For example, a small-cap company might be a specialist manufacturer or a regional retailer that is growing quickly but is still a fraction of the size of the industry's leaders.

Small-cap stocks tend to be more volatile than large-cap stocks. They may have less diversified businesses, less access to financing and more sensitivity to economic downturns. Their shares are often traded less frequently, which can make them harder to buy or sell without affecting the price.

Research suggests small-cap stocks have at times outperformed large-cap stocks over long periods, a pattern called the size premium, but the effect has been inconsistent. Many investors include small-cap funds as part of a diversified portfolio.

definition: Smart beta is an investment approach that tracks an index built using rules other than market capitalization, such as factors like value or low volatility, or equal weighting, typically through low-cost exchange-traded funds.
explanation: Traditional index funds weight each company by its market value, so the largest companies dominate. Smart beta funds use alternative rules to choose and weight holdings, aiming to improve returns, reduce risk or both.

Common smart beta approaches include equal weighting, where each company has the same weight; fundamental weighting, based on measures such as sales or dividends; and factor-based indices targeting value, momentum, quality, size or low volatility.
For example, an equal-weighted index of 500 large companies gives each company a 0.2% weight, increasing exposure to smaller companies compared with a standard market-weighted index.

Smart beta sits between passive and active investing. It follows transparent rules like an index fund, but deviates from the market like an active strategy. Fees are usually higher than for standard index funds but lower than for active funds. Like factor investing, smart beta strategies can underperform the broad market for long periods, and the name is a marketing term rather than a guarantee of smarter results.

definition: A smart contract is a computer program stored on a blockchain that automatically carries out the terms of an agreement when specified conditions are met.
explanation: Smart contracts work on an if-then basis. For example, if a payment is received, then a digital asset is transferred. Because they run on a blockchain, they are visible to participants and very difficult to alter once deployed, and they execute without needing a trusted intermediary.
The idea was described by computer scientist Nick Szabo in the 1990s and became practical with the launch of the Ethereum blockchain in 2015, which was designed to run such programs.
For example, an insurance smart contract could automatically pay farmers if official weather data show rainfall below a set level, without anyone having to file a claim.

Smart contracts underpin decentralized finance, non-fungible tokens and many other blockchain applications. Despite their name, they are not necessarily legal contracts. They are only as reliable as their code; errors or vulnerabilities can be exploited, and once deployed, faulty contracts can be hard to fix. They also depend on accurate external data, provided by services called oracles.

definition: Socially responsible investing is an investment approach that considers ethical, social or environmental values when choosing investments, often by excluding companies or industries that conflict with those values.
explanation: Socially responsible investing, often shortened to SRI, has its roots in religious and ethical investing, where investors avoided businesses such as alcohol, tobacco, gambling or weapons. Over time, it has broadened to include environmental issues, human rights, labour practices and governance.

The most common SRI method is negative screening, excluding certain sectors or companies. Other approaches include positive screening, choosing companies with strong practices, and shareholder engagement, using ownership to encourage change.
For example, an SRI fund might exclude companies that make weapons, produce tobacco or derive significant revenue from coal, while otherwise investing broadly.

SRI overlaps with ESG investing and impact investing. SRI focuses mainly on aligning investments with values; ESG investing considers environmental, social and governance factors partly as financial risks; and impact investing seeks measurable positive outcomes. Exclusions can make a portfolio less diversified, and their effect on returns has been widely debated, with research producing mixed results.

definition: SOFR, the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, is a benchmark interest rate in the United States based on the cost of overnight borrowing secured by US Treasury securities in the repurchase agreement market.
explanation: SOFR was chosen to replace US dollar LIBOR, which was based on banks' estimates of their borrowing costs and was vulnerable to manipulation. SOFR is based on actual transactions, measuring the cost of borrowing cash overnight using Treasury securities as collateral.
It is published each business day by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, based on a very large volume of daily transactions, which makes it robust and hard to manipulate.

SOFR is used as the reference rate for many loans, floating-rate bonds, derivatives such as interest rate swaps, and adjustable-rate mortgages. For example, a business loan might charge SOFR plus 2 percentage points.

Because SOFR is an overnight rate secured by collateral, it does not include the bank credit risk that LIBOR did, and it is backward-looking. Methods such as compounding SOFR over a period, or using term SOFR rates derived from futures markets, are used to set interest for longer periods. Other countries have similar benchmarks, such as SONIA in the United Kingdom and €STR in the euro area.

definition: A soft landing is when a central bank slows down an overheating economy enough to bring inflation under control, without causing a recession.
explanation: When inflation rises because demand is too strong, central banks raise interest rates to cool the economy. The challenge is to slow growth enough to reduce inflation without pushing the economy into a downturn with rising unemployment.
A soft landing is achieved when growth slows gradually, inflation returns towards its target and unemployment stays relatively low. It is often compared to a pilot bringing a plane down smoothly.

For example, the US economy in the mid-1990s is often cited as a soft landing: the Federal Reserve raised interest rates in 1994 and 1995, inflation stayed low and the economy continued to grow without a recession.

Soft landings are difficult because monetary policy works with long and uncertain delays, and policymakers must rely on imperfect data. Raising rates too much or too quickly can cause a hard landing, a recession. Raising them too little can leave inflation high. Whether a soft landing has occurred is often clear only in hindsight.

definition: Solvency is the ability of a person or business to meet all its long-term financial obligations, meaning its assets are worth more than its debts.
explanation: Solvency looks at the overall financial position. A solvent business has enough assets, over time, to cover everything it owes. An insolvent one owes more than it owns or cannot pay its debts as they become due.

Solvency is different from liquidity. Liquidity is about having cash available now; solvency is about the long-term balance between assets and debts. A company can be solvent but illiquid, owning valuable factories but lacking cash this month. It can also be liquid but heading towards insolvency, holding cash today while losing money and building up debts it will never be able to repay.

For example, a business with assets of 2 million and debts of 1.5 million is solvent, because its assets exceed its liabilities by 500,000. If losses shrink its assets to 1.2 million while debts stay at 1.5 million, it becomes insolvent.

Lenders, investors and regulators watch solvency closely. Banks and insurers must meet minimum solvency or capital requirements, and directors of a company that becomes insolvent often have special legal duties to protect creditors.

definition: A solvency ratio is a measure of an insurer's or company's ability to meet its long-term obligations, comparing its available capital or resources with its liabilities or capital requirements.
explanation: For insurers, the solvency ratio usually compares the capital they hold with the minimum capital regulators require. Under the European Union's Solvency II framework, and similar regimes, the key measure divides eligible own funds by the solvency capital requirement.

For example, an insurer with eligible own funds of 150,000,000 and a solvency capital requirement of 100,000,000 has a solvency ratio of 150%. A ratio above 100% means it meets the requirement; insurers typically aim for a comfortable buffer above this level.
The solvency capital requirement is calibrated so that an insurer meeting it should be able to absorb losses from a severe event that would occur, on average, only once in 200 years.

For non-financial companies, solvency ratios are used more loosely to describe measures of long-term financial health, such as comparing cash flow with total liabilities, or debt with equity. Different organisations define solvency ratios differently, so the specific calculation should always be checked.

definition: The Sortino ratio measures an investment's return above a target or risk-free rate for each unit of downside risk, counting only volatility from returns that fall below the target.
explanation: The Sharpe ratio uses total volatility, treating large gains and large losses as equally risky. Most investors, however, only worry about losses. The Sortino ratio, named after Frank Sortino, focuses on harmful volatility.
It is calculated by subtracting a target return, often the risk-free rate, from the investment's return and dividing by the downside deviation, a measure of how much returns fall below the target.
For example, a fund with an annual return of 10%, a target rate of 3% and a downside deviation of 8% has a Sortino ratio of about 0.88.

The Sortino ratio is especially useful for comparing investments with uneven return patterns, such as strategies that produce occasional large gains. Two funds with the same Sharpe ratio can have different Sortino ratios if one has more of its volatility on the upside. Like other ratios based on past returns, it depends on the period measured and may not predict future performance.

definition: Sources and uses is a summary table in a transaction, such as an acquisition or leveraged buyout, showing where the money to fund the deal comes from and how it will be spent.
explanation: The table has two sides that must always balance. Sources list the funding: new debt, equity from investors, cash on the target's or acquirer's balance sheet, and sometimes seller financing or rollover equity from existing owners. Uses list the payments: the purchase price for the equity, repayment of the target's existing debt, transaction fees and financing fees.

For example, a buyer acquiring a company might need 600,000,000 in total: 500,000,000 for the shares, 80,000,000 to repay the target's existing debt and 20,000,000 for fees. It might fund this with 350,000,000 of new debt and 250,000,000 of equity.

The sources and uses table is one of the first things built in a transaction model. It determines how much debt and equity are needed, which drives the analysis of returns, leverage and earnings per share.
It also provides a clear summary for lenders, investors and boards of how the deal will be financed.

definition: A sovereign default is when a national government fails to make interest or principal payments on its debt on time, or forces creditors to accept less favourable terms.
explanation: Governments can default for several reasons: large debts relative to their economy, a collapse in revenues, rising interest costs, inability to borrow new money, a currency crisis or political choices. Default may be outright, with payments stopped, or achieved through a restructuring that reduces what creditors receive.

Well-known examples include Argentina in 2001, Greece's debt restructuring in 2012, which imposed large losses on private bondholders, and Russia in 1998. Several countries have defaulted more than once.
For example, when a government defaults, holders of its bonds may see the value of their investments fall sharply, and the country may lose access to international borrowing for years.

Unlike companies, governments cannot be forced into bankruptcy and liquidated, so defaults are usually resolved through negotiation. Consequences can include higher future borrowing costs, banking crises, currency collapse and recession.
